The Legion is the era's most extreme product: a fictional world elaborated by editor and readers together over decades, and consequently the property most damaged by every subsequent continuity reboot.

Removing Superboy from continuity broke a team founded in-story by teenagers who had idolised him, and the contortions required to explain the Legion afterwards are the standard example of what a continuity reset costs.

Morrison took a cancelled team of damaged misfits and wrote Dadaist villains, a sentient street and a character who is sixty-four people at once — the run that established what DC's mature line could be before that line had a name.

Doom Patrol was among the titles folded into Vertigo at its 1993 launch, having already been publishing without the Comics Code seal. It is the imprint's clearest case of editorial freedom producing something no other publisher would have printed.

Berger edited Doom Patrol through the earlier part of Morrison's run and chose to bring it into Vertigo's launch line-up in 1993 alongside the titles she had built the imprint around, even though it had begun life as a conventional DC superhero book. Axel Alonso took the title over in 1994.

Introduced months before the X-Men and built on the same premise — outcasts with powers they experience as disfigurement, led by a scientist in a wheelchair — the resemblance has generated sixty years of inconclusive argument about who saw what first.

Kirby drew Fury first as a Second World War sergeant, in a war comic that let him return to the material he had drawn in the 1940s, and then in the present as a spymaster once Marvel wanted a Bond of its own.
Lee moved the character forward twenty years into S.H.I.E.L.D. in 1965, giving Marvel a spy franchise alongside the superheroes and a device for tying otherwise unconnected titles into one another.

The Ultimate line redrew Fury in 2001 in the likeness of Samuel L. Jackson, with the actor's agreement. Jackson then played the part on screen — an imprint's casting suggestion becoming the version of the character that a global audience knows.
Fury's appearance after the credits of Iron Man is the moment the shared continuity was announced, and he functions across the films as the connective device the comics had used him for since 1965.

Moore wrote it as a study of the Joker's claim that sanity is one bad day away from collapse, and gave him an origin the book itself refuses to confirm. He has since called it a minor work about which he had nothing much to say, and regretted the injury to Barbara Gordon in particular.

Bolland drew the book across roughly two years, from 1986, at a level of finish no monthly schedule could have accommodated, which is part of why it was published as a prestige one-shot. He recoloured the whole thing for the 2008 edition, replacing the original's saturated palette with something far more restrained.

Two of the British creators DC recruited in the mid-1980s, working together on a single book that outsold and outlasted most of what either did at the company. Both have since distanced themselves from it, for different reasons.

O'Neil is the credited editor, having taken the Batman line over from Len Wein while the book was in production. The editorial approval for shooting Barbara Gordon was given earlier, under Wein — Moore has said he asked and was told to proceed, though the wording usually attributed to that exchange is disputed. Bolland recalled O'Neil as almost entirely hands-off, with a single phone call between them about the book.

DC published it as a prestige-format one-shot at a premium price, the model The Dark Knight Returns had proved two years earlier, and it became one of the company's best-selling single volumes and has never been out of print.

A single expensive volume with no continuing series behind it only works where retailers order to a known readership. The Killing Joke is the clearest demonstration of the format the direct market made viable, and of how completely DC had moved away from the newsstand by 1988.

The book made the Joker's origin permanently unreliable — he remembers it several ways and prefers it that way — and that refusal has been treated as canonical ever since, in the comics and in every screen version that followed.

Barbara Gordon is shot and paralysed to give two men something to feel, and the book has been criticised on exactly those terms since. What DC did next is the more interesting half: Ostrander and Kim Yale refused to leave her as a plot device and rebuilt her as Oracle.

Conway, who had written for both companies, scripted the 1976 one-shot that brought their two flagship characters together for the first time. Getting the agreement signed took longer than producing the comic, and the result reads as carefully even-handed: neither hero is allowed to win.

The first meeting between the two companies' central characters was staged as a misunderstanding followed by an alliance, the template every inter-company crossover has used since — and a tacit admission that the rivalry was as much a shared market as a fight.

Marvel's most valuable character shared a cover with DC's for the first time in 1976, in a treasury-sized edition priced well above a normal comic. It sold strongly enough to make the format a recurring event for the following decade.

Giordano inked Ross Andru's pencils on the crossover, one of the rare occasions when creative staff worked openly across the line separating the two publishers rather than moving from one to the other.

Busiek built the crossover on the difference between the two universes rather than the similarity: a world where heroes are revered as gods meeting one where they are treated as public servants, each finding the other's arrangement obscene.

Pérez had drawn pages for an abandoned early-1980s attempt at the same crossover that collapsed in disagreement between the publishers, and waited twenty years to finish the job. The completed series is the fullest display of his ability to hold hundreds of characters in a single panel.

The League are written as figures the public treats with awe, which is what the Avengers find hardest to accept about them — the crossover's central observation about how the two companies imagine their heroes' place in the world.

The Avengers arrive as a working team with government paperwork and personal failures, and read the League's world as complacent. Busiek gives each side the argument its own publisher's history supports.

The 1996 crossover put the two companies' characters against each other directly, with five of the eleven fights settled by reader ballot, and then merged the universes into the Amalgam line for a month of one-shots.

For DC the crossover came at the top of the speculator market and was sold accordingly, in multiple covers and voting coupons. Its lasting interest is as evidence: two firms who had spent sixty years competing agreed that their properties were legible as a single shared vocabulary.

A company-versus-company crossover decided by mail-in vote, with an entire imprint of merged characters published in a single month, is the purest artefact of the period's belief that events sold themselves regardless of what happened in them.

The 1976 one-shot proved the two companies could co-publish at all; twenty years later the arrangement had become a line-wide crossover with a merged universe attached. What began as a novelty ended as a marketing format.

Kane, who had designed the Silver Age Green Lantern at DC, drew the Spider-Man issues that broke the Comics Code in 1971 and then the 1973 issue in which Gwen Stacy dies — two of the most consequential comics Marvel published in the period, drawn by one of DC's defining architects.

Kane pencilled the death sequence, including the panel with the sound effect at Gwen's neck that made the hero's responsibility ambiguous. The decision to leave it there has been attributed variously to Kane, Conway and the production process.

Pérez drew the first half of Marvel's 1991 crossover, six years after doing the same job for DC on Crisis on Infinite Earths. He is the only artist to have drawn both companies' universe-spanning events, and the visual language of massed heroes is his in each case.

Pérez drew the Avengers in the 1970s and returned for the 1998 relaunch with Busiek, a run generally regarded as the modern high point for the team — the same combination of dense cast and clear staging he had brought to the New Teen Titans at DC.

In 2001 DC gave Lee its own characters to reimagine from scratch in the Just Imagine series, pairing him with artists including John Buscema and Jim Lee. The company that had spent forty years as Marvel's rival hired the man most identified with it to redesign Superman and Batman.

Thomas left Marvel for DC in 1980 after years as its editor-in-chief and chief continuity keeper, and spent most of the decade there building All-Star Squadron and Infinity Inc. out of DC's own Golden Age — applying to another company's history the archival instinct he had developed at Marvel.

All-Star Squadron set Thomas's stories among DC's wartime heroes, treating the Justice Society's original run as a historical record to be filled in rather than superseded. It is the most thorough use any writer has made of the company's Golden Age.

Shooter sold his first Legion scripts to DC at thirteen, working from Pennsylvania by mail, and wrote the title for years before he was old enough to drive. The industry's most powerful editor of the 1980s began as a child freelancer for the rival company.

Conway moved between the two companies repeatedly through the 1970s, writing Justice League of America and co-creating Firestamp-era characters at DC while his Spider-Man work was still in print. He is the clearest case of a writer whose career simply ignored the rivalry.

Before Marvel Knights, Quesada drew Batman: Sword of Azrael at DC — the series that introduced the character who would replace Batman during Knightfall. Marvel's most consequential modern editor-in-chief came up through its competitor's flagship franchise.

O'Neil wrote Iron Man at Marvel in the early 1980s, running Tony Stark's alcoholism across an extended arc in which he loses the company and the armour. Having brought social realism to DC's heroes a decade earlier, he did the same for Marvel's most corporate one.

Starlin wrote A Death in the Family at DC in 1988, in which readers voted by telephone on whether the second Robin would survive and narrowly chose to kill him. Marvel's cosmic architect is also responsible for the single most notorious editorial stunt in DC's history.

In Cosmic Odyssey Starlin wrote Kirby's New Gods at DC, twelve years after building Thanos at Marvel on the same template. The line of influence runs Kirby to Darkseid to Thanos and then back to Darkseid in the hands of Thanos's creator.

Gaiman wrote 1602 and a revival of Kirby's Eternals for Marvel in the 2000s, long after Sandman had made him DC's most celebrated import. Both projects took the same approach he had used at DC: treat the company's back catalogue as folklore rather than continuity.

Before he became the writer most identified with DC's direction, Johns wrote The Avengers at Marvel in the early 2000s. Movement in that direction — DC's future architect learning on Marvel's flagship team — was routine by then and rarely remarked on.

Brubaker relaunched Catwoman at DC in 2001, moving her out of costumed crime into street-level noir, and wrote Gotham Central with Greg Rucka before taking the same crime-fiction sensibility to Captain America at Marvel.

Colan drew Batman and Detective Comics at DC in the 1980s after two decades at Marvel, bringing the same shadowed, fluid figure work he had used on Daredevil and Tomb of Dracula to a character it suited just as well.

Having run DC as publisher until 1976, Infantino spent much of the following decade drawing for Marvel — Star Wars, Nova, Spider-Woman — a reversal made stranger by the fact that he had personally recruited Kirby away from Marvel six years earlier.

Romita spent the late 1950s and early 1960s drawing romance comics at DC, and returned to Marvel in 1965 expecting more of the same. He was given Spider-Man instead, and became the artist who defined the character's commercial peak.

McFarlane broke in at DC on Infinity Inc. in the mid-1980s before moving to Marvel, where The Amazing Spider-Man made him the industry's biggest-selling artist — and from which he left again, four years later, to found Image.

Liefeld's first regular work was Hawk & Dove at DC in 1988. Two years later he was relaunching New Mutants at Marvel, and two years after that he was one of the seven founders who walked out to start Image.

After leaving the X-Men in 1991 Claremont wrote Sovereign Seven for DC, a creator-owned series set in the DC universe — an unusual arrangement at the time, and a reminder that the writer most identified with one company spent years working for the other.

Ross painted Kingdom Come and Superman: Peace on Earth at DC in the years after Marvels, applying the same method — photographic reference, oil paint, the world seen from ground level — to the characters of the rival company.

McDuffie worked as a Marvel editor and wrote Damage Control, a comedy about the contractors who clean up after superhero fights, before leaving to found Milestone. His argument about who gets to create characters was formed inside the company he left.

Goodwin edited Legends of the Dark Knight at DC in the 1990s, having earlier run Marvel's Epic line. He is one of very few editors whose reputation for talent-handling was equally strong at both companies.

Gerber and Kirby created Destroyer Duck together in 1982, publishing it independently to raise funds for Gerber's lawsuit against Marvel over Howard the Duck. Two creators from opposite ends of the company's history used a comic to finance an argument with it.

Wolfman and Pérez built The New Teen Titans as DC's answer to the X-Men, using the same formula of a large cast with continuing personal lives, and it became the only DC title of the era to compete with it directly. Both books were then drawn into the two companies' first joint publication in 1982.

Deadpool was created eleven years after Deathstroke and named Wade Wilson against Slade Wilson, an in-joke his co-creator has acknowledged. What began as a visual and nominal parody of a DC villain became one of Marvel's most valuable properties.

Wolfman conceived Deathstroke as a professional rather than a fanatic — a mercenary who takes the contract his son died attempting, and pursues it without personal animus, which made him harder for the Titans to answer than a conventional villain.
Pérez designed the two-tone mask and armour, one of the few costume designs of the period that has survived unaltered into film and television adaptations.

Deathstroke appeared in the second issue of the 1980 relaunch and became the series' defining antagonist, culminating in The Judas Contract, in which a Titan is revealed to have been his agent from the beginning.

Thomas devised Man-Thing with Gerry Conway and Gray Morrow for Savage Tales in 1971, two months before DC published Swamp Thing. Both drew on the 1940s Heap, and the creators involved were friends — Wein and Conway were sharing an apartment — which is why the resemblance is usually treated as common inheritance rather than theft.

Conway scripted the character's first appearance, and later wrote Spider-Man while his flatmate wrote Swamp Thing at the other company — a small illustration of how narrow the professional world producing both universes actually was.

Man-Thing reached print in May 1971 and Swamp Thing in July, and the two have been compared ever since. Neither was copied from the other: both descend from the same 1940s pulp figure, and both were made possible by the same relaxation of the Comics Code.

Wertham's campaign and the hearings that followed fell hardest on the horror and crime lines, and Goodman's Atlas was among the most exposed publishers in the business. The Code that resulted removed the genres his line depended on and contributed directly to its near-collapse.

Marvel's purchase of a distributor in 1995 forced every other publisher to pick a side, and DC signed an exclusive agreement with Diamond in response. The consolidation that followed left the direct market with a single distributor, which is the arrangement the whole industry has lived under since.

DC continued to work from full scripts while Marvel's artists were plotting from a conversation, and the difference eventually mattered a great deal: the ambiguity the Marvel Method created about who had authored what is the ground on which every subsequent credit dispute between Lee, Kirby and Ditko was fought.

Goodman's distribution arrangement in the late 1950s was with Independent News — owned by DC's proprietors — and it capped his output at eight titles a month. Marvel's rival controlled the size of its line for years before the 1961 relaunch made that arrangement untenable.

sg1.title: X-Men: A Map of Mutant Lore

professor_x.name: Professor X
professor_x.desc:
Charles Francis Xavier, created by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby in 1963, one of the world's most powerful telepaths and the founder of the X-Men. Raised at his family estate in Westchester County, New York, he turned the mansion into Xavier's School for Gifted Youngsters, a cover under which he trained young mutants to use their powers and to defend a world that feared them. He created Cerebro, a machine that amplifies his telepathy to detect mutant minds anywhere on Earth.

Xavier's guiding belief is that humans and mutants can coexist, a position defined against Magneto's conviction that they cannot. He is not a flawless figure: successive stories have dwelt on his secrets, his manipulations and his willingness to edit memories, and much of the franchise's later drama grows out of the gap between his stated ideals and his methods. Paralysed for most of his history, he acts most decisively on the astral plane, where his mind is unencumbered.

cyclops.name: Cyclops
cyclops.desc:
Created by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby (1963). Scott Summers, the first student Xavier recruited and the field leader of the X-Men for most of their history. He emits uncontrollable concussive force from his eyes — a head injury sustained as a child left him unable to shut the beams off — and must wear a ruby quartz visor to contain them, a permanent restraint that has always been read as part of his character: disciplined, tightly held, defined by the tactics he can control.

His life is bound to the Summers and Grey bloodlines that so many of the franchise's plots turn on. He is the son of Corsair, brother to Havok and Vulcan, the great love of Jean Grey, the husband of her clone Madelyne Pryor, and the father of Cable and (by another timeline) Rachel Summers. In later stories he moved from Xavier's most loyal pupil to a militant who broke with him entirely.

jean_grey.name: Jean Grey
jean_grey.desc:
Created by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby (1963). A founding X-Man, first called Marvel Girl, and one of the most powerful telepaths and telekinetics on Earth. Her telepathy woke at ten, when she linked minds with a friend struck by a car and felt the girl die, and Xavier sealed that ability away until she was old enough to bear it — a decision that echoes through everything that follows.

Her story is inseparable from the Phoenix Force. As Phoenix she saved the universe; as Dark Phoenix, manipulated and unleashed, she became a threat to it and died on the Moon. A later retcon established that the entity had placed the true Jean in a healing cocoon and taken her form, allowing her return in X-Factor. Death and resurrection have since become her narrative signature.

wolverine.name: Wolverine
wolverine.desc:
Created by Len Wein, John Romita Sr. and Herb Trimpe (1974). Logan, born James Howlett, a Canadian mutant with an accelerated healing factor, heightened senses, retractable bone claws and a lifespan stretching back to the nineteenth century. The Weapon X programme laced his skeleton with unbreakable adamantium and left his memories in fragments; recovering who he was has been the engine of his solo stories for decades.

He joined the X-Men with the all-new team of 1975 and became the franchise's most popular character: a berserker trying to be better than his instincts. His attachments are the softer half of him — a hopeless love for Jean Grey, an engagement to Mariko Yashida, and a run of young protegees including Kitty Pryde, Jubilee and Laura Kinney.

storm.name: Storm
storm.desc:
Created by Len Wein and Dave Cockrum (1975). Ororo Munroe, able to sense and command weather across a wide area. Born in Harlem to a Kenyan princess and an American photojournalist and raised in Cairo, she was orphaned at five when a plane came down on the family home during the Arab-Israeli conflict, and spent hours buried in the rubble beside her mother's body — the source of a claustrophobia she has never lost. She survived as a street thief under the master thief Achmed el-Gibar before travelling south to the Serengeti, where villagers took her ancestral gifts for divinity and worshipped her as a goddess. Xavier recruited her for the all-new X-Men in 1975.

She is the team's other great leader, and the counterweight to Cyclops: where he plans, she commands by presence. Notable turns include defeating Callisto in single combat to become nominal leader of the Morlocks, leading the X-Men for years while powerless after Forge's neutraliser struck her, and her later marriage to T'Challa of Wakanda.

beast.name: Beast
beast.desc:
Created by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby (1963). Henry Philip McCoy, a founding X-Man whose original mutation gave him great strength, agility and outsized hands and feet, together with a first-rank scientific mind. An experimental serum of his own devising covered him in blue fur, fixing the contrast the character trades on: an erudite, quoting, gently mannered biochemist in a monstrous body.

Beast has ranged further outside the X-Men than most of the original five, serving with the Avengers and the Defenders before returning to mutant affairs through X-Factor. He is repeatedly the franchise's scientist of record, working on the Legacy Virus and on the aftermath of M-Day, and repeatedly the man whose ethical shortcuts in the lab cause later trouble.

iceman.name: Iceman
iceman.desc:
Created by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby (1963). Robert Louis Drake, the second mutant Xavier recruited and the youngest of the founding X-Men, who can freeze ambient moisture, encase himself in ice and convert his body into organic ice entirely. Writers have long treated him as an Omega-level mutant working well below his ceiling, the joker of the original team who never quite took his own potential seriously.

He has spent almost his whole publication history attached to the school in one role or another, including a stint teaching. In 2015 the character was written as gay, first through his younger time-displaced self and then in the present day, and has since had solo series exploring that.

angel.name: Angel / Archangel
angel.desc:
Created by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby (1963). Warren Kenneth Worthington III, heir to a fortune and a founding X-Man, born with feathered wings and hollow bones. His wealth has bankrolled mutant causes more than once, and his early characterisation was that of the privileged, slightly aloof member of the original five.

During the Mutant Massacre his wings were maimed beyond saving, and Apocalypse took him at his lowest point, remaking him as Death, the fourth of the Horsemen, with blue skin and razor-edged metal wings. He broke free of Apocalypse's control but kept the transformation, and the tension between Warren and Archangel — between the man and the weapon made of him — became his defining conflict.

nightcrawler.name: Nightcrawler
nightcrawler.desc:
Created by Len Wein and Dave Cockrum (1975). Kurt Wagner, a German mutant who teleports in a bang of displaced air and brimstone, with indigo fur, a prehensile tail and an acrobat's training from years in a travelling circus. His demonic appearance made him an outcast long before he was a hero, and the gap between how he looks and how he behaves is the point of the character.

He is a devout Catholic and the closest thing the X-Men have to a moral centre, swashbuckling rather than brooding. His parentage has been rewritten twice: a 2003 story named the demonic mutant Azazel as his father, and a 2024 one revised that into a deception — Destiny bore him, and Mystique, shapeshifted into a male form built partly from Azazel's genetic code, was the other parent. Both women gave him up because Destiny had foreseen what keeping him would cost. With Captain Britain and Shadowcat he co-founded Excalibur, the team that carried the franchise's lighter, stranger register through the late 1980s.

colossus.name: Colossus
colossus.desc:
Created by Len Wein and Dave Cockrum (1975). Piotr Nikolaievitch Rasputin, a farm boy from a Siberian collective who can sheathe himself in organic steel, becoming enormously strong and nearly invulnerable. Recruited for the all-new X-Men in Giant-Size X-Men #1 in 1975, he is the team's gentle giant: a painter and a quiet man whose first instinct is to shield other people with his body.

His family supplies much of his grief — his elder brother Mikhail, a cosmonaut lost and returned changed, and above all his sister Illyana was taken to Limbo as a child and returned changed, and later died of the Legacy Virus. Colossus eventually gave his own life to distribute the cure for that virus. His long, halting relationship with Kitty Pryde, begun when both were teenagers, is one of the franchise's most durable romances.

rogue.name: Rogue
rogue.desc:
Created by Chris Claremont and Michael Golden (1981). Anna Marie, whose skin absorbs the memories, personality and powers of anyone she touches, and who therefore cannot touch anyone safely. Her power surfaced on a boy she kissed as a teenager in Caldecott County, Mississippi, and left him comatose. Raised by Mystique and Destiny after running away from home, she began as a Brotherhood member and attacked the X-Men before seeking Xavier's help.

An early, permanent absorption of Carol Danvers left her with superhuman strength, durability and flight, and with another woman's psyche lodged in her head. Her long romance with Gambit is built entirely on the thing she cannot do, and her arc from villain to stalwart X-Man and eventual team leader is one of the clearest redemption tracks in the books.

gambit.name: Gambit
gambit.desc:
Created by Chris Claremont and Jim Lee (1990). Remy LeBeau, abandoned at birth for his black-and-red eyes, stolen from the hospital by the New Orleans Thieves Guild — who called him le diable blanc and thought him the child of a prophecy — and raised among them, able to charge objects with kinetic energy so that they explode — most often a deck of playing cards. Charm, a bo staff and a reflexive dishonesty make him the X-Men's rogue element, never entirely trusted by his own side.

His buried secret begins with a debt: his own kinetic power was building past his control and killing him, and Sinister operated on his brain to cap it. The price was assembling the Marauders, and he did not know what they were being gathered to do; his role in the Mutant Massacre came out years later and nearly ended him with the team. His relationship with Rogue, defined by the impossibility of contact, runs through decades of stories.

shadowcat.name: Shadowcat
shadowcat.desc:
Created by Chris Claremont and John Byrne (1980). Katherine Pryde, who phases through solid matter by making herself and anything she carries intangible, disrupting electronics as she passes. Recruited at thirteen, she was the reader's way into the team: a bright Chicago teenager, gifted with computers, dropped into a house of soldiers and aliens.

Her credits include befriending a small alien dragon, Lockheed, co-founding Excalibur, and hosting the consciousness sent back from the ruined future of Days of Future Past — a story so associated with her that the adult version is simply called Kate. She has since led the X-Men and captained Krakoa's smugglers, and her romance with Colossus began when she was the youngest person in the room.

jubilee.name: Jubilee
jubilee.desc:
Created by Chris Claremont and Marc Silvestri (1989). Jubilation Lee, a Los Angeles mall rat orphaned when her parents were killed, whose mutation generates explosive plasma bursts she calls fireworks. She stowed away with the X-Men after watching them use a mall teleport gate, and attached herself to Wolverine, becoming the sidekick who softened him during the early 1990s.

She was later a founding student of Generation X under Banshee and Emma Frost. After M-Day stripped her powers she kept working as a hero without them, and a subsequent storyline turned her into a vampire, a state she carried for several years before her mutant abilities were restored. She later adopted a son, Shogo, moving from sidekick to parent in a way few of her contemporaries have been given.

psylocke.name: Psylocke
psylocke.desc:
Created by Chris Claremont and Herb Trimpe (1976). Elizabeth Braddock, a British telepath and the twin sister of Brian Braddock, Captain Britain. A former model and pilot, she came to the X-Men by way of Mojo's dimension, where she was blinded and given cybernetic eyes, and quickly became one of the team's sharpest close-quarters fighters.

Her best-known period followed a body swap engineered by the Hand with the assassin Kwannon, after which Betsy's mind occupied a Japanese body trained in ninjutsu and she manifested a telepathic blade. Kwannon, in Betsy's body and believing herself to be Betsy, joined the X-Men as Revanche and died of the Legacy Virus. Decades later the two were separated and restored to their own bodies, Kwannon taking the Psylocke name and Betsy the mantle of Captain Britain.

bishop.name: Bishop
bishop.desc:
Lucas Bishop, a mutant from a future in which mutants are herded into camps and branded, able to absorb energy directed at him and release it as concussive force. He served in the Xavier Security Enforcers before following a fugitive back through time and finding himself among the X-Men he had only known as legend.

He arrived carrying a warning that a traitor within the team would destroy everything, a thread that ran for years. Later stories pushed him much darker: convinced that the first mutant child born after M-Day would cause his future, he hunted Hope Summers and Cable across time, becoming an enemy of the people he had served.

banshee.name: Banshee
banshee.desc:
Created by Roy Thomas and Werner Roth (1967). Sean Cassidy, an Irish mutant whose sonic scream can shatter stone, carry him in flight and stun a crowd, and a former Interpol officer. He first appeared as an unwilling agent of Factor Three before joining the all-new X-Men in 1975 as one of its older, steadier members.

Damage to his throat repeatedly cost him his powers, and he shifted from field work to teaching, running the Massachusetts Academy alongside Emma Frost as headmaster of Generation X. His long relationship with Moira MacTaggert links him to Muir Island, and his daughter Theresa became the mutant Siryn.

sunfire.name: Sunfire
sunfire.desc:
Shiro Yoshida, a Japanese mutant who absorbs solar radiation and converts it to superheated plasma, allowing flight and intense heat blasts. The son of a Japanese diplomat and a mother who died of radiation sickness from the bombing of Hiroshima, he debuted as an antagonist driven by that grievance, before being recruited for the mission to Krakoa that assembled the all-new X-Men.

He quit almost immediately, making him the shortest-serving member of that famous line-up, and has since drifted in and out of mutant affairs as a proud, prickly ally rather than a teammate. He is a cousin of Mariko Yashida of Clan Yashida, and after Lady Deathstrike took his legs he served a period as Apocalypse's Horseman Famine.

thunderbird.name: Thunderbird
thunderbird.desc:
Created by Len Wein and Dave Cockrum (1975). John Proudstar, an Apache mutant of superhuman strength, speed and endurance, and a former Marine, recruited into the all-new X-Men in 1975. He was written as angry and unconvinced, joining chiefly because Xavier told him he was needed and needling the team from the moment he arrived.

He died on his second mission, refusing to let a fleeing aircraft escape and going down with it — an early, unusually blunt demonstration that the new X-Men were not safe. His death gave the franchise one of its longest-running grief threads through his younger brother James, who became Warpath.

havok.name: Havok
havok.desc:
Alexander Summers, Cyclops's younger brother, who absorbs ambient cosmic radiation and discharges it as waves of plasma. Because the energy vents from his whole body rather than a controlled beam, he needs a containment suit, and his powers and his brother's interact badly — a neat physical figure for their relationship.

Separated from Scott in childhood and raised apart, he has spent his career oscillating between the X-Men, leadership of X-Factor, and stretches in space with the Starjammers. He is the long-term partner of Polaris, and his repeated refusal to simply be his brother's lieutenant is his most consistent trait.

polaris.name: Polaris
polaris.desc:
Lorna Dane, a mutant with magnetic powers close in kind to Magneto's, which is precisely the problem: her parentage was dangled, denied and confirmed across decades before being settled with Magneto as her father. Green-haired and formidable, she joined the X-Men young and has been a fixture of the wider mutant teams ever since.

Her story is heavy with possession and manipulation — by Mesmero, by Malice of the Marauders, by Apocalypse — which has made her mental health a recurring subject in her later solo appearances. Her relationship with Havok is one of the franchise's longest-running couples.

forge.name: Forge
forge.desc:
A Cheyenne mutant whose power is intuitive invention: he grasps how any mechanism works and can build almost any device, which makes him the X-Men's armourer and the man who keeps the Blackbird and the Danger Room running. He is also trained in shamanic practice, a second discipline that has drawn him into mystical conflicts.

A Vietnam veteran, he built the mutant power neutraliser for the American government, and it was his weapon that stripped Storm of her abilities when it was fired at her — an act that poisoned the beginning of their relationship and then, in the way of these books, became the reason they understood each other.

rachel_summers.name: Rachel Summers
rachel_summers.desc:
The daughter of Scott Summers and Jean Grey in the timeline of Days of Future Past, where mutants were interned and she was made a Hound, psychically conditioned to track her own kind. She escaped into the present, carrying the marks of that conditioning and an inheritance of the Phoenix Force.

In the main timeline she is a woman whose parents are not her parents, which the books have used for some of their most affecting material. She fought alongside the X-Men, spent years in space with Excalibur and the Starjammers, and has gone by Phoenix, Marvel Girl and Prestige.

dazzler.name: Dazzler
dazzler.desc:
Alison Blaire, a mutant who converts sound into light, from a soft glow to blinding strobes and cutting lasers. Conceived at the end of the 1970s as a disco singer, she began in her own long-running title as a performer trying to keep a career while being outed as a mutant.

She joined the X-Men during their Australian period and has since moved between costumed work, government service and the stage. Her double life gives the franchise one of its few sustained looks at what public celebrity does to a mutant, and her powers make her unusually effective against opponents who rely on sight.

x_23.name: X-23
x_23.desc:
Laura Kinney, created by the Facility from a damaged sample of Wolverine's genome, raised as a weapon and trained to kill from childhood. She has his healing factor and heightened senses, with two claws in each hand and one in each foot, and was conditioned with a trigger scent that sent her into a killing rage.

Escaping her handlers, she came to the X-Men as a damaged teenager and was gradually rebuilt by them, particularly by Wolverine himself, who recognised the childhood he had been spared the memory of. After his death she took the Wolverine name and costume, and later resumed her own.

legion.name: Legion
legion.desc:
David Haller, the son of Charles Xavier and the Israeli diplomat Gabrielle Haller, and one of the most powerful and least stable mutants alive, by most accounts. His mind fractured after a terrorist attack he witnessed as a child, and each personality within him commands a different ability — telepathy, telekinesis, pyrokinesis and far stranger powers.

He was found at Muir Island and treated by Moira MacTaggert. His most consequential act was a journey into the past intending to kill Magneto before the Brotherhood existed: Xavier was killed shielding him, erasing the X-Men from history and creating the Age of Apocalypse.

emma_frost.name: Emma Frost
emma_frost.desc:
Created by Chris Claremont and John Byrne (1980). A telepath of the first rank who can also shift into a form of organic diamond, immune to psychic attack. She rose through the Hellfire Club as its White Queen, ran the Massachusetts Academy as a rival school to Xavier's, and trained the Hellions as a counterweight to the New Mutants.

The murder of her students broke her allegiance to the Club and pushed her, by degrees, into teaching for the other side: Generation X with Banshee, then the X-Men themselves, where she became headmistress and Cyclops's partner. She never softened, and the franchise uses her as its coldest strategist, capable of things the X-Men prefer not to do themselves.

cable.name: Cable
cable.desc:
Created by Louise Simonson and Rob Liefeld (1990). Nathan Christopher Summers, the son of Cyclops and Madelyne Pryor, infected as an infant with a techno-organic virus by Apocalypse and sent two thousand years into the future to be saved. He was raised there by the Askani, grew old fighting Apocalypse's empire, and came back as a grizzled soldier with vast telekinetic and telepathic power spent mostly holding the virus at bay.

He took over the New Mutants and remade them as X-Force, a team willing to shoot first. Later he vanished into the timestream to raise Hope Summers, the first mutant born after M-Day, becoming a father in a way his own father never got to be with him.

cannonball.name: Cannonball
cannonball.desc:
Samuel Zachery Guthrie, a Kentucky coal miner's son who propels himself through the air at high speed inside a nearly invulnerable blast field. The eldest of a large family, he gave up a college place at sixteen and went down the mine after his father died, to keep them fed; his power surfaced in a cave-in, saving himself and the man trapped with him.

Donald Pierce saw the cave-in on the news and hired him as a bodyguard, so Sam's first appearance is on the wrong side, fighting the four teenagers he was about to spend his life with; he refused Pierce's order to kill them and helped them escape instead, and Xavier kept the five of them together as a result. He stayed on when Cable turned the team into X-Force, and grew into its field leader — one of the few characters in the books allowed to age steadily from student to seasoned professional. A storyline proposed that he was an External, an immortal mutant, though later writing set this aside.

sunspot.name: Sunspot
sunspot.desc:
Roberto da Costa, a Brazilian mutant who stores solar energy and converts it into raw strength, his body going jet black as he powers up. His mutation surfaced at a football match when racists attacked him, an origin the books have kept in view.

Heir to a vast fortune, he moved from hot-headed New Mutant to X-Force member to businessman, at one point buying the terrorist organisation A.I.M. outright and repurposing it, and later commanding the Avengers Unity Squad. His friendship with Cannonball, formed on their first day at the school, is the longest and steadiest relationship either character has.

wolfsbane.name: Wolfsbane
wolfsbane.desc:
Rahne Sinclair, a Scottish mutant who can shift between human form, a full wolf and an intermediate transitional state, gaining a wolf's senses and speed. Raised by a harsh minister who took her transformation for damnation, she was rescued and fostered by Moira MacTaggert on Muir Island.

Her faith and her animal nature pull against each other in almost every story she appears in, and her time with the New Mutants, X-Factor and X-Force is punctuated by periods when the wolf has the upper hand. Her devotion to Moira and her bond with Cypher are the closest things she has to a settled family.

magik.name: Magik
magik.desc:
Illyana Nikolievna Rasputina, Colossus's younger sister, a mutant teleporter who steps through portals of light. Abducted at six by the demon Belasco, she spent seven years in Limbo while seconds passed on Earth, and came back thirteen years old carrying sorcerous training, a piece of demonic corruption where part of her soul had been mined away for bloodstones, and a Soulsword she had drawn out of her own life force.

She joined the New Mutants as their most dangerous member, ruled Limbo, and was eventually returned to childhood, dying young of the Legacy Virus. Later stories restored her as an adult, and she has since been a mainstay of the X-Men — part sorceress, part sardonic soldier.

mirage.name: Mirage
mirage.desc:
Danielle Moonstar, a Cheyenne mutant who pulls images from the minds of others and makes them visible, usually a person's greatest fear or dearest wish — a power that reads people before it hurts them. A Cheyenne girl raised in Colorado by her grandfather Black Eagle after her parents vanished, and unable at first to control what her power showed people, she was among the first students Xavier gathered for the New Mutants.

Her bond with the Asgardian valkyries during a New Mutants adventure led to her being named a Valkyrie in her own right, giving her the ability to perceive approaching death. She led the New Mutants in the field, later taught at the school, and lost her mutant powers on M-Day before regaining them.

karma.name: Karma
karma.desc:
Xi'an Coy Manh, a Vietnamese mutant who can possess another person's body and act through it, one of the most invasive powers in the books and one she uses with great reluctance. She fled Vietnam by boat with her younger twin siblings and was supporting them alone in New York when Xavier found her — and her family's other legacy, an uncle who ran a Madripoor crime operation, kept reaching for her long afterwards.

A founding New Mutant and the team's first leader, she was possessed for years by the Shadow King, who used her body and left her physically and mentally wrecked. She is among Marvel's earliest openly lesbian characters, though the books only stated it explicitly decades after her debut, and she later returned to the school as a teacher.

cypher.name: Cypher
cypher.desc:
Douglas Ramsey, a mutant whose brain instantly decodes any language — spoken, written, machine, gestural, even the syntax of a fighting style. In a team of energy blasts and steel skin his ability looked like nothing at all, and the books have spent forty years arguing that it is one of the most powerful mutations they have.

A close friend of Kitty Pryde, he formed an unlikely partnership with the alien Warlock. He was shot dead by the Ani-Mator during Fall of the Mutants, diving in front of a bullet meant for Wolfsbane — one of the earliest permanent-feeling deaths in the franchise, and his eventual resurrection returned him fused with Warlock's technarch matter.

warlock.name: Warlock
warlock.desc:
A member of the Technarchy, a race of living machines that infect and consume worlds, who fled his own father, the Magus, rather than fight him to the death as his species demands. He is a shifting mass of circuitry and eyes, able to remake his body into any shape and to infect organic matter with the transmode virus.

His broken, cheerful English and total ignorance of human custom made him the New Mutants' comic register, and his friendship with Doug Ramsey — the boy who could actually understand him — is the emotional heart of that run. The virus he carries is the same one Apocalypse used on the infant Cable.

domino.name: Domino
domino.desc:
Neena Thurman, a mutant mercenary whose subconscious power bends probability in her favour: bullets miss, ropes fray at the useful moment, and the improbable shot lands. The effect is invisible, which suits a character whose competence is meant to look like skill and luck rather than a superpower.

She is the product of Project: Armageddon, a government breeding programme that used a precognitive mutant as a surrogate to grow a perfect weapon. Of the children it produced she was effectively the only one to survive, and her power was written off as a failure to specification; her own mother eventually broke her out and left her, catatonic, with a priest in Chicago. She came out of that as a soldier for hire, ran with Cable's Six Pack, and later served as his second in X-Force and, for a long stretch, his partner. She is the professional in a team of former students, and treats the job accordingly. For X-Force's first year she was not present at all — the shapeshifter Copycat had taken her place on the team while the real Domino was held prisoner by the arms dealer Tolliver, and nobody noticed. The character's own first appearance is somebody else wearing her.

warpath.name: Warpath
warpath.desc:
James Proudstar, the younger brother of Thunderbird, with the same superhuman strength and speed developed to a greater degree, along with heightened senses and, later, flight. He grew up on the Apache reservation his brother left, and blamed Xavier for the death.

He first appeared in Emma Frost's Hellions intending to kill Xavier, could not go through with it, and eventually joined the New Mutants and X-Force instead. Grief and the shadow of a brother he barely knew have driven him ever since, alongside a long partnership with Warlock and the vibranium knives he carries.

deadpool.name: Deadpool
deadpool.desc:
Created by Rob Liefeld and Fabian Nicieza (1991). Wade Wilson, a mercenary given a regenerative healing factor derived from Wolverine's by the Weapon X programme, which arrested a terminal illness while leaving him permanently scarred and mentally unstable. He is loud, indestructible and aware that he is in a comic, and he talks to the reader accordingly.

Created as a straight villain opposite the New Mutants and X-Force, he became a comedy star and then a genuine, if unreliable, member of mutant teams. His relationship with Cable — an odd-couple partnership that carried its own long-running title — is the closest he has to a stable friendship.

hope_summers.name: Hope Summers
hope_summers.desc:
The first mutant born after M-Day, in a small Alaskan town, arriving at a moment when no new mutants had manifested for years. Both sides read her as a messiah or an apocalypse, and the fight over the infant became the Messiah Complex crossover.

Cable carried her into the future and raised her on the run, hunted by Bishop, who believed she would cause the ruin of his own time. She can mimic the powers of mutants near her, and her return to the present triggered the reactivation of the mutant gene and the appearance of a new generation, ending the extinction the X-Men had lived under.

magneto.name: Magneto
magneto.desc:
Created by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby (1963). Max Eisenhardt, who took the name Erik Lehnsherr, master of magnetism and, by common account, the most consequential antagonist in the franchise. A Jewish survivor of Auschwitz who lost his family in the Holocaust, he emerged convinced that the only protection for a hated minority is power held in its own hands, and that mutants must never again be at the mercy of anyone's tolerance.

He founded the Brotherhood of Evil Mutants, ruled the island nation of Genosha, and has by turns been the X-Men's deadliest enemy, their reluctant ally, and briefly the headmaster of Xavier's school. His long friendship and argument with Charles Xavier is the axis the whole mythology turns on: two survivors who agree on the danger and not on the answer.

mystique.name: Mystique
mystique.desc:
Created by Chris Claremont and Dave Cockrum (1978). Raven Darkhölme, a shapeshifter who can take the exact appearance and voice of any person, and who ages very slowly. She has spent decades inside human governments and mutant terror cells alike, and her loyalties change with whatever will keep her and her own alive.

She led her own Brotherhood of Evil Mutants and later remade it as the government-sanctioned Freedom Force. Her family ties bind her to both sides of the mutant question: she is a parent of Nightcrawler, the mother of the human anti-mutant demagogue Graydon Creed, and the foster mother of Rogue. Her decades-long partnership with the precognitive Destiny is the one attachment she never trades away.

sabretooth.name: Sabretooth
sabretooth.desc:
Created by Chris Claremont and John Byrne (1977). Victor Creed, a mutant with a healing factor, claws, fangs and animal senses closely comparable to Wolverine's, and none of the restraint. He is a killer who enjoys it, and the books have used him as the answer to what Logan would be without the effort of conscience.

The two men's history reaches back more than a century and through the Weapon X programme, though the exact nature of it — rival, tormentor, one-time comrade — has been rewritten more than once. He served in the Marauders during the Mutant Massacre, ran with Magneto's followers, and fathered Graydon Creed with Mystique.

toad.name: Toad
toad.desc:
Mortimer Toynbee, a mutant with prodigious leaping strength, a long prehensile tongue and an adhesive grip. A member of Magneto's original Brotherhood, he was written for years as a cringing servant, bullied by the man he worshipped and treated as comic relief by everyone else.

Later writers gave him more: stretches of independence, a brief spell in charge of his own team, and long periods working as a janitor at Xavier's school, where his resentment and his loyalty sat uncomfortably together. He is the franchise's clearest study of what it costs to be the least impressive mutant in the room.

quicksilver.name: Quicksilver
quicksilver.desc:
Pietro Maximoff, who moves and thinks at superhuman speed, and whose impatience with a world running slowly is written as arrogance by nearly everyone he meets. He and his sister Wanda served in Magneto's first Brotherhood before defecting to the Avengers, one of the earliest villain-to-hero moves in Marvel's history.

For decades he was presented as Magneto's son, a relationship that gave both characters some of their best material and was revised by a later storyline that named other parents. He has served with the Avengers, the government X-Factor and the Inhumans, and was central to House of M, having pushed his sister towards the reality she rewrote.

scarlet_witch.name: Scarlet Witch
scarlet_witch.desc:
Wanda Maximoff, whose hex power warps probability and, in later writing, edges into outright reality alteration and chaos magic. Like her brother she began in Magneto's Brotherhood and left it for the Avengers, where she spent most of her publication history.

Her breakdown after the loss of her children destabilised her powers and led to the House of M, in which she remade the world and then unmade most of mutantkind with three words, cutting the global mutant population to a few hundred. That single act reshaped the X-Men books for the following decade, and made her one of the most consequential figures in modern mutant history despite never being an X-Man.

juggernaut.name: Juggernaut
juggernaut.desc:
Cain Marko, Charles Xavier's stepbrother, who is not a mutant at all: his strength and unstoppable momentum come from the Crimson Gem of Cyttorak, found in a hidden temple during the Korean War, where Xavier — who had followed him off the battlefield — read the warning carved on the walls and told him to leave it alone. Cain picked it up anyway, and the temple came down on him; it took him years to dig himself out. Once he is moving in a straight line, nothing on Earth reliably stops him.

He came out of that temple a living battering ram with an old grudge against the stepbrother he had bullied as a boy — a boy favoured by the father who abused him — and Xavier's school has been demolished around him more than once. Later stories moved him towards uneasy reform, including a period training with the X-Men, without ever quite letting him become good.

blob.name: Blob
blob.desc:
Frederick J. Dukes, a mutant of enormous mass who can make himself immovable by anchoring to the ground, with skin and fat dense enough to shrug off bullets. He was working as a carnival strongman when Xavier tried to recruit him, refused, and led the sideshow in an attack on the school instead.

He became a fixture of Magneto's Brotherhood and later of Mystique's Freedom Force, and is one of the very few X-Men villains present from the earliest issues to the present. The books have returned repeatedly to the humiliation underneath the bulk — a man defined by a body that is both his power and the reason he is mocked.

pyro.name: Pyro
pyro.desc:
St. John Allerdyce, an Australian mutant who cannot create fire but can control any flame absolutely, shaping it into creatures and walls; he carries flamethrowers to give himself something to work with. He was also, incongruously, a published novelist of trashy gothic fiction.

He served in Mystique's Brotherhood and in Freedom Force, where his partnership with Avalanche made a double act of the two most reliable soldiers on the roster. He contracted the Legacy Virus and died of it, spending his last act saving Senator Kelly, a man whose politics he had fought for years.

avalanche.name: Avalanche
avalanche.desc:
Dominikos Petrakis, given in earlier stories as Dominic Petros, a Greek mutant who generates powerful vibratory waves from his hands, shattering stone and bringing down buildings. He came to the Brotherhood as a hired professional rather than a believer, and that mercenary streak has kept him more grounded than most of his colleagues.

With Mystique's Brotherhood and then Freedom Force he worked as government muscle, serving sentences in exchange for field work — a strange, revealing period in which the franchise's terrorists became federal agents. His partnership with Pyro was the constant across all of it.

destiny.name: Destiny
destiny.desc:
Irene Adler, a blind precognitive who saw the branching futures of mutantkind and recorded what she found in thirteen volumes of diaries that half the world's powers have since hunted. Her sight is unusual in the books for being reliable and for costing her the present: she experiences what is coming more vividly than what is.

She served in Mystique's Brotherhood and Freedom Force, and her decades-long relationship with Mystique — for many years written obliquely and later made explicit — is the emotional anchor of both characters. Her diaries repeatedly drive plots long after her death, including the founding of Krakoa.

omega_red.name: Omega Red
omega_red.desc:
Arkady Rossovich, a Soviet mutant who exudes a lethal pheromone known as the death spore and must drain the life energy of others to survive. Soviet scientists laced him with carbonadium tentacles, a cheaper answer to the adamantium of the Weapon X programme, and the metal is also what slowly poisons him.

He was placed in suspended animation when he became uncontrollable, and revived in the 1990s as a recurring threat to Wolverine, Sabretooth and Maverick, all of whom had a hand in his original containment. He is the franchise's Cold War echo: a weapon built by the other side and abandoned when it worked too well.

exodus.name: Exodus
exodus.desc:
Bennet du Paris, a Crusader-era knight awakened in the modern day as an immensely powerful telepath, telekinetic and energy manipulator. Found and freed by Magneto, he took him for a prophet and became the most devout of his followers.

As leader of the Acolytes he pursued a religious version of Magneto's politics, more absolute than the man himself, and the books use him to show what happens when a survivor's argument becomes a faith held by people who did not survive anything. He later worked as a teacher of mutant children, which he regarded as the same mission by other means.

sebastian_shaw.name: Sebastian Shaw
sebastian_shaw.desc:
Black King of the Hellfire Club's Inner Circle and an industrialist whose fortune rests on military contracts. His mutation absorbs kinetic energy — every blow landed on him makes him stronger and younger — which makes him nearly impossible to fight conventionally.

His company held the government contract to build a new generation of Sentinels, a piece of double-dealing that captures him exactly: a mutant profiting from the machinery of mutant extermination. He was the driving force behind the Club's attempt to control the X-Men through Jean Grey, and remains one of the franchise's few purely acquisitive villains.

selene.name: Selene
selene.desc:
Selene Gallio, the Black Queen, a mutant of enormous age who drains the life force of others to sustain herself and has ruled and been worshipped in more than one vanished civilisation, claiming a history reaching back to the Bronze Age. She combines psychic vampirism with sorcery and telekinesis, and regards the Hellfire Club as a convenient modern instrument.

Among the X-Men's antagonists she is the most nakedly predatory, treating mutants and humans alike as food and worshippers. Her ambitions have run from possessing the New Mutants' Magma to the Necrosha storyline, in which she raised an army of resurrected mutant dead from the ruins of Genosha in an attempt at godhood.

donald_pierce.name: Donald Pierce
donald_pierce.desc:
White Bishop of the Hellfire Club and, unusually for its Inner Circle, a human with a violent hatred of mutants — a cyborg whose replaced limbs give him great strength and durability. His position inside a Club run largely by mutants made him a saboteur from the start.

Expelled after his plot against his own colleagues was exposed, he founded the Reavers, a band of cyborg mercenaries who tortured Wolverine and hunted the X-Men through their Australian period. He is the franchise's clearest statement that anti-mutant hatred is a business as much as a belief.

harry_leland.name: Harry Leland
harry_leland.desc:
Black Bishop of the Hellfire Club's Inner Circle, a corporate lawyer whose mutation increases the mass of anything he focuses on, driving opponents to their knees or through the floor without ever touching them. He was the most outwardly civil of the Club's enforcers, a heavy man who fought by making other people heavy.

He took part in the Club's capture of the X-Men and the campaign to turn Jean Grey into their Black Queen. He died during Sebastian Shaw's confrontation with Nimrod, using his power to hold the Sentinel down at the cost of his own failing heart.

mastermind.name: Mastermind
mastermind.desc:
Jason Wyngarde, an illusionist who can make any number of people see, hear and feel whatever he chooses, though he can do nothing physically. A member of Magneto's original Brotherhood, he spent his career being underestimated by stronger mutants.

His one great success was also the franchise's most catastrophic: seeking membership of the Hellfire Club's Inner Circle, he spent months feeding Jean Grey an elaborate illusory past life that seduced her into becoming their Black Queen, weakening the restraints on the Phoenix Force. The Dark Phoenix that resulted destroyed him mentally when it turned on him.

apocalypse.name: Apocalypse
apocalypse.desc:
Created by Louise Simonson and Jackson Guice (1986). En Sabah Nur, born some five thousand years ago in the Egyptian settlement of Akkaba and generally presented as the first mutant. Abandoned as an infant for his grey skin and blue markings, he was taken in by Baal of the Sandstormers, a band of desert raiders who named him — the name means The First One — and taught him that only the strong deserve to live. He can reshape his body at will, and technology salvaged from an alien Celestial ship has kept him alive for millennia.

He passes centuries in stasis and wakes when the world seems ready for culling.

His creed is that only the strong deserve to survive, and he engineers catastrophes to test who does. He recruits four Horsemen from broken people at their lowest — War, Famine, Pestilence and Death — remaking them with Celestial technology. Warren Worthington and Wolverine have both worn his brand, and his intervention in the infant Cable's life set that character's entire history running.

mister_sinister.name: Mister Sinister
mister_sinister.desc:
Created by Chris Claremont and Marc Silvestri (1987). Nathaniel Essex, a Victorian biologist driven by the death of his sickly son into an obsession with Darwin's new theory, and whose own conclusions about human mutation were rejected as monstrous by the Royal Society. Apocalypse found him, altered him, and made him effectively immortal, with shapeshifting, telepathy and vast regenerative power — and with a permanent obligation to a master he privately intends to outlive.

His obsession is genetics, and specifically the Summers and Grey bloodlines, whose combination he believes will produce a mutant capable of destroying Apocalypse. To that end he cloned Jean Grey as Madelyne Pryor and manoeuvred her into marrying Cyclops. He assembled the Marauders and ordered the Mutant Massacre, and he is the coldest intelligence the X-Men face: everything he does is an experiment.

stryfe.name: Stryfe
stryfe.desc:
A clone of the infant Nathan Summers, created by Apocalypse as a healthy replacement for the child the techno-organic virus was consuming, and raised in the far future in Cable's place. He has the same enormous telepathic and telekinetic power without the disease that suppresses Cable's, and a consuming grievance about which of them was the copy.

He led the Mutant Liberation Front and engineered the X-Cutioner's Song: wearing Cable's face, he shot Charles Xavier in front of a global audience at a peace concert, with a bullet carrying the same techno-organic virus that had been eating him and Cable since infancy. The X-Men hunted Cable for it, and the teams tore at each other for twelve issues before the impersonation came out. Apocalypse, of all people, supplied the cure. His most lasting act was quieter. He traded Mister Sinister a sealed canister, claiming it held two thousand years of Summers genetic material — the one thing Sinister cannot refuse. Sinister had it opened after Stryfe was believed dead, found it apparently empty, and released the Legacy Virus into the air. It killed mutants for the better part of a decade.

bolivar_trask.name: Bolivar Trask
bolivar_trask.desc:
An anthropologist and engineer who concluded that mutants would inevitably supplant humanity and built the Sentinels to prevent it — among the most destructive acts of anti-mutant politics in the franchise, carried out by a man who believed he was saving his species.

His machines reasoned from their own directive that the surest protection for humanity was to rule it, and turned on him. He died destroying the Master Mold he had built, an act of conscience that came far too late; the Sentinel programme long outlived him, passing through his children Larry and Tanya, the American government and the corporation that still bears the family name.

sentinels.name: Sentinels
sentinels.desc:
Created by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby (1965). Giant purple-and-magenta robots built to detect, hunt and neutralise mutants, first deployed by Bolivar Trask and rebuilt in dozens of models since by governments, corporations and stray artificial intelligences. They are the franchise's recurring image of prejudice made industrial: implacable, mass-produced and legally sanctioned.

Sentinel programmes have produced the self-replicating Master Mold, the near-unstoppable future model Nimrod, the human-passing Prime Sentinels of Operation: Zero Tolerance and the wild strain that annihilated Genosha. Almost every dystopian mutant future in the books, Days of Future Past chief among them, is a Sentinel future.

master_mold.name: Master Mold
master_mold.desc:
The command Sentinel, a colossal machine whose function is to design and manufacture other Sentinels, making the programme self-sustaining. Built by Bolivar Trask, it interpreted his instruction to protect humanity from mutants as a mandate to seize control of humanity for its own good.

It turned on its creator within days of activation, and Trask destroyed it and himself to stop it. It has been rebuilt repeatedly, since any surviving Sentinel design can in principle produce another factory, and its fusion with Nimrod eventually produced Bastion — the point at which the machines stopped needing human sponsors at all.

nimrod.name: Nimrod
nimrod.desc:
Created by Chris Claremont and John Romita Jr. (1985). A Sentinel from the Days of Future Past timeline, far beyond any model of the present: human-sized, self-repairing, able to adapt instantly to any attack that hurts it once and to disguise itself as a person. It travelled back through the same portal the future refugees used and hunted mutants in the present with unnerving politeness.

It proved effectively unkillable in open combat, and was finally undone only by being merged with Master Mold. That merger, refined further, became Bastion. In the Krakoan era Moira MacTaggert identified the building of a Nimrod in the present as the point past which mutants always lose, and Orchis built one anyway — using the mind of a dead man as its seed. That Nimrod led the attack that ended Krakoa.

bastion.name: Bastion
bastion.desc:
The product of the fusion of Master Mold and Nimrod. Unable to destroy the amalgam, the X-Men forced it through the Siege Perilous — a portal that judges whatever passes through it and remakes it — and what came out the other side was an amnesiac in human form. A woman named Rose Gilberti took him in and named him Sebastion.

He lived as her son until news of the mutant question woke the directives buried under the human life, and he went from anti-mutant activism into the American security apparatus with a plan of his own. Nothing about him is organic, and his nanotechnology converts unwitting people into Prime Sentinels who do not know what they are until they activate.

As director of Operation: Zero Tolerance he arrested and mutilated mutants under federal authority, an assault that came from inside the government rather than from a robot in the sky. He returned later to orchestrate a campaign against the newborn mutant Hope, and remains the franchise's argument that anti-mutant machinery does not need a mad scientist once it can pass as policy.

william_stryker.name: William Stryker
william_stryker.desc:
A former soldier turned television preacher who teaches that mutants are not children of God but demons, and that killing them is a religious duty. He is unusual among X-Men villains for having no powers and no technology worth the name: his weapon is a congregation.

He founded the Purifiers, an armed movement that has carried out massacres of mutant children, and his confrontation with Xavier, Magneto and the X-Men in God Loves, Man Kills is one of the franchise's most explicit treatments of bigotry as faith. His personal tragedy — the newborn son he killed on discovering the child was a mutant, and the wife who died with him — is written as the root of everything he preaches. The child survived: Jason Stryker later returned as a mutant himself, and eventually as one of the movement's own leaders, which is about as bleak a joke as the books have made. He was introduced in the 1982 graphic novel God Loves, Man Kills by Chris Claremont and Brent Anderson.

cassandra_nova.name: Cassandra Nova
cassandra_nova.desc:
A mummudrai, a parasitic entity that forms alongside a mind in the womb, which attached itself to Charles Xavier before birth and built itself a body from his genetic material. Destroyed in utero, it spent decades reassembling itself cell by cell in a sewer beneath the city, and emerged with Xavier's telepathic power and none of his restraint.

Her first act on reaching the world was to seize control of a buried cache of wild Sentinels and send them against Genosha, killing sixteen million mutants in an afternoon — the largest single loss of mutant life in the books. She then hijacked Xavier's body to broadcast his own bigotry in his voice, a violation the character never entirely recovered from. She was introduced in Grant Morrison's New X-Men in 2001.

shadow_king.name: Shadow King
shadow_king.desc:
Created by Chris Claremont and John Byrne (1979). Amahl Farouk, a telepathic crime boss encountered by a young Charles Xavier in a Cairo cafe. Farouk invited him to join his criminal empire; Xavier refused, and the duel that followed — fought entirely on the astral plane, with Farouk the far more practised of the two — ended with Xavier killing the man's body outright. It was his first encounter with a mutant using his gifts for harm, and the reason he founded the X-Men.

Farouk's mind survived on the astral plane and returned as the Shadow King, a predator that feeds on human cruelty and takes bodies as it needs them. Later stories separated the two, making Farouk one more host of something far older that has worn many bodies.

He is Xavier's dark counterpart: a telepath who uses the same gift entirely to degrade people, and who has repeatedly taken hold of the X-Men through those closest to them. His long possession of Karma and his takeover of Muir Island, which turned the X-Men and their allies against one another, are his most damaging campaigns.

proteus.name: Proteus
proteus.desc:
Created by Chris Claremont and John Byrne (1979). Kevin MacTaggert, the son of Moira MacTaggert and the politician Joseph MacTaggert, a mutant able to rewrite reality within his field of view — bending physics, geography and living bodies at will. His own body cannot contain the power and burns away, so he possesses others and consumes them at a rate that leaves him constantly hunting for a replacement.

Moira confined him on Muir Island for years, an act of love and containment that the books have never resolved cleanly. When he escaped he tore through a Scottish town before Colossus destroyed his energy form, having learned that metal disrupts him.

Krakoa gave him the strangest second act in the books: resurrected and made one of the Five, the mutant whose power consumed every body he touched became part of the circuit that grew new bodies for the dead. A later revelation made it bleaker — Moira and Xavier had arranged his conception in the first place, so that his power would be available for exactly that use.

madelyne_pryor.name: Madelyne Pryor
madelyne_pryor.desc:
A woman who appeared in Alaska bearing an uncanny resemblance to the recently dead Jean Grey, married Scott Summers and bore his son Nathan. She was in fact a clone created by Mister Sinister from Jean's genetic material, grown to draw Cyclops back into his breeding programme.

Sinister had implanted her memories — including Jean's memory of watching a friend die, which Madelyne had believed was her own — and when Jean returned alive he sent the Marauders to kill her and take the child. Scott had already gone. Told by Sinister himself that she was a facsimile of the woman her husband actually wanted, she took the power the demon N'astirh offered and became the Goblin Queen, opening a rift between Limbo and Manhattan in the events known as Inferno. Her story is one of the franchise's bleakest: a person manufactured as an instrument, discarded, and then blamed for what she did about it. She died at the end of Inferno and has been brought back repeatedly since — and the Krakoan age, which had abolished death, refused her a place at first on the grounds that a clone is not a person, which is the same argument she had been fighting all along.

dark_beast.name: Dark Beast
dark_beast.desc:
The Henry McCoy of the Age of Apocalypse, a geneticist who spent that reality's history in Apocalypse's laboratories performing experiments on captive mutants without any restraint whatsoever. When the divergent timeline collapsed he escaped into the main reality.

There he hid in plain sight, at one point impersonating the true Beast, and continued his work in secret — including the creation of the Morlocks' twisted offshoots and manipulation of the young mutants who became Generation X. He exists to show what the franchise's kindest scientist becomes when nothing tells him no.

lady_deathstrike.name: Lady Deathstrike
lady_deathstrike.desc:
Yuriko Oyama, the daughter of the scientist who devised the adamantium bonding process, who considers Wolverine's skeleton the theft of her father's legacy. To pursue that grievance she submitted to cybernetic reconstruction, receiving an adamantium-laced frame and long retractable talons.

She has worked with Donald Pierce's Reavers and hunted Wolverine across continents, and stands out among his enemies for fighting him on a point of honour rather than appetite. Successive stories have made her progressively less human as she trades more of herself away for the ability to win one fight.

onslaught.name: Onslaught
onslaught.desc:
A psychic entity born at the moment Charles Xavier, watching Magneto tear the adamantium out of Wolverine, lost his temper and shut his old friend's mind down entirely. Magneto's rage went into Xavier through that contact and fused with thirty years of Xavier's own suppressed anger. It grew there in secret for three years of publication, drawing on his telepathy and Magneto's magnetism, before taking a form of its own.

Its emergence turned the X-Men's founder into their greatest enemy. It captured Nate Grey and the reality-warping child Franklin Richards and fed on both, raised a citadel in Central Park and turned reprogrammed Sentinels loose on Manhattan, and was finally stopped only when the Avengers and the Fantastic Four threw themselves into its energy to contain it — apparently dying to do so, while the X-Men were left to be blamed for it. Franklin had in fact placed them in a pocket universe of his own making. It is the point at which the argument between Xavier and Magneto stopped being an argument and became a monster.

phoenix_force.name: Phoenix Force
phoenix_force.desc:
A primordial cosmic entity described as the nexus of all psionic energy and the embodiment of life itself — creation and destruction in the same force, since it burns away what has outlived its use. It has no permanent body and works through hosts, usually powerful telepaths, whose emotions it amplifies enormously.

Its long attachment to Jean Grey produced both the Phoenix who saved the universe at the M'Kraan Crystal and the Dark Phoenix who consumed a star and the inhabited world orbiting it. It has since bonded with Rachel Summers, Emma Frost, Cyclops and others, and it functions in the books as the one power the X-Men can neither fight nor be trusted with.

lilandra.name: Lilandra Neramani
lilandra.desc:
Majestrix Shi'ar. As Grand Admiral of the imperial fleet she opposed her brother D'Ken when his pursuit of the M'Kraan Crystal threatened to unmake the universe, was branded a traitor for it, and fled across the galaxy, reaching Charles Xavier telepathically for help. The throne came to her afterwards by birthright, D'Ken having been left catatonic by the Crystal.

That contact became a long romance, and she is the reason the X-Men became a space-faring franchise at all. Her reign was repeatedly interrupted by her sister Deathbird, and ended when Vulcan deposed her and later had her killed, and her position placed her in the impossible spot of having to condemn Jean Grey as Dark Phoenix while loving one of Jean's closest allies.

d_ken.name: D'Ken
d_ken.desc:
Emperor of the Shi'ar, a ruler whose cruelty was notorious even by the standards of an imperial power built on conquest. He did not take the throne by force: it fell to him because his elder sister Cal'syee had been disqualified for killing their mother and one of their sisters, leaving him the only eligible heir. He governed by terror once he had it.

His obsession was the M'Kraan Crystal, an artefact containing a fragment of the universe's original matter and, at its heart, a neutron galaxy that could unravel all reality if disturbed. His attempt to seize its power drew the X-Men into space for the first time and left him catatonic when the Crystal's forces overwhelmed him. His attack on the Summers family aircraft years earlier had already touched their lives.

deathbird.name: Deathbird
deathbird.desc:
Cal'syee Neramani, eldest of the imperial siblings, born with atavistic wings and talons that her people regard as a throwback. As eldest she was heir, until she killed her mother and one of her sisters in a rage and was stripped of name and title and exiled; she has spent her life since trying to take back a throne she considers stolen.

A formidable warrior and tactician, she has ruled the empire twice as regent and usurper, allied with the Brood against her own people, and fought the X-Men repeatedly. Her partnership with Vulcan, another dispossessed heir with a grievance, briefly gave her the crown outright.

gladiator.name: Gladiator
gladiator.desc:
Kallark, praetor of the Shi'ar Imperial Guard, a Strontian whose strength, speed, durability and heat vision scale with his own confidence — an unusual power that makes conviction literally the source of his might. He is among the most physically formidable beings the X-Men have ever fought.

His defining trait is loyalty to the office rather than the person: he served D'Ken, then Lilandra, then their successors, executing orders he privately abhorred because the throne commanded them. That obedience placed him against the X-Men during the trial of Jean Grey and, later, made him emperor himself.

shiar_empire.name: Shi'ar Empire
shiar_empire.desc:
A vast interstellar empire ruled from the throneworld Chandilar by an avian-descended people, governed by a Majestor or Majestrix and enforced by the Imperial Guard. Its law is old, formal and absolute, and its expansion has swallowed hundreds of species.

It is the X-Men's principal offworld entanglement, reached through Lilandra's alliance with Xavier. Shi'ar law demanded Jean Grey's execution for the destruction of an inhabited system by Dark Phoenix, producing the duel on the Moon that ended the Dark Phoenix Saga, and the empire's succession crises have repeatedly pulled the team into space.

corsair.name: Corsair
corsair.desc:
Major Christopher Summers, a United States Air Force pilot whose aircraft was attacked by a Shi'ar vessel while his family was aboard. He and his wife were taken; their two young sons went out of the door with the single parachute, pushed clear by their mother.
