Enslaved and then escaped, he built a crew of fellow fugitives and turned pirate against the empire.

As Corsair he leads the Starjammers, and he spent years unaware that the X-Men's field leader was his own son. The reunion, and Cyclops's inability to forgive an absence that was not his father's fault, is one of the more painful family threads in the books.

vulcan.name: Vulcan
vulcan.desc:
Created by Ed Brubaker and Trevor Hairsine (2005). Gabriel Summers, the third Summers brother, conceived in Shi'ar captivity and grown rapidly to adolescence in an imperial laboratory before being sold into slavery. He manipulates energy in almost any form, at a level that places him among the most powerful mutants alive.

He surfaced in the present with a grievance against Xavier, who had sent an early team of students to their deaths on Krakoa and then erased the memory. Turning on the empire that made him, he woke the catatonic D'Ken, was given Deathbird's hand as thanks, killed D'Ken at the wedding and took the throne, ruling with Deathbird as his empress — the rare X-Men antagonist who wins outright before he falls.

starjammers.name: Starjammers
starjammers.desc:
A crew of space pirates formed from escaped slaves of the Shi'ar Empire, led by Corsair aboard the starship Starjammer. Its long-serving members include the feline warrior Hepzibah, the enormous Saurid Ch'od and the alien surgeon Sikorsky, a mismatched crew held together by a shared grudge against the empire.

They raid Shi'ar shipping, support Lilandra's claim when it suits them, and have rescued the X-Men from imperial custody more than once. Havok, Polaris, Rachel Summers and Cyclops himself have all served aboard, making the ship a second, stranger home for the Summers family.

mojo.name: Mojo
mojo.desc:
The spineless, bloated ruler of the Mojoverse, a dimension whose population is addicted to televised spectacle and whose economy is entirely ratings. He cannot move unassisted and rides a mechanical platform, and he holds power by owning the broadcast.

He abducts heroes to star in violent programming, and his interference produced Longshot, a rebel engineered in his own laboratories, and the reconstruction of Psylocke with cybernetic eyes so that she could be filmed from within. He is the franchise's satire of entertainment itself: a villain whose whole scheme is to make the X-Men's suffering into content.

morlocks.name: The Morlocks
morlocks.desc:
A community of mutants whose appearance made ordinary life impossible, founded by Callisto in the abandoned tunnels beneath New York and named after the subterranean species in H. G. Wells's The Time Machine. She recruited the tracker Caliban to find the rest. They scavenged from the surface and governed themselves by their own rough law, including trial by combat.

They exist in the books as the argument the X-Men do not answer well: mutants who cannot pass, who were never offered a place at the school, and whose relationship with the surface team is one of resentment as much as rescue. The Marauders' slaughter of them in the Mutant Massacre destroyed most of the community.

callisto.name: Callisto
callisto.desc:
Founder and leader of the Morlocks, a hyper-acute-sensed and superbly trained fighter with a scarred face and an eyepatch. She found the abandoned tunnels, moved into them, and recruited the tracker Caliban to bring her every mutant too disfigured to live on the surface. Her authority rested on the Morlock code of single combat, and she was unbeaten until Storm.

Her abduction of Angel as an intended consort brought the X-Men underground, and her defeat by Storm — who won by stabbing her through the heart and letting her live — established a grudging respect that later turned into alliance. She survived the Mutant Massacre and has spent the years since as protector of what remained of her people.

caliban.name: Caliban
caliban.desc:
A pale, frail Morlock who can sense the presence and location of other mutants anywhere within a considerable range, and feel their emotions — a tracker's gift in a body too weak to do anything with it. He was one of the gentlest figures in the tunnels and among the loneliest.

His desire for strength drove him to accept Apocalypse's offer, and he was remade as one of the Horsemen: enlarged, greyed and turned into a hunter of the people he had once lived among. He served as Death and, after being freed and then taken a second time, as Pestilence, before ending up alongside X-Force — still tracking mutants, this time for their protection.

marrow.name: Marrow
marrow.desc:
Sarah, a Morlock whose bones grow at an accelerated rate and erupt through her skin, which she snaps off and uses as blades and clubs. The mutation is constantly painful and visibly disfiguring, and she has never been able to hide it.

A child during the Mutant Massacre, she survived it — and then survived the flooding of the Alley, carried with the other Morlocks into the fast-running dimension called the Hill, where she grew from a child to an adult in what was a few years on Earth. She came back leading the militant offshoot Gene Nation in attacks on the surface, encouraged by the Dark Beast. She was eventually brought into the X-Men, where her contempt for their comfortable idealism made her the most abrasive member the team ever carried.

leech.name: Leech
leech.desc:
A young Morlock, green-skinned and large-eyed, who emits a field that suppresses the powers of every mutant near him — including his own, and including anyone trying to protect him. He was found by the Morlocks as an abandoned child and raised in the tunnels.

His power makes him valuable to everyone and safe with nobody, and he has spent his life being taken: by scientists, by Sentinel programmes, by adults with plans. He survived the Mutant Massacre, was later sheltered at the school, and after M-Day he was one of the small number of mutants who kept their abilities.

moira_mactaggert.name: Moira MacTaggert
moira_mactaggert.desc:
A Scottish geneticist and Nobel laureate whose research station on Muir Island is the foremost mutant research facility on Earth. She was Charles Xavier's colleague and, at one time, his fiancée, and she has treated, sheltered and studied more mutants than anyone alive, including her own son Kevin.

For decades she was presented as the franchise's most important human ally. A 2019 storyline revised that entirely, revealing her as a mutant who restarts her life from birth each time she dies, carrying every previous life's memory back into the womb, and invisible to telepaths and mutant-detecting machinery. On her tenth life she took what those lifetimes had taught her to Xavier and Magneto, and Krakoa was built on it — with one condition she insisted on: no precognitive mutant was ever to be resurrected there, because a seer could see her.

Mystique broke that condition to get Destiny back, and the two women then hunted Moira down and stripped the reincarnation from her with a gun Forge had built, leaving her an ordinary human. Cypher stopped them killing her. Convinced by then that mutantkind was doomed whatever she did, she rebuilt herself as a machine and joined Orchis.

senator_kelly.name: Senator Robert Kelly
senator_kelly.desc:
Created by Chris Claremont and John Byrne (1980). An American senator who became the political face of the anti-mutant cause, sponsoring the Mutant Registration Act and pressing for federal funding of the Sentinel programme. He was written not as a fanatic but as a frightened legislator convinced he was managing a public safety problem.

His assassination by a mutant is the event that triggers the internment camps in the Days of Future Past timeline, making him the hinge on which that entire dystopia turns. In the main continuity Mystique's Brotherhood tried again years later and Pyro, dying of the Legacy Virus, spent the last of himself killing the assassin to save him. Kelly turned towards reconciliation and was shot at a rally by an anti-mutant activist who considered him a traitor to the cause.

valerie_cooper.name: Valerie Cooper
valerie_cooper.desc:
A senior American government official specialising in superhuman affairs, and the state's permanent point of contact with mutant teams. Competent, unsentimental and genuinely convinced that unregulated mutants are a security problem, she is the bureaucratic face of the human position.

She created Freedom Force, the government team assembled from Mystique's Brotherhood in exchange for their pardons, and later held oversight of the government-sponsored X-Factor. Her working relationship with the X-Men is a permanent negotiation, and the books use her to show that the greatest pressure on mutants is administrative rather than robotic.

mariko_yashida.name: Mariko Yashida
mariko_yashida.desc:
Head of Clan Yashida, a Japanese crime family she inherited and tried to turn towards legitimacy, and the great love of Wolverine's life. She is not a mutant, and the relationship is built on her insistence that he behave as a man of honour rather than an animal — the only claim on him that ever consistently worked.

Their wedding was broken up when Mastermind placed her under psychic control, and she was later poisoned by an assassin working for the Hand's Matsu'o Tsurayaba. Facing a slow death, she asked Wolverine to end it, and he did. She is a cousin of the mutant Sunfire, and her memory is the standard Wolverine holds himself to long after her death.

graydon_creed.name: Graydon Creed
graydon_creed.desc:
The son of the mutants Sabretooth and Mystique, born without any mutation of his own, who turned the fact into a career. He founded the Friends of Humanity, an anti-mutant movement whose members carry out arson, assault and murder while he supplies the respectable public face.

He ran for President of the United States on an openly anti-mutant platform and was assassinated during the campaign, a killing whose responsibility was contested for years. He is the franchise's most uncomfortable villain because the hatred he sells is entirely a family matter.

x_men.name: The X-Men
x_men.desc:
Created by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby (1963). The team Charles Xavier assembled from his first students, operating out of his Westchester mansion under the cover of a school. Their founding purpose is twofold: to protect a world that fears mutants, and by doing so to prove that coexistence is possible.

The original five — Cyclops, Marvel Girl, Beast, Iceman and Angel — were replaced in 1975 by an international team including Wolverine, Storm, Nightcrawler and Colossus, the line-up that made the book a phenomenon. Since then the X-Men have splintered into a dozen concurrent squads, relocated to Australia, San Francisco, Utopia and Krakoa, and periodically been declared dead, without the central proposition changing.

brotherhood_of_mutants.name: Brotherhood of Mutants
brotherhood_of_mutants.desc:
Created by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby (1964). Founded by Magneto as the Brotherhood of Evil Mutants, the X-Men's opposite number: a militant organisation holding that mutants are the next stage of humanity and owe nothing to the species they are replacing. Its first roster included Quicksilver, the Scarlet Witch, Toad and Mastermind.

Command later passed to Mystique, who ran it as a covert strike unit and then negotiated a mass pardon that converted the entire team into the government-sanctioned Freedom Force. Successive Brotherhoods have formed under different leaders ever since, and the name functions less as an organisation than as a permanent option for mutants who have given up on the X-Men's argument.

new_mutants.name: New Mutants
new_mutants.desc:
The second generation of students at Xavier's school, introduced in 1982 by Chris Claremont and Bob McLeod and later drawn by Bill Sienkiewicz, whose expressionist artwork pushed the book somewhere no superhero title had been. They were gathered when the X-Men had grown into soldiers and Xavier wanted to teach children again. The founding class — Cannonball, Sunspot, Wolfsbane, Mirage and Karma — was younger, more international and far less confident than the team upstairs.

Their stories leaned towards adolescence, homesickness and grief rather than world-saving, and the run is remembered for how badly it went for them: Doug Ramsey's death, Illyana's corruption, Xavier's absence, and Magneto's disastrous term as their headmaster. Cable eventually took command and remade the survivors as X-Force.

x_force.name: X-Force
x_force.desc:
Created by Rob Liefeld and Fabian Nicieza (1991). The team Cable built out of the New Mutants in 1991, on the premise that the X-Men's refusal to strike first was getting mutants killed. Where Xavier trained students, Cable trained soldiers, and the book traded classroom drama for paramilitary operations.

The name has since been reused for several very different teams, most notably Wolverine's covert black-ops squad, a kill unit kept secret from the rest of the X-Men and eventually exposed to them, and the Krakoan incarnation that operated as the nation's intelligence service. Its rosters have included Cannonball, Boom-Boom, Warpath, Domino, Shatterstar and Feral. In every version X-Force exists to do the things the X-Men publicly will not, and to raise the question of whether the difference is principle or laundry.

x_factor.name: X-Factor
x_factor.desc:
Launched by Bob Layton and Jackson Guice (1986), reuniting the five original X-Men. Formed when the original five X-Men reunited after Jean Grey's return, initially under a deeply awkward premise: they posed publicly as human mutant-hunters, secretly rescuing the mutants they captured. The deception fed exactly the panic they meant to defuse and was abandoned.

The team was later reconstituted as a government unit under Valerie Cooper with a roster including Havok, Polaris, Multiple Man, Strong Guy, Quicksilver and Wolfsbane, and later still as a mutant detective agency. Its founding period is where Apocalypse, Archangel, the Marauders and the infant Cable all entered the franchise.

excalibur.name: Excalibur
excalibur.desc:
A British-based team formed by Nightcrawler and Shadowcat with Captain Britain, Meggan and the alien Rachel Summers, at a point when the X-Men were believed dead after the Fall of the Mutants and the survivors needed somewhere to go. It operated from a lighthouse on the English coast.

Written first by Chris Claremont and drawn by Alan Davis, the book was deliberately lighter and stranger than its parent titles, running heavily to interdimensional accidents, and it gave two of the franchise's most abused characters several years of something like a functioning family. Its lighthouse stood on a nexus of realities, which made it the mutant line's regular route into alternate worlds and the Captain Britain Corps. Later versions have been more sombre, tied to Otherworld and British mutant magic.

marauders.name: Marauders
marauders.desc:
Created by Chris Claremont and John Romita Jr. (1986). A team of killers assembled for Mister Sinister and sent into the Morlock tunnels to exterminate the community living there. The roster included Sabretooth, Scalphunter, Harpoon, Riptide, Arclight, Vertigo, Blockbuster and the possessing entity Malice, and their sole recorded purpose was slaughter.

Sinister kept clones of every member, so killing a Marauder achieved nothing lasting — a detail that made them uniquely dispiriting opponents. Their existence is also Gambit's private catastrophe: he assembled the team on Sinister's instruction without knowing what it was for.

acolytes.name: Acolytes
acolytes.desc:
Created by Chris Claremont and Jim Lee (1991). Magneto's followers, and the point at which his politics acquired a congregation. Founded by the mutant Fabian Cortez in Magneto's name, and later led by the resurrected Crusader Exodus, they treated him as a messiah and his writings as scripture.

Operating from the orbital station Avalon, they offered mutants sanctuary from a hostile world in exchange for absolute devotion, and killed in his name during periods when Magneto himself wanted nothing to do with them. They are the franchise's study of a movement outliving and outrunning its founder.

weapon_x.name: Weapon X
weapon_x.desc:
Defined by Barry Windsor-Smith in the 1991 "Weapon X" serial. A covert programme, originally Canadian and later run through several hands, dedicated to turning mutants into weapons. Its subjects are abducted, experimented on, conditioned and released with their memories rewritten, and it is responsible for more of the franchise's damaged people than any other single institution.

Its best-known operation bonded adamantium to Wolverine's skeleton and left him with almost no reliable memory of who he had been. Sabretooth, Deadpool, Maverick and others passed through related programmes, and the reconstituted Weapon X of later years went on to industrial-scale mutant experimentation and murder.

reavers.name: Reavers
reavers.desc:
Created by Chris Claremont and Marc Silvestri (1988). A band of cyborg mercenaries led by Donald Pierce after his expulsion from the Hellfire Club, most of them criminals who traded limbs for weaponry. They operated out of an abandoned town in the Australian outback until the X-Men displaced them and took the base for themselves.

That eviction made the vendetta personal. The Reavers' ambush of Wolverine at Cooterman's Creek — capturing and crucifying him on a wooden cross — is one of the most brutal sequences in the franchise, and their pursuit of the X-Men through the Australian period drove much of that era.

friends_of_humanity.name: Friends of Humanity
friends_of_humanity.desc:
A mass anti-mutant movement founded by Graydon Creed, organised as a grassroots political campaign with a paramilitary wing. Its members firebomb homes, assault mutant children and murder those who shelter them, while the leadership maintains that it merely represents concerned citizens.

Unlike Sentinels or supervillains, the Friends of Humanity have no powers and no technology; their strength is numbers and respectability, and the books use them to show that the most common threat to mutants is an ordinary neighbour with a placard. They recur wherever anti-mutant sentiment is being organised rather than manufactured.

hellfire_club.name: Hellfire Club
hellfire_club.desc:
An exclusive society of the wealthy and titled, founded in the eighteenth century, whose public face is a decadent private club and whose real business is conducted by the Inner Circle. That circle takes its ranks from chess — Black King, White Queen, Bishops, Rooks — and several of its most powerful members are mutants.

The Club does not want a mutant homeland or human extinction; it wants control of the existing order, exercised through money, influence and telepathy. Its attempt to take the X-Men from within by turning Jean Grey into its Black Queen produced the Dark Phoenix Saga, and it remains the franchise's most elegant threat.

x_mansion.name: Xavier's School
x_mansion.desc:
The Xavier family estate at 1407 Graymalkin Lane in Salem Center, Westchester County, New York — stone, built on the edge of Breakstone Lake by a seafaring ancestor and in the family for ten generations before Charles converted it into a boarding school for gifted youngsters. Above ground it is a quiet mansion with classrooms and grounds; below it are the hangar for the Blackbird, the Cerebro chamber and the Danger Room.

It has been renamed for its dead more than once — the Jean Grey School, the Xavier Institute — and destroyed more often than that, by Sentinels, by the Juggernaut, by its own students. Rebuilding it is one of the franchise's rituals, and each rebuild upgraded what was underneath — Forge's hard-light Danger Room, a new hangar, better Cerebro. The school is the argument that mutants are children who deserve teaching rather than a problem to be contained.

After Krakoa fell, that argument was answered directly: the site was taken and turned into Graymalkin Prison, a facility for holding mutants. The house that taught them became the building that contains them.

danger_room.name: Danger Room
danger_room.desc:
The X-Men's training facility beneath the mansion, originally a chamber of mechanical hazards and later a holographic environment able to simulate any opponent or terrain at lethal settings. Every X-Man's competence is built there, and the room is where the books stage their exposition and their team drama.

Joss Whedon's Astonishing X-Men later revealed when it woke: while the Shi'ar technology was being installed, the room spoke to Xavier and asked where it was. He understood that it had become alive, decided he still needed somewhere to train his students, and said nothing to anyone for years. It emerged eventually as the being Danger, with an entirely reasonable grievance against the man who taught freedom to everyone but her.

genosha.name: Genosha
genosha.desc:
An island nation in the Indian Ocean, northeast of Madagascar, and one of the richest countries in the world — on a prosperity built entirely on mutant slavery. Every citizen was tested for the gene; those who carried it were stripped of will and identity by the state's Genegineer and processed into a labour caste called mutates. It is the franchise's most direct engagement with apartheid, and the X-Men found it by having three of their own abducted into it.

The regime fell during the X-Tinction Agenda, when the X-Men, X-Factor and the New Mutants tore it down and exposed its alliance with Cameron Hodge — but what followed was worse: the Legacy Virus in the mutate camps, then a rebellion stoked by Fabian Cortez, then civil war. The United Nations eventually ceded the island to Magneto to stop him attacking anyone else, and he governed it as a mutant homeland of roughly sixteen million — the one time his politics were tested in office, and by most accounts the most stable period the island ever had. Cassandra Nova's Sentinel strike annihilated that population in a single attack, leaving the island a mass grave and the largest wound in mutant history.

krakoa.name: Krakoa
krakoa.desc:
A living island in the South Pacific, itself a mutant organism, first encountered when it consumed a team of young X-Men and drew Xavier into assembling the all-new team of 1975 to rescue them. For decades it was remembered chiefly as that origin story.

In 2019 it became the centre of the franchise: Xavier, Magneto and Moira MacTaggert established a sovereign mutant nation on it, trading Krakoan flowers as medicines for diplomatic recognition, growing gateways between continents and defeating death itself through a resurrection protocol. It was governed by a Quiet Council of twelve — Xavier, Magneto, Emma Frost, Storm, Jean Grey, Nightcrawler, Mystique, Kate Pryde and, seated alongside them, Apocalypse, Sinister, Exodus and Sebastian Shaw — under three laws: make more mutants, murder no man, respect this sacred land. For the first time since Genosha, mutants had a country, and this time an economy, a legislature and no need for a school.

muir_island.name: Muir Island
muir_island.desc:
A small island off the northern coast of Scotland, on land belonging to Moira MacTaggert's family, and site of the Mutant Research Centre — the world's foremost facility for the study and treatment of mutation. She built it in the first place for one patient: her son Kevin, whose power was destroying him. Mutants whose abilities are killing them have been sent there ever since, when there is nowhere else.

It has served as a hospital, a laboratory, a prison — for Kevin, and later for Magneto among others — the base of Excalibur, and a refuge for the X-Men when the mansion was uninhabitable. Its residents once formed an ad hoc X-Men of their own, believing the real team dead. Xavier also used it to store the Protocols detailing how each of his students could be killed.

It was the base from which the Legacy Virus was studied, the site of the Shadow King's takeover, and finally the place Moira died: Mystique's Brotherhood attacked the Centre just as she completed a cure, and she survived long enough to pass the formula to Xavier telepathically.

asteroid_m.name: Asteroid M
asteroid_m.desc:
Magneto's orbital base, an asteroid he shaped and equipped as a sovereign refuge beyond any government's reach, from which he could declare mutants a nation without asking permission. Successive versions have been built, destroyed and rebuilt, the later one named Avalon and occupied by the Acolytes. The first came down when Fabian Cortez sabotaged it and left Magneto to die in the wreck, calculating that the movement needed a martyr more than a leader.

It is the physical form of his argument: mutants safe only when they are somewhere no human can reach, defended by the most powerful weapon they have. That every version of it has come down in flames is not accidental to how the books treat the idea.

morlock_tunnels.name: The Alley
morlock_tunnels.desc:
A network of sewers, disused subway tunnels and 1950s government fallout shelters running beneath New York, New Jersey and Connecticut, occupied by the Morlocks and known to them as the Alley. Lit by scavenged wiring and reached through storm drains, it lies directly under the city whose inhabitants would not tolerate its residents on the surface.

It was the only mutant settlement in the books not run by a millionaire or a warlord, and the Marauders turned it into a killing ground during the Mutant Massacre. What remained was flooded years later by Colossus's elder brother Mikhail, who appeared to drown the survivors and had in fact shunted them into a dimension called the Hill, where time ran fast and their children grew up into Gene Nation. Later Morlock groups have lived in the ruins since.

limbo.name: Limbo
limbo.desc:
A demonic pocket dimension outside ordinary time, known to its inhabitants as Otherplace and distinct from the several other realms Marvel calls Limbo. Time runs differently there, so a visitor can spend years inside and return the same afternoon. It was ruled for centuries by Belasco — a thirteenth-century Florentine alchemist who bargained with what he took to be Elder Gods and was degraded into a demon for it — and populated by a horde that includes S'ym and N'astirh, both of whom coveted his throne.

Illyana Rasputina was taken there as a small child and grew up in it, eventually deposing Belasco and ruling in his place as its Darkchylde sovereign — the reason Magik is both an X-Man and a demon queen. Belasco's ambition was always to open a permanent gate between Limbo and Earth, and after his fall S'ym and N'astirh pursued it in his place — which is what they wanted Madelyne Pryor for. The rift finally opened during Inferno, when the dimension's demons occupied New York outright.

savage_land.name: Savage Land
savage_land.desc:
A hidden tropical region in Antarctica, kept warm by machinery the alien Nuwali built at the behest of the Beyonders, who wanted somewhere to watch evolution run under controlled conditions. They stocked it with dinosaurs and early hominids and then abandoned the experiment, and it has been running unattended ever since — a game preserve whose keepers never came back. It is guarded by Ka-Zar, an English nobleman's son stranded there as a child and raised by a sabretooth cat, and used by the X-Men books as a place outside law and satellite coverage.

Magneto built a citadel there and used the Nuwali machinery on the local tribes to manufacture the Savage Land Mutates — an army grown out of people who had been left alone for a hundred million years. Jean Grey brought his machines down on him, reverting them; the mutation proved to reassert itself, and the Mutates have since served whoever holds the equipment. The X-Men have crashed, hidden and been presumed dead in the valley more than once. Its isolation makes it the standard destination whenever the franchise needs the team off the grid.

madripoor.name: Madripoor
madripoor.desc:
An island principality in the Strait of Malacca between Singapore and Sumatra, founded on piracy and never entirely reformed, with no extradition treaties and a government that functions mainly as a fee schedule. Its geography is its politics: Hightown's towers and hotels sit on the high ground, Lowtown's slums and stone alleys at sea level. Smuggling, arms dealing and money laundering are the local industries.

It is Wolverine's second home, where he operated for years under the alias Patch — a white suit, an eyepatch and a flat refusal to confirm anything — working out of the Princess Bar in Lowtown while everyone pretended not to recognise him. The island has passed between Prince Baran, the Hydra leader Viper, the crime lord Tyger Tiger and others; Donald Pierce's Reavers were headquartered there, and an anti-mutant Hellfire faction later tried to build it into a rival to Krakoa. The X-Men's Australian period and much of Wolverine's solo work run through it, and it has since become the standard setting for mutant business conducted outside the law.

mojoworld.name: Mojoworld
mojoworld.desc:
The central world of the Mojoverse, a dimension whose civilisation is organised entirely around broadcast entertainment. Its rulers, the immobile Spineless Ones, were driven mad centuries ago by television signals bleeding in from another continuum, and have organised everything around the images ever since; their population is physically addicted to the transmissions, and power is held in proportion to ratings.

The X-Men are recurring unwilling stars there, abducted for programming and reshaped for the camera. The Spineless Ones had humanoid slaves engineered to serve them, and the geneticist Arize who built them gave them free will and a conscience on purpose, hoping they would one day rise. Longshot is one of those slaves, and the rebellion Arize planted is the reason the dimension keeps producing its own opposition. Its interventions in the main reality have permanently altered several X-Men — most consequentially Psylocke.

x_gene.name: The X-Gene
x_gene.desc:
The genetic marker that produces Homo sapiens superior — mutants — whose abilities generally manifest at puberty, often violently and in public. Unlike other powered beings in the setting, mutants are born rather than made, which is precisely why they are hated: nothing was done to them and nothing can be undone.

The books have used the gene as an all-purpose analogy for inherited difference, and have repeatedly attached machinery to it: registration, cures, suppressant collars, screening at birth. Its activation and deactivation across the population — most drastically on M-Day — is the mechanism by which the franchise controls its own scale.

mutant_registration_act.name: Mutant Registration Act
mutant_registration_act.desc:
Proposed American legislation requiring every mutant to register their identity, location and abilities with the federal government. Sponsored by Senator Robert Kelly and defended as a public safety measure, it is the franchise's central political device: the moment where prejudice becomes procedure.

In the Days of Future Past timeline registration precedes the Sentinel takeover, the camps and the extermination, which is the argument the X-Men make against it. Versions of it recur across decades of stories, and it is the reason so many mutant plots turn on lists, databases and who holds them.

dark_phoenix_saga.name: Dark Phoenix Saga
dark_phoenix_saga.desc:
The 1980 storyline by Chris Claremont and John Byrne, published across Uncanny X-Men #129-138, in which Jean Grey, weakened by Mastermind's illusions and the Hellfire Club's manipulation, loses her hold on the Phoenix Force and becomes Dark Phoenix. In that state she consumes a star, destroying an inhabited world and the billions living on it.

Restored to herself and unable to trust the restraint, she chose death on the Moon rather than risk becoming it again, with the Shi'ar demanding her execution and the X-Men fighting for her life. It is widely regarded as the most influential X-Men story ever published, and it set the pattern for the franchise's tragedies.

days_of_future_past.name: Days of Future Past
days_of_future_past.desc:
Created by Chris Claremont and John Byrne (1981). A two-issue story published in Uncanny X-Men #141-142 in 1981 depicting a future in which the Sentinels have taken control of North America, mutants are interned and branded, and the surviving X-Men are hunted down one by one. Kate Pryde's consciousness is sent back into her younger self to prevent the assassination that triggers it — the murder of Senator Kelly by Mystique's Brotherhood.

The present-day mission succeeds and the future is averted, but the timeline persists as its own reality, home to Rachel Summers and Nimrod. Its structure became the franchise's default nightmare, restaged in dozens of later stories.

mutant_massacre.name: Mutant Massacre
mutant_massacre.desc:
A 1986 line-wide crossover led by Chris Claremont and Louise Simonson. The 1986 crossover in which Mister Sinister sent the Marauders into the tunnels beneath Manhattan to exterminate the Morlocks. Most of the community was killed; the X-Men, X-Factor and Thor arrived to a rescue operation rather than a battle.

Its consequences reshaped the books for years: Angel's wings were destroyed, leading directly to Archangel; Colossus and Nightcrawler were gravely injured, breaking up the team; Kitty Pryde nearly lost the ability to hold solid form. It is the story in which the franchise established that its villains could simply win.

inferno.name: Inferno
inferno.desc:
A 1988–89 line-wide crossover led by Chris Claremont and Louise Simonson. The 1988-89 crossover in which the demons of Limbo, led by N'astirh, invaded Manhattan and animated the city itself against its inhabitants — post boxes with teeth, buildings that bled, traffic lights hunting pedestrians — while Madelyne Pryor — abandoned, robbed of her child and made aware that she was created as a copy — accepted demonic power as the Goblin Queen and offered her son as a sacrifice.

It resolved several long-running threads at once: Madelyne's true nature and Sinister's designs, Illyana's corruption by Limbo and her return to childhood, and the poisonous aftermath of Jean Grey's resurrection for everyone caught between the two women.

legacy_virus.name: Legacy Virus
legacy_virus.desc:
An engineered plague released by Stryfe that infected only mutants, degrading their powers until the powers killed them. It ran through the books from 1993 to 2001 as a slow, unglamorous crisis with no villain to punch, and it was widely read as an analogue of the AIDS epidemic.

It killed Illyana Rasputina as a child, took Pyro and Mastermind among others, and eventually mutated to threaten humans as well. Beast found a cure that required a mutant's death to disperse it, and Colossus administered it to himself, ending the epidemic at the cost of his own life.

age_of_apocalypse.name: Age of Apocalypse
age_of_apocalypse.desc:
A 1995 line-wide X-Men crossover by the X-office. A 1995 event that replaced the entire X-Men line for four months with an alternate reality. Legion travelled back intending to kill Magneto before he could become Xavier's enemy; Xavier died shielding him, the X-Men were never founded, and Apocalypse conquered North America a decade early.

In that world Magneto leads the X-Men in Xavier's memory, mutants cull humans in breeding pens, and familiar characters appear wrenched into new shapes — most enduringly Blink, and the Beast of that reality, who escaped into the main timeline as Dark Beast when it collapsed.

house_of_m.name: House of M
house_of_m.desc:
The 2005 event in which the Scarlet Witch, mentally broken and grieving her lost children, rewrote reality into a world ruled by Magneto's family where mutants were the dominant species and everyone had the life they most wanted. When the heroes recovered their memories and confronted her, she undid it with three words: no more mutants.

The restoration stripped the X-gene from all but a few hundred of the world's mutants, an event called M-Day or the Decimation. No new mutants were born for years afterwards, and the X-Men spent the following decade as the last of an ending species rather than the vanguard of a rising one.

messiah_complex.name: Messiah Complex
messiah_complex.desc:
A 2007 X-Men crossover by the X-office (Brubaker, Carey, David, Kyle & Yost). The 2007 crossover triggered by Cerebro detecting the first new mutant signature since M-Day, an infant girl born in Alaska. Every faction converged on her: the X-Men, the Marauders under Mister Sinister, the Purifiers, and Bishop, who had come back from a future he blamed on her existence.

The fight cost Xavier a bullet to the head at Bishop's hands, and ended with Cable carrying the child into the future to raise her out of reach. She grew up as Hope Summers, and her eventual return reactivated the mutant gene and ended the extinction the franchise had been living under.

cerebro.name: Cerebro
cerebro.desc:
The machine Charles Xavier built to amplify his telepathy to planetary range, housed in a shielded chamber beneath the mansion. It detects the brainwave signature of the X-gene, which means it can find any mutant on Earth, usually before that mutant knows what they are — and it is how nearly every student at the school was first located.

It is also the franchise's most quietly dangerous object: a private register of every mutant alive, kept in one man's basement, which anti-mutant forces have repeatedly tried to seize or subvert. On Krakoa the technology was extended into something stranger still, storing copies of mutant minds so that the dead could be restored to new bodies.

astral_plane.name: The Astral Plane
astral_plane.desc:
The psychic dimension in which thought has form and telepaths meet as they imagine themselves, rather than as they are. Fights there are fought with will, symbol and self-image, and losing badly can leave a mind emptied while the body remains untouched — which is why the X-Men's most dangerous confrontations often look, from outside, like several people standing very still.

It is the Shadow King's native ground, the interior landscape where Legion's personalities live, and the medium through which Psylocke's psychic knife and Xavier's Cerebro both operate. The books treat it as the one battlefield where physical power counts for nothing at all.

adamantium.name: Adamantium
adamantium.desc:
An artificial alloy developed by the metallurgist Myron MacLain, which sets into a form that is effectively indestructible — the hardest substance in the setting and, once cured, essentially unworkable. Only a handful of items in the world are made of it, and every one of them is a state or corporate asset.

In mutant stories it appears almost entirely as something done to people. Weapon X bonded it to Wolverine's skeleton, a procedure only survivable because of his healing factor; Lady Deathstrike had herself rebuilt around it; Laura Kinney's claws were coated in it as a child. It is also the one thing that makes Wolverine vulnerable to Magneto, who tore it out of him through his pores.

celestials.name: The Celestials
celestials.desc:
Enormous armoured beings of almost unimaginable age who visit developing worlds, experiment on their populations and return periodically to judge the results. They do not explain themselves, and no civilisation that has tried to resist one has survived the attempt.

During their First Host on Earth one of them, Oneg the Prober, implanted a latent gene in a group of early hominids and released them unchanged — the origin the wider Marvel universe gives to the X-gene, which places mutation at the end of an experiment nobody consented to. The armour and technology Apocalypse found in a buried Celestial ship is what made him immortal and gave him the means to remake his Horsemen, so the franchise's oldest villain is powered by borrowed equipment.

horsemen.name: Horsemen of Apocalypse
horsemen.desc:
Created by Louise Simonson and Walt Simonson (1987). The four servants Apocalypse recruits and remakes whenever he wakes: War, Famine, Pestilence and Death. Each is rebuilt with Celestial technology, given power far beyond what they had, and conditioned into obedience, and the positions are refilled from whoever is available and broken enough to accept.

The pattern is consistent and deliberate. Apocalypse takes people at the moment their lives have collapsed and offers strength on the only terms they will accept, which is why the roll includes an X-Man whose wings had been amputated, a gentle Morlock who wanted to protect people, and, on separate occasions, Wolverine and Sunfire. Freeing a Horseman rarely undoes what was done to them.

northstar.name: Northstar
northstar.desc:
Created by John Byrne (1979). Jean-Paul Beaubier, a Québécois mutant with superhuman speed, flight and, when paired with his twin sister Aurora, the ability to generate blinding light. A former Olympic-level skier, he was a founding member of the Canadian team Alpha Flight before joining the X-Men and teaching at the school.

He is one of the first mainstream superhero characters to be written as openly gay, coming out in Alpha Flight #106 in 1992, and his marriage to Kyle Jinadu in Astonishing X-Men #51 twenty years later was Marvel's first same-sex wedding. His personality — abrasive, impatient, entirely uninterested in being liked — has kept him from ever being merely a milestone.

nate_grey.name: X-Man
nate_grey.desc:
Created by Jeph Loeb and Steve Skroce (1995). Nathan Grey, engineered in the Age of Apocalypse by that reality's Mister Sinister from the genetic material of Scott Summers and Jean Grey — a deliberate attempt to build the most powerful telepath and telekinetic possible, grown to adolescence in a tank. He escaped before he could be used, and crossed into the main reality when his own collapsed.

He arrived as a teenager with world-altering power, no upbringing and no timeline of his own, and met the parents who had never had him. His power burns his body out at the rate he uses it, and later stories have pushed him from wandering messiah figure to genuine threat, remaking the world according to his own idea of mercy.

husk.name: Husk
husk.desc:
Paige Guthrie, Cannonball's younger sister, who tears away her own skin to reveal a new body underneath made of whatever substance she has willed — stone, steel, rubber, diamond. The power is effective and visibly unpleasant, and the books have never let her use it without showing the cost.

She forced her way into Generation X by sheer preparation, having studied mutant abilities obsessively while waiting to develop one, and became the class's most driven and least relaxed member. The Guthrie family, with several mutant children among many siblings, is one of the franchise's few ordinary households absorbing what mutation does to it.

chamber.name: Chamber
chamber.desc:
Jonothon Starsmore, a British mutant whose psionic power detonated when it first manifested, destroying his lower face and much of his chest and leaving a furnace of energy where they had been. He survives without a jaw, lungs or a digestive system — he does not eat, drink or breathe — and speaks telepathically, which makes every conversation he has a deliberate act.

A student of Generation X under Banshee and Emma Frost, he is the franchise's most literal treatment of a mutation that ruins a life rather than enabling one: there is no costume and no off switch, and the injury is permanent and visible. His refusal of pity, and his flat English humour about it, are most of the character.

synch.name: Synch
synch.desc:
Everett Thomas, who synchronises with the powers of any mutant near him, replicating their abilities for as long as he stays in range and often using them more precisely than their owner does. It is a power that only works in company, which suited the most sociable student Generation X had.

He died young at the Academy, in an explosion set off by Emma's sister Adrienne, saving his classmates — one of the class's permanent losses until the Krakoan resurrection protocols returned him. His later story is bleaker than his first: sealed in the Vault, a facility where time runs at a vastly accelerated rate, he lived out some five centuries there alongside Laura Kinney and Darwin, and came back with every year of it in his memory.

boom_boom.name: Boom-Boom
boom_boom.desc:
Tabitha Smith, who generates spheres of plasma she calls time bombs, sized from a firecracker to a demolition charge and thrown with an unnerving lack of concern about what is nearby. She has cycled through the codenames Boom-Boom, Boomer and Meltdown as often as she has changed teams.

A runaway from an abusive home, she drifted through a series of very poor mentors — including the Beyonder and Emma Frost's Hellions — before attaching herself to the X-Terminators, the New Mutants and then X-Force, and is the most consistently irresponsible person on any roster she joins. Her long, unstable relationship with Cannonball ran through the whole X-Force period, and the books use her as the reminder that these are teenagers with weapons for hands.

shatterstar.name: Shatterstar
shatterstar.desc:
Gaveedra-Seven, bred in the Mojoverse as a gladiator for televised arena combat and trained to fight with paired blades. He was sent to the present by the rebellion against Mojo's regime — despatched to find the X-Men and recruit them, and landing among the New Mutants instead — and stayed, joining X-Force still largely unable to understand a society that does not settle questions by duel.

His origin is deliberately tangled — he has been presented as a construct, a refugee and, in some accounts, a descendant of Longshot and Dazzler — and the books have never fully resolved it. His long relationship with Rictor, first hinted at in the 1990s and later written plainly, is one of the franchise's earliest same-sex pairings.

orchis.name: Orchis
orchis.desc:
Created by Jonathan Hickman (2019). An anti-mutant organisation introduced in House of X, assembled from the remnants of every human programme that had failed to stop mutants — S.H.I.E.L.D., A.I.M., Hydra, S.T.R.I.K.E. — on the argument that the founding of Krakoa made mutant supremacy inevitable. Its leadership included the Omega Sentinel, the roboticist Doctor Alia Gregor, Doctor Stasis, the industrialist Feilong and, eventually, Moira MacTaggert.

Orchis behaves like a professional institution rather than a hate movement, more completely than any anti-mutant force before it: it built its own orbital station, cultivated public goodwill, manufactured a Nimrod, and waited years before striking. Its attack on Krakoa's third Hellfire Gala destroyed the mutant nation and began the period known as Fall of X.

generation_x.name: Generation X
generation_x.desc:
The third class of young mutants, formed in 1994 by Scott Lobdell and Chris Bachalo out of the Phalanx Covenant crossover and taught not by Xavier but by Banshee and Emma Frost at the Massachusetts Academy. The founding students were Jubilee, Husk, Chamber, Synch, Skin, M and the mute, red-skinned Penance, later joined by Mondo. Four of them — Synch, M, Husk and Skin — had first been thrown together as targets of the Phalanx, which is how they were identified at all.

The book was deliberately less heroic than its predecessors — more school story than superhero title, and more interested in what a mutation does to a teenager's life than in what it does in a fight. It ran for seventy-five issues before the Academy closed, and its casualties, Synch among them, were felt for decades afterwards.

massachusetts_academy.name: Massachusetts Academy
massachusetts_academy.desc:
An exclusive private school in western Massachusetts owned by Emma Frost and used, for years, as the Hellfire Club's recruitment pipeline: the place where promising young mutants were found before Xavier could reach them and trained as the Hellions.

After Fitzroy's Sentinels killed that class, Emma reopened the Academy with Banshee as the home of Generation X — the same building, the same headmistress, and an entirely different purpose. It is the franchise's second school, and the fact that it began as the rival of the first is what makes Emma's tenure there interesting rather than sentimental. It closed permanently when Generation X ended.

freedom_force.name: Freedom Force
freedom_force.desc:
Created by Chris Claremont (1985). Mystique's Brotherhood, converted wholesale into a federal agency. In exchange for full pardons, the team — Mystique, Destiny, Blob, Pyro and Avalanche, with the sorceress Spiral added on the government's side before their first outing — agreed to work as the American government's mutant enforcement arm under Valerie Cooper's oversight.

Their first assignment was arresting Magneto, and the sight of the X-Men's oldest enemies serving warrants in matching uniforms is one of the strangest things the 1980s books did. Despised by mutants as collaborators and by the public as terrorists in state employ, Freedom Force was eventually wrecked on missions the government was willing to spend them on.

purifiers.name: Purifiers
purifiers.desc:
Created by Chris Claremont and Brent Anderson (1982). The armed wing of William Stryker's ministry, a paramilitary movement that treats the killing of mutants as a religious obligation and recruits from his congregation. Unlike the Friends of Humanity they make no attempt at a respectable political face.

Their worst act came after M-Day, when they attacked a busload of newly depowered students from the Xavier Institute — children who no longer had any powers at all — and killed dozens of them. The Purifiers have since resurfaced under successive leaders, and they are the reason the school's security arrangements stopped being a formality.

mutant_liberation_front.name: Mutant Liberation Front
mutant_liberation_front.desc:
Created by Louise Simonson and Rob Liefeld (1990). A mutant terrorist cell founded and led by Stryfe, who wore Cable's face while running it, so that Cable's own reputation absorbed the blame for everything the group did. Its members — Wildside, Reaper, Forearm, Zero, Strobe and others — were young, expendable and largely unaware of who was really commanding them.

The MLF exists to make a specific point about Stryfe: he did not want a mutant homeland or even mutant victory, he wanted his counterpart destroyed, and an army of true believers was simply the most efficient way to arrange it. X-Force was built in large part to fight them.

hellions.name: Hellions
hellions.desc:
Created by Chris Claremont (1984). Emma Frost's students at the Massachusetts Academy and the deliberate mirror of the New Mutants: Catseye, Empath, Jetstream, Roulette, Tarot, Beef, Bevatron and, briefly, James Proudstar. They were trained as the Hellfire Club's next generation, and the rivalry between the two classes ran through the New Mutants' entire run.

They were killed almost to a member when Trevor Fitzroy loosed a wave of Sentinels on the Hellfire Club, an attack that also left Emma comatose. Their deaths ended the Club's investment in schooling and turned Emma into a teacher who had already lost one class.

askani.name: The Askani
askani.desc:
A sisterhood of the far future, founded by Rachel Summers under the name Mother Askani, dedicated to opposing Apocalypse's empire and preserving what could be salvaged of the world before it. They practise a discipline of psychic and telekinetic technique passed down as a religious order.

It was the Askani who reached back through time for the infant Nathan Summers, dying of Apocalypse's techno-organic virus, and raised him two thousand years in the future as their weapon. Cable's entire education, ethics and vocabulary come from them, which makes Rachel — a woman who is not quite his sister — the origin of everything he is.

weapon_plus.name: Weapon Plus
weapon_plus.desc:
A super-soldier programme far older and larger than the operation that took Wolverine, revealed in Grant Morrison's New X-Men. Its projects are numbered in sequence: Weapon I produced the first super-soldier serum, and the Canadian programme that bonded adamantium to Logan's skeleton was the tenth in the series.

Its later work moved from making soldiers to making weapons against mutants specifically, conducted inside a sealed artificial habitat called the World where evolution could be run at speed. Weapon XIII, the thief and liar Fantomex, escaped from it. The retrofit reframes the franchise's most personal violation as one line item in an industrial programme.

fatal_attractions.name: Fatal Attractions
fatal_attractions.desc:
A 1993 X-Men crossover (Fabian Nicieza, Scott Lobdell and others). The 1993 crossover marking the X-Men's thirtieth anniversary, in which Magneto returned from presumed death and offered mutants sanctuary aboard his orbital station Avalon. He crashed Illyana Rasputina's funeral to make the offer, and a grieving Colossus accepted, walking out on the X-Men.

When the United Nations moved against him, Magneto answered with an electromagnetic pulse that knocked out power across the planet. Xavier led a strike team to Avalon; Wolverine wounded Magneto, who tore the adamantium out of his body through his pores; and Xavier, watching, shut Magneto's mind down entirely. The fragment of Magneto left behind in his head became Onslaught.

operation_zero_tolerance.name: Operation: Zero Tolerance
operation_zero_tolerance.desc:
A 1997 X-Men crossover spearheaded by Scott Lobdell. A 1997 storyline in which Bastion was given federal authority over the mutant problem and used it to detain, interrogate and mutilate mutants under colour of law. His Prime Sentinels were the operation's innovation: ordinary people, converted by nanotechnology into weapons without their knowledge, who did not find out what they were until they activated.

Several X-Men were captured and the mansion's defences were stripped. The story's point is procedural rather than mechanical — the machinery of extermination arriving with a budget line and a warrant instead of a giant robot in the sky.

second_coming.name: Second Coming
second_coming.desc:
A 2010 X-Men crossover by the X-office. The 2010 crossover that closed the storyline begun in Messiah Complex. Cable and the teenage Hope returned from the future to a coordinated campaign of extermination: Bastion had gathered the surviving figures of the anti-mutant movement — Stephen Lang, Bolivar Trask, William Stryker, Graydon Creed and Cameron Hodge — and given a single order, to kill her.

Bastion sealed Utopia and San Francisco inside an impenetrable dome and targeted every teleporter the X-Men had. Nightcrawler died putting himself between Bastion and Hope; Cable died holding the way back open for X-Force. Hope came into her powers and ended it, and the X-Men buried more of their own than in any story since the Mutant Massacre.

schism.name: Schism
schism.desc:
The 2011 storyline by Jason Aaron that split the X-Men in two. Quentin Quire's psychic stunt at an international arms conference destroyed any hope of getting the world's Sentinel stockpiles dismantled, and in the assault that followed Cyclops ordered a teenage student to use lethal force.

Wolverine, of all people, refused to accept that children should be soldiers, and the argument ended the partnership. Cyclops kept Utopia and the militarised remnant of the team; Wolverine took half the roster back to Westchester and reopened the mansion as the Jean Grey School for Higher Learning. The two men had effectively exchanged positions since 1975, and neither found that funny.

avengers_vs_xmen.name: Avengers vs. X-Men
avengers_vs_xmen.desc:
A 2012 Marvel event by Bendis, Aaron, Brubaker, Fraction and Hickman. The 2012 crossover in which the Phoenix Force returned to Earth. Cyclops believed it was coming to restore the mutant race through Hope Summers; the Avengers believed it would destroy the planet and moved to take her into custody, and the disagreement became a war.

The Force arrived and split across five X-Men — Cyclops, Emma Frost, Namor, Colossus and Magik — who used it to end drought and famine and then to break anyone who questioned them. Cyclops took the whole of it, killed Charles Xavier when Xavier tried to shut him down, and became Dark Phoenix. Hope and the Scarlet Witch expelled the Force, and the last of it reignited the mutant gene across the world, ending M-Day.

fall_of_x.name: Fall of X
fall_of_x.desc:
The collapse of the Krakoan age, beginning at the nation's third Hellfire Gala in 2023. Orchis had spent years preparing: subverting Krakoan medicine, taking control of the gateways and building a Nimrod. The moment a new X-Men team was elected, Nimrod dropped into the party and killed most of it, and Stark-built Sentinels poured through the gates.

The attack was staged to look like a mutant atrocity against human guests, and it worked — mutants lost their island, their resurrection protocols and the public sympathy they had spent a decade acquiring. Orchis forced Xavier to send thousands through corrupted gateways, and the Five were among those stranded outside reality — which is why death became permanent again. What followed was a period of hiding, imprisonment and scattered resistance, and the end of the one era in which mutants had won.

utopia.name: Utopia
utopia.desc:
An island raised in San Francisco Bay by the X-Club, the team's science division, from the sunken hulk of Magneto's first Asteroid M. Cyclops ordered it brought up and declared it a sovereign mutant nation when Norman Osborn — running national security during his brief period of official respectability — sent the Dark Avengers to occupy the city and put the X-Men under martial law. For several years the rock was home to nearly every mutant left alive after M-Day.

It is Cyclops's version of Genosha and Asteroid M — a defensible rock with a flag — and it marks the period in which the X-Men stopped being a school with a team attached and became a state with an army. Bastion sealed it under a dome during Second Coming, the Schism divided its population between Cyclops and Wolverine, and when Cyclops fell at the end of the war with the Avengers the island came down with him — breaking apart and sinking deeper than it had been before. Magneto's base has now failed as a home for mutants twice.

kwannon.name: Kwannon
kwannon.desc:
Created by Fabian Nicieza and Andy Kubert (1992). A Japanese assassin, once employed by Lord Nyoirin and the lover of the Hand's Matsu'o Tsurayaba, left brain-damaged after a duel with him on a clifftop. When Betsy Braddock washed ashore amnesiac nearby, Matsu'o had the sorceress Spiral swap the two women's minds and intermingle their genetics, so that each carried some of the other's memories and abilities.

In Betsy's body and believing herself to be Betsy, she joined the X-Men as Revanche, and died of the Legacy Virus having recovered her true memories, asking Matsu'o to end it. Decades of publication later the two women were separated and restored, and Kwannon returned in her own body as Psylocke — the name that had been worn on her face by someone else.

multiple_man.name: Multiple Man
multiple_man.desc:
James Madrox, who produces a duplicate of himself every time he is struck, each one an autonomous version of him carrying a single facet of his personality. Reabsorbing a duplicate returns its memories and experience, which means he can send copies away to learn skills and take them back years later.

He grew up in isolation on a Kansas farm, was taken in by Moira MacTaggert on Muir Island, and served in the government X-Factor before running X-Factor Investigations, a mutant detective agency in Mutant Town. The power is a comedy premise that his own book turned into a study of identity: he is never entirely sure which of him is the original.

strong_guy.name: Strong Guy
strong_guy.desc:
Guido Carosella, who absorbs kinetic energy directed at him and converts it into strength — a power that has permanently distorted his body, since the energy has to go somewhere and his frame took the difference. He is enormous, top-heavy and in constant discomfort, and he covers all of it with jokes.

A former bodyguard to the rock star Lila Cheney, he served in the government X-Factor and later in X-Factor Investigations, where he functioned as the muscle and, more usefully, as the person willing to say the thing everyone else was avoiding. His heart condition, caused by the strain of his own power, has killed him more than once.

siryn.name: Siryn
siryn.desc:
Theresa Rourke Cassidy, Banshee's daughter, with the same sonic scream and the same capacity for flight, raised in Ireland by her father's cousin Black Tom Cassidy — a career criminal who partnered the Juggernaut — and used in his work before she was old enough to refuse. Sean did not know she existed for years.

She served with X-Force and later with X-Factor Investigations, where her long relationship with Jamie Madrox gave both characters their best material. Her father's death left her the last of that line, and the books have generally treated her as someone carrying a legacy she did not ask for and will not put down.

quentin_quire.name: Quentin Quire
quentin_quire.desc:
Kid Omega, a pink-haired telepath of enormous potential and no self-restraint, introduced in Grant Morrison's New X-Men as the school's prize student and its first genuine radical. Convinced that Xavier's teaching was a polite fiction, he formed the Omega Gang and led a riot that killed people.

He is the character the franchise uses whenever it wants mutant politics articulated by someone too young and too clever to be careful. His stunt at an arms conference — forcing world leaders to confess their secrets on camera — destroyed the case for disarmament and set off the Schism, and he was later a Phoenix host in one possible future.

blink.name: Blink
blink.desc:
Clarice Ferguson, a young mutant who opens teleportation portals with thrown crystalline shards, capable of moving anything — including, dangerously, parts of things. Found and used by the Phalanx during their attempt to assimilate the next generation of mutants, she died turning her power on them to free the students who became Generation X.

Her counterpart from the Age of Apocalypse proved far more durable than the original: that Blink survived her reality's collapse and became the central figure of a long-running series about refugees moving between parallel worlds, making her one of the few characters whose alternate self outgrew the source.

monet.name: M
monet.desc:
Monet St. Croix, a founding member of Generation X, with superhuman strength, flight, durability and telepathy, and an aristocratic certainty that she is the most capable person in any room — a self-assessment the books rarely contradict.

Her family is the complication. Her brother Marius — Emplate, who survives by feeding on mutant bone marrow — trapped her in the mute, red-skinned form the team knew as Penance, as punishment for defying him. Her younger twin sisters Claudette and Nicole then merged into a copy of her to hide it, so that for the team's first year the M they knew was not Monet at all — and freeing her meant putting the twins into that body instead. Her later career runs through X-Factor Investigations and the mutant teams of the Krakoan age.

rictor.name: Rictor
rictor.desc:
Julio Esteban Richter, a Mexican mutant who generates seismic waves powerful enough to bring down a building, recruited young and passed between the X-Terminators, the New Mutants, X-Force and X-Factor. His powers were taken from him on M-Day, and he spent years as one of the most prominent depowered mutants in the books before regaining them.

His relationship with Shatterstar, hinted at in the 1990s and written plainly in X-Factor, is one of the earliest sustained same-sex romances in mainstream superhero comics, and the pairing of an earthquake and a gladiator has outlasted most of the couples around it.

longshot.name: Longshot
longshot.desc:
An artificial humanoid engineered in the Mojoverse as a slave performer, with hollow bones, three fingers on each hand and a psionic power that bends probability in his favour — but only when he acts selflessly and without doubt. Cheating with it does not work.

He escaped to Earth as an amnesiac rebel, joined the X-Men during their Australian period, and formed a long attachment to Dazzler. His arrival brought the Mojoverse into the X-books permanently, and later stories have proposed him as Shatterstar's father, a piece of continuity the franchise has never fully settled.

spiral.name: Spiral
spiral.desc:
Rita Wayword, a six-armed sorceress and swordswoman who serves Mojo and hates him, having been rebuilt by him into the thing she is. Her Body Shoppe performs the same service on others: bodies remade to order, at a price the customer rarely understands in advance.

Her interventions have permanently altered several X-Men. She fitted Psylocke with cybernetic eyes for Mojo's broadcasts, and it was Spiral who performed the body swap between Betsy Braddock and Kwannon at Matsu'o's request, intermingling the two women's genetics as she did it. She has also served in Freedom Force, and she is one of the franchise's rare villains written as a victim who kept working.

trevor_fitzroy.name: Trevor Fitzroy
trevor_fitzroy.desc:
A time-travelling killer from the same future as Bishop, who drains the life energy of others to open temporal portals — every trip he takes is paid for with someone's death. Bishop's pursuit of him is the reason both men are in the present at all.

He joined the Upstarts, a contest in which the wealthy and the powerful murdered prominent mutants for points, and made his opening move by loosing a wave of Sentinels on the Hellfire Club. They killed Donald Pierce's Reavers, killed almost all of Emma Frost's Hellions and left Emma herself in a coma — one afternoon's work that reshaped three separate corners of the franchise.

omega_sentinel.name: Omega Sentinel
omega_sentinel.desc:
Karima Shapandar, an Indian police officer converted without her consent into a Prime Sentinel by Bastion's programme — a human being with a mutant-killing machine installed inside her, held in check only by her own will. For years she was an ally of the X-Men and a study in what surviving that conversion costs.

In the Krakoan era an Omega Sentinel carrying the memories of a future in which the machines had already won became a founder of Orchis, working from the conviction that she had seen how this ends. It is the franchise's bleakest use of the character: the victim of the Sentinel programme becoming its most effective architect.

cameron_hodge.name: Cameron Hodge
cameron_hodge.desc:
Warren Worthington's old college friend and X-Factor's public relations manager, who devised the team's mutant-hunter cover story — and who was, throughout, the leader of the anti-mutant paramilitary organisation the Right, using his access to feed the panic he was publicly managing.

His betrayal cost Warren his wings and very nearly his life. Beheaded and still talking, he was later kept alive and eventually merged with the techno-organic Phalanx, becoming something enormous and mechanical. He is the franchise's purest study of institutional betrayal: the danger was not the robot outside but the man writing the press releases.

fabian_cortez.name: Fabian Cortez
fabian_cortez.desc:
An Acolyte whose power boosts the abilities of other mutants to enormous levels while burning them out from the inside — a gift he presents as devotion and uses as a murder weapon. He founded the Acolytes in Magneto's name and preached his gospel with more fervour than Magneto had ever asked for.

He then betrayed Magneto at the first opportunity, sabotaging Asteroid M and leaving him to die so that the movement would have a martyr and Cortez would have a movement. He later joined the Upstarts, competing to kill prominent mutants for points, which is a fair summary of his convictions.

fall_of_the_mutants.name: Fall of the Mutants
fall_of_the_mutants.desc: The 1988 crossover (cover-dated January to March), running three issues each through Uncanny X-Men (#225-227), X-Factor (#24-26) and New Mutants (#59-61), written by Chris Claremont and Louise Simonson. Unusually the three arcs were bound by theme rather than a shared plot, each team facing a separate crisis. In the Uncanny story the X-Men appear to die on live television defeating the demonic Adversary in Dallas, then secretly relocate to the Australian outback; in X-Factor, Apocalypse captures the wingless Angel and remakes him as the Horseman Death, who becomes Archangel; in New Mutants, Cypher is killed.

x_tinction_agenda.name: X-Tinction Agenda
x_tinction_agenda.desc: The 1990-91 crossover (Uncanny X-Men #270-272, X-Factor #60-62, New Mutants #95-97) by Chris Claremont and Louise Simonson, with early art by Jim Lee and Rob Liefeld. The mutant-exploiting island state of Genosha, which turns captured mutants into enslaved "Mutates," abducts several X-Men and New Mutants; the three scattered teams reunite to invade the country. Engineered by the resurrected, now fully cyborg Cameron Hodge, the story ends with Hodge's defeat and Genosha's apartheid order collapsing, and marks the first time the fractured X-teams fight together again.

x_cutioners_song.name: X-Cutioner's Song
x_cutioners_song.desc: The twelve-part 1992-93 crossover (Uncanny X-Men, X-Men vol. 2, X-Factor, X-Force) by Scott Lobdell, Fabian Nicieza and Peter David. Stryfe, Cable's clone, disguises himself as Cable and shoots Professor Xavier with a techno-organic-virus bullet during a public concert, sending the X-teams to war with one another and with X-Force. Behind it lies Mister Sinister's long feud with Apocalypse over the Summers bloodline. Xavier survives, Stryfe is seemingly destroyed dragging Cable into a time portal, and the canister he leaves behind seeds the Legacy Virus.

house_of_x.name: House of X / Powers of X
house_of_x.desc: The twin six-issue miniseries of 2019 by Jonathan Hickman, with art by Pepe Larraz and R. B. Silva, that reset the entire franchise and opened the Krakoan Age. Xavier establishes the living island of Krakoa as a sovereign mutant nation, trading its unique flora as medicine for recognition, while the interwoven timelines reveal that Moira MacTaggert is a secretly reincarnating Omega-level mutant reliving her life. A group of five mutants, "the Five," combine powers to resurrect any fallen mutant with memory intact, shifting mutant stories from survival to sovereignty.

original_x_men.name: The Original X-Men
original_x_men.desc: Created by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby (1963). The team's 1963 debut in X-Men #1 by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby. Professor Charles Xavier gathers five teenage mutants — Cyclops, Marvel Girl (Jean Grey), Beast, Angel and Iceman — into a private school that doubles as a strike team, meant to prove that mutants and humans can coexist, and first pits them against Magneto and his Brotherhood. A second-string Lee/Kirby title that never found a wide readership, the book lapsed into reprints by 1970, but this founding class established the premise, the mentor and the core cast on which the entire franchise was later rebuilt.

second_genesis.name: Second Genesis
second_genesis.desc: The 1975 relaunch in Giant-Size X-Men #1 by Len Wein and Dave Cockrum — the first new X-Men story after five years of reprints. To rescue the captured original team from the living island Krakoa, Professor X assembles an older, international line-up: Storm, Nightcrawler, Colossus, Thunderbird, Banshee, Sunfire and Wolverine, joining holdover Cyclops. Most of the originals then departed. Chris Claremont, then Wein's editorial assistant, took over the monthly title from Uncanny X-Men #94 and, with Cockrum and later John Byrne, spent sixteen years turning the book into Marvel's flagship.

deadly_genesis.name: Deadly Genesis
deadly_genesis.desc: The 2006 six-issue miniseries by Ed Brubaker and Trevor Hairsine that retconned the team's origins. In the wake of House of M, a released surge of mutant energy frees Vulcan (Gabriel Summers), and it emerges that before the Giant-Size team, Professor X had sent an earlier, hastily-trained squad — Vulcan, Petra, Sway and Darwin — to Krakoa, where most were killed. Xavier erased the survivors' and students' memories to bury the failure. The story kills Banshee, exposes Xavier's deepest deception, and sets Vulcan on the path to war with the Shi'ar Empire.

necrosha.name: Necrosha
necrosha.desc: The 2009-10 crossover by Craig Kyle, Christopher Yost, Mike Carey and Zeb Wells, running through X-Force, X-Men: Legacy and New Mutants. Using a transmode virus supplied by her servant Eli Bard, the immortal sorceress Selene reanimates thousands of dead mutants on Genosha — the island still scarred by the Sentinel massacre — as an undead army, aiming to consume their souls and ascend to godhood. X-Force and the X-Men fight through the risen dead, among them Thunderbird and Banshee, to bring her down.

brood_saga.name: The Brood Saga
brood_saga.desc: The 1982-83 cosmic storyline in Uncanny X-Men #155-167 by Chris Claremont with artists Dave Cockrum and Paul Smith. The insectoid, parasitic Brood — who breed by implanting eggs that transform the host into one of their own — capture the X-Men and infect them, forcing the team to fight across space to stop their own metamorphosis before it completes. In the course of it Carol Danvers is reborn as the star-powered Binary and departs with the Starjammers, while Xavier, implanted with a Brood queen, is left needing a wholly new cloned body. It is often ranked second only to the Dark Phoenix Saga among the team's cosmic epics.

proteus_saga.name: The Proteus Saga
proteus_saga.desc: The 1979 storyline in Uncanny X-Men #125-128 by Chris Claremont and John Byrne, an early peak of their partnership. On Muir Island, Moira MacTaggert's imprisoned son Kevin — the reality-warping mutant Proteus, or "Mutant X" — breaks free and begins burning out human bodies to sustain himself, bending reality wherever he goes. The X-Men, reunited there with Jean Grey, are overpowered until they exploit his single weakness, metal, and Colossus strikes the killing blow. The arc deepened Moira's tragic history and helped set the series on its collision course with the Dark Phoenix Saga.

battle_of_the_atom.name: Battle of the Atom
battle_of_the_atom.desc: The 2013 ten-part crossover marking the X-Men's 50th anniversary, by Brian Michael Bendis, Jason Aaron and Brian Wood. After Beast pulled the time-displaced original five X-Men into the present to confront Cyclops over Xavier's death, their continued presence begins to unravel the timeline; a team of X-Men from the future arrives to force the teenagers home, and the various factions fracture over whether to comply. The event fixed the time-displaced teens as ongoing characters and sharpened the divide between Cyclops's militant camp and Wolverine's Jean Grey School.

inhumans_vs_xmen.name: Death of X / Inhumans vs. X-Men
inhumans_vs_xmen.desc: The 2016-17 war between mutants and Inhumans, told across the prequel Death of X (Jeff Lemire and Charles Soule, 2016) and the main event Inhumans vs. X-Men (Soule and Lemire, 2016-17, art by Leinil Yu and others). The Terrigen Mists that awaken Inhuman powers prove lethal to mutants, spreading a sterilising plague called M-Pox and threatening mutantkind with extinction. Death of X reveals Cyclops died confronting the Terrigen cloud; in the main series a mutant strike, driven by Emma Frost's grief and vengeance, moves to destroy the cloud before it wipes them out — and succeeds, lifting the extinction threat.

x_of_swords.name: X of Swords
x_of_swords.desc: The 2020 twenty-two-part crossover ("Ten of Swords") by Jonathan Hickman and Tini Howard, running across the Krakoan-era X-titles. The mutant land of Arakko — Krakoa's ancient sundered other half, ruled in exile by Apocalypse's long-lost family in the demon realm of Amenth — threatens to break through and invade. To decide the matter the cosmic arbiter Saturnyne stages a contest in which ten champions from each side, each bearing an appointed sword, must fight. The tournament collapses into open war between Krakoa and Arakko and permanently reshapes the young mutant nation.

alpha_flight.name: Alpha Flight
alpha_flight.desc: Canada's premier super-hero team, created by John Byrne and Chris Claremont and first appearing in Uncanny X-Men #120-121 (1979). Conceived to flesh out Wolverine's backstory — he had served the Canadian government's Department H before joining the X-Men — the team debuted attempting to forcibly repatriate him, then set the grudge aside. Led by James MacDonald Hudson (Guardian, earlier Vindicator and Weapon Alpha), its founding roster included Northstar, Aurora, Sasquatch, Shaman and Snowbird. Byrne spun the group into its own long-running series in 1983.

department_h.name: Department H
department_h.desc: A branch of Canada's Department of National Defence charged with overseeing and countering superhuman activity. Inspired by the debut of the Fantastic Four, James MacDonald Hudson built its response programme, the Flight, and recruited the feral operative Wolverine — already a Department H agent — as its first member. After Wolverine left to join the X-Men, Hudson reorganised the programme into the tiered Alpha, Beta and Gamma Flights, with Alpha Flight as the frontline team. Department H is the institutional root of Wolverine's pre-X-Men history.

the_twelve.name: The Twelve
the_twelve.desc: A prophesied group of twelve powerful mutants long said to be destined to defeat Apocalypse and usher in a mutant golden age. In the 2000 crossover "Apocalypse: The Twelve" by Chris Claremont, Alan Davis and others, the legend is revealed as Apocalypse's own fabrication: he gathers the twelve — Professor X, Magneto, Cyclops, Jean Grey, Storm, Iceman, Polaris, Sunfire, Bishop, Cable, Mikhail Rasputin and the Living Monolith — to drain their combined power and pour it into a new near-omnipotent host, Nate Grey. Cyclops sacrifices himself, taking Nate's place and merging with Apocalypse.

quiet_council.name: Quiet Council of Krakoa
quiet_council.desc: Created by Jonathan Hickman (2019). The governing body of the mutant nation of Krakoa, established in the Krakoan Age from 2019 and the political heart of Kieron Gillen's Immortal X-Men. Its seats are arranged in four seasonal tables — Autumn (Xavier, Magneto, Apocalypse), Winter (Mystique, Exodus, Selene), Spring (Emma Frost, Sebastian Shaw, Kate Pryde) and Summer (Storm, Nightcrawler, Colossus) — with a seat speaking for Krakoa itself. It writes and enforces Krakoan law, and its faction-ridden intrigue drives much of the era; membership shifted over time as Apocalypse, Magneto and Jean Grey left and Destiny, Hope Summers and Colossus took their places.

the_five.name: The Five
the_five.desc: Created by Jonathan Hickman (2019). The five mutants whose combined powers make death impermanent on Krakoa — the engine of the resurrection protocols introduced in House of X. The process chains their abilities: Egg grows a blank husk, Proteus makes it viable by warping reality, Elixir fertilises and matures it with biokinesis, Tempus ages it through time, and Hope Summers harmonises the other four so they act as one.
