A telepath, usually Professor X working from a Cerebro backup, then imprints the dead mutant's mind into the new body. Their work turned death into a revolving door for mutantkind.

x_statix.name: X-Statix
x_statix.desc: A team of media-obsessed, celebrity super-hero mutants created by Peter Milligan and Mike Allred, who took over X-Force (vol. 2) in 2001 before the book was retitled X-Statix. A pointed satire of fame and reality television, the team — led by Mister Sensitive (the Orphan) and including U-Go Girl, Doop and the Anarchist — treated superheroics as a sponsor-driven entertainment brand, and its members died with startling regularity. Most of the original line-up was killed off by 2004; several were later resurrected in the Krakoan era as the X-Cellent.

holocaust.name: Holocaust
holocaust.desc: A villain of the Age of Apocalypse, the monstrous son of that reality's Apocalypse, created by Scott Lobdell and Joe Madureira in 1995. Originally a being of raw energy called Nemesis, he was reduced to a burnt husk when Magneto blasted away his flesh; he thereafter renamed himself Holocaust and sealed his energies inside a crystalline containment armour, sustaining his form by draining the life-force of others. One of Apocalypse's Horsemen, he murdered that reality's Scarlet Witch and warred with Rogue's X-Men, and in the storyline's finale crossed over into the main Marvel reality to keep menacing the X-Men.

sugar_man.name: Sugar Man
sugar_man.desc: A grotesque, many-limbed mutant geneticist introduced in the Age of Apocalypse in 1995, with no prior counterpart in the main Marvel reality. In that timeline he was a torturer and overseer of Apocalypse's mutant breeding and processing pens. In the crossover's finale he fled into the past of the main universe and, arriving decades early, festered in continuity — most notably shaping the horrors of Genosha's slave state — before the present-day X-Men finally caught up with him. He is defined by cruelty, cunning and a long prehensile tongue.

abyss.name: Abyss
abyss.desc: A Horseman of the Age of Apocalypse, the mutant Nils Styger, revealed as the half-brother of Nightcrawler. His body is a living void: he can unravel into ribbons coiled around a bottomless darkness that draws in and consumes whatever comes near. In that reality he served Apocalypse until Banshee sacrificed himself to kill him. A separate version later appeared in the main Marvel timeline where, Apocalypse never having conquered the world, he was no villain at all.

forearm.name: Forearm
forearm.desc: A founding member of the Mutant Liberation Front, created by Louise Simonson and Rob Liefeld in New Mutants #86 (1990). Michael McCain is a hulking mutant with two extra arms growing from his torso and the superhuman strength, stamina and durability to make them count — a brute enforcer in Stryfe's terrorist cell. Forearm proved one of the MLF's most durable fixtures, surviving through the team's changes of leadership and repeated imprisonments, and in later years turned up among the Krakoan-era Dark Riders.

reaper.name: Reaper
reaper.desc: A founding member of the Mutant Liberation Front, introduced by Louise Simonson and Rob Liefeld in 1990. Pantu Hurageb is a bio-electric mutant who wields a scythe and can paralyse or kill with a touch that disrupts a victim's nervous system. A cold and vicious operative in Stryfe's ranks, he lost a hand to Shatterstar in X-Force's very first clash with the group, and stayed with the MLF through its later incarnations under Reignfire and Wildside.

wildside.name: Wildside
wildside.desc: A founding and later leading member of the Mutant Liberation Front, created by Louise Simonson and Rob Liefeld in 1990. Richard Gill projects hallucinations so vivid the mind treats them as real, in time potent enough to genuinely wound. Sadistic and chaotic, he came to want, in his own words, simply "an excuse for mayhem," and eventually rose to head a version of the MLF. Even after settling into an uneasy retirement on Krakoa he stayed thoroughly unpleasant, and was recruited as a covert agent by the anti-mutant organisation Orchis.

thumbelina.name: Thumbelina
thumbelina.desc: A founding member of the Mutant Liberation Front, created by Louise Simonson and Rob Liefeld in 1990. Kristina Anderson can shrink to minuscule size while proportionally increasing her density and strength, making her a tiny, dense and dangerous striker in Stryfe's cell. She was among the MLF rounded up and imprisoned during X-Cutioner's Song. In later years she left crime behind, and as a citizen of Krakoa served with the mutant espionage agency S.W.O.R.D.

zero.name: Zero
zero.desc: The Mutant Liberation Front's teleporter, a techno-organic android built in the far future and brought to the present by Stryfe, whom he served as escape-hatch, transport and messenger. Zero relocated the MLF instantly in and out of its raids, making the team maddeningly hard to pin down. After breaking from Stryfe and his creator Tyler, Zero undertook an unusual arc — largely in the pages of Excalibur — toward genuine sentience and a life of his own, a strange redemption for a thing built purely as a weapon.

scalphunter.name: Scalphunter
scalphunter.desc: A Marauder and Mister Sinister's most trusted assassin, created by Chris Claremont and John Romita Jr. in Uncanny X-Men #210-211 (1986). John Greycrow can instinctively operate — and often generate — any weapon he lays hands on, making him a walking armoury and the field leader of Sinister's kill-team. He was a central perpetrator of the Mutant Massacre and, infamously, the one who shot Madelyne Pryor. In the Krakoan era he broke with the Marauders, reclaimed his birth name Greycrow, and served among the Hellions.

arclight.name: Arclight
arclight.desc: A Marauder created by Chris Claremont and John Romita Jr. in 1986. Philippa Sontag, a former US Army soldier, unleashes concussive shockwaves and seismic tremors from her body, backed by superhuman strength and durability. One of Mister Sinister's core assassins, she took part in the Mutant Massacre of the Morlocks and stayed a fixture of the Marauders — and of Sinister's vault of Marauder clones — through their many deaths and resurrections.

harpoon.name: Harpoon
harpoon.desc: A Marauder created by Chris Claremont and John Romita Jr. in 1986. The Inuit mutant Kodiak Noatak charges thrown weapons — his signature energy harpoons — with a destructive bio-energy that can also disrupt other mutants' powers on contact. A killer in Mister Sinister's employ, he took part in the Mutant Massacre, where one of his spears left Kitty Pryde locked in an intangible, phasing state that nearly killed her.

vertigo.name: Vertigo
vertigo.desc: A Marauder created by Chris Claremont and John Romita Jr. in 1986. Vertigo projects a psionic field that overwhelms a victim's balance and equilibrium, inducing crippling disorientation, nausea and collapse — a quiet but devastating power able to drop even formidable mutants. One of Mister Sinister's assassins, she took part in the Mutant Massacre and, like her teammates, was repeatedly killed and re-cloned by Sinister. (She is distinct from the Savage Land Mutate of the same name.)

riptide.name: Riptide
riptide.desc: A Marauder created by Chris Claremont and John Romita Jr. in 1986. Janos Quested spins his body at blinding speed, throwing off a vortex that flings razor-sharp calcified projectiles like a living cyclone of blades. Savage and unstable, he was one of Mister Sinister's Mutant Massacre killers — and pushed the normally gentle Colossus so far during that slaughter that the armoured X-Man snapped his neck, a rare killing that haunted Piotr for years afterward.

scrambler.name: Scrambler
scrambler.desc: A Marauder created by Chris Claremont and John Romita Jr. in 1986. Kim Il Sung can scramble any system he touches — disrupting machinery, biological processes or another mutant's powers and sending them into sudden malfunction and loss of control. One of Mister Sinister's Mutant Massacre assassins, he was among the Marauders seemingly killed in the final battle on Muir Island, only to return later as one of Sinister's ever-ready clones.

black_tom.name: Black Tom Cassidy
black_tom.desc: A mutant criminal created by Chris Claremont and Dave Cockrum in X-Men #101 (1976), the cousin and lifelong rival of Banshee. Thomas Cassidy channels destructive energy — concussive force and heat — through wood, usually the shillelagh he carries, and he and Banshee are naturally immune to each other's powers. Having gambled away the family estate of Cassidy Keep to Sean, he turned to crime, befriended Cain Marko in prison and became the longtime partner and scheming brains behind the Juggernaut. For years he secretly raised Banshee's daughter Siryn as his own protégée before the truth came out.

sauron.name: Sauron
sauron.desc: A mutate villain created by Roy Thomas and Neal Adams in X-Men #59-60 (1969). Dr. Karl Lykos, cursed to drain life-energy to survive, absorbed too much mutant power and transformed into Sauron — a monstrous, pterodactyl-like predator he named for Tolkien's dark lord. In that form he flies, hypnotises his prey and feeds on mutant energies. A recurring foe long tied to the Savage Land, he lurches between villainy and reluctant heroism as Lykos struggles to keep the beast within him caged.

arcade.name: Arcade
arcade.desc: A flamboyant, homicidal assassin-for-hire created by Chris Claremont and John Byrne in Marvel Team-Up #65-66 (1978). Arcade disdains guns for elaborate, death-trap-laden amusement parks called Murderworld, in which he toys with his targets for sport as much as for pay. A frequent tormentor of the X-Men and Spider-Man — hired more than once to kill them, including by Black Tom Cassidy and the Juggernaut — he treats murder as an art form and an elaborate game.

nastirh.name: N'astirh
nastirh.desc: A scheming demon of Limbo, created by Louise Simonson and Jon Bogdanove in X-Factor #32 (1988) and a central architect of the Inferno crossover. A master of both sorcery and a techno-organic virus, N'astirh manipulated Madelyne Pryor, the Goblin Queen, into helping him rip open a portal between Limbo and Earth above Manhattan — part of a scheme to conquer both realms. His invasion was ultimately repelled and he was destroyed, leaving his fellow demon S'ym to seize Limbo's throne.

sym.name: S'ym
sym.desc: A hulking demon of Limbo, created by Chris Claremont and Brent Anderson in Uncanny X-Men #160 (1982). S'ym wields immense superhuman strength — greater than Colossus's, and enough to snap one of Wolverine's claws — paired with a crude, brutal cunning. Once bound to serve Illyana Rasputin as Limbo's ruler, he chafed against her, and allying with N'astirh he seized the realm during Inferno; after N'astirh's death he was left its sole master.

belasco.name: Belasco
belasco.desc: An ancient demon-sorcerer, created by Bruce Jones and Brent Anderson in Ka-Zar the Savage #11 (1982) and woven into X-Men lore as the corrupter of Magik. Belasco once ruled the hell-dimension of Limbo and schemed to summon his masters, the Elder Gods, to remake the Earth. He abducted the child Illyana Rasputin and spent years twisting her toward darkness as his intended vessel, the Darkchylde — until she mastered the Soulsword, defeated him and took Limbo for herself.

brood.name: The Brood
brood.desc: A ravenous insectoid alien race resembling monstrous scorpion-wasps, created by Chris Claremont and Dave Cockrum and introduced in Uncanny X-Men #155 (1982). The Brood breed parasitically, implanting an egg in a host whose body and powers are consumed and remade into a new Brood while a fading shadow of the original mind lingers in torment. Ruled by a Queen and driven purely to spread, they menaced the X-Men most memorably in the Brood Saga, when they infected the entire team — a piece of cosmic body-horror in the mould of the era's alien-invasion films.

death_horseman.name: Death (Horseman)
death_horseman.desc: The most storied of Apocalypse's four Horsemen, a title passed down a long line of mutants forcibly converted to his cause. The first and most famous bearer was Angel — Warren Worthington, whom Apocalypse rescued after his wings were maimed and remade with lethal bio-metallic wings, the transformation that turned him into Archangel. Set against his fellow Horsemen for leadership, Death emerged victorious. Later mutants twisted into the role of Death include Caliban, Wolverine, Gambit and Psylocke, each granted a dark, augmented power set.

war_horseman.name: War (Horseman)
war_horseman.desc: Apocalypse's Horseman of War, the role of raw destruction. The first modern bearer was Abraham Kieros, an embittered ex-soldier and paraplegic whom Apocalypse restored and empowered to unleash devastating force. Over the millennia and across timelines the mantle has fallen to a striking range of others — among them the Hulk, the Shi'ar renegade Deathbird, the cosmic Gazer and even Colossus — each remade into a living engine of war in service of Apocalypse's creed of survival of the fittest.

famine_horseman.name: Famine (Horseman)
famine_horseman.desc: Apocalypse's Horseman of Famine, whose power is to drain and wither — sapping the strength, will or life from others. The first bearer was Autumn Rolfson, an isolated, anorexic teenager whose resentment made her easy for Apocalypse to twist. The role has since passed to figures such as Rory Campbell (better known as the Sentinel-hunter Ahab) and Sunfire, each augmented into an agent of decay and starvation for Apocalypse's cause.

pestilence_horseman.name: Pestilence (Horseman)
pestilence_horseman.desc: Apocalypse's Horseman of Pestilence, the bringer of disease. The first modern bearer was Plague, a Morlock recruited during the Mutant Massacre whose powers already spread sickness. The role has since been carried by others, including the Morlock Caliban and, in later incarnations, Polaris — each remade by Apocalypse into a vector of plague, corruption and contagion.

cecilia_reyes.name: Cecilia Reyes
cecilia_reyes.desc: A Puerto Rican trauma surgeon and reluctant mutant hero, created by Scott Lobdell and Carlos Pacheco in X-Men #65 (1997). Cecilia Reyes involuntarily throws up a protective psioplasmic force field whenever she is threatened. Wanting nothing to do with heroics, she turned Xavier down flat — but when the anti-mutant Operation: Zero Tolerance exposed and hunted her, she was forced onto the X-Men, growing close to Beast before drifting back to medicine. In the Krakoan era she took up practice in the mutant nation's Healing Gardens.

maggott.name: Maggott
maggott.desc: One of the strangest mutants ever to wear an X, created by Scott Lobdell and Joe Madureira in Uncanny X-Men #345 (1997). Japheth, a flamboyant South African who speaks in exaggerated Afrikaans slang, externalises his digestive system as two huge sentient slugs, Eany and Meany; they devour matter and return to his body, and while they feed he gains vast superhuman strength. Briefly an X-Man and later a passing member of Generation X, he never quite found a lasting place on the team.

joseph.name: Joseph
joseph.desc: A clone of Magneto, created by Scott Lobdell and Roger Cruz in Uncanny X-Men #327 (1995). Found near a South American orphanage with no memory, Joseph was long taken to be a mysteriously de-aged, amnesiac Magneto; he joined the X-Men and courted Rogue while trying to atone for the older man's crimes. He was ultimately revealed as a clone grown by the mutant Astra, and died battling the true Magneto — only to be resurrected years later by Astra as a warped, villainous shadow of himself.

fantomex.name: Fantomex
fantomex.desc: A suave, morally slippery adventurer created by Grant Morrison and Igor Kordey in New X-Men #128 (2002). A product of the Weapon Plus program — Weapon XIII — Fantomex has three brains, an external nervous system that manifests as a sentient techno-organic flying craft named E.V.A., a healing factor, and "misdirection," the power to weave hypnotic illusions. A thief and mercenary as often as a hero, he became a fixture of the black-ops Uncanny X-Force.

sage.name: Sage
sage.desc: A mutant with a mind like a supercomputer, created by Chris Claremont and John Byrne as Tessa in Uncanny X-Men #132 (1980) and reintroduced as Sage in 2001. Possessing perfect recall, superhuman analytical processing and the rare gift of 'jump-starting' another mutant's latent powers, she was first presented as Sebastian Shaw's cool aide in the Hellfire Club — until a retcon revealed her as one of Xavier's earliest recruits, planted inside the Club as his deep-cover spy for years. She later led and served on numerous X-teams, from X-Treme X-Men to Krakoa's X-Force.

darwin.name: Darwin
darwin.desc: A mutant whose body adapts instantly to any threat, created by Ed Brubaker and Pete Woods in X-Men: Deadly Genesis #2 (2006). Armando Muñoz's reactive evolution lets him survive almost anything — breathing underwater, shrugging off the vacuum of space, turning to stone or energy as danger demands. Introduced retroactively as a member of the secret team Xavier sent to Krakoa before the all-new X-Men, Darwin was the rare survivor of that doomed mission — his powers simply refusing to let him die — and later worked with X-Factor Investigations.

petra.name: Petra
petra.desc: A geokinetic mutant able to shape and command earth and stone, created by Ed Brubaker in X-Men: Deadly Genesis (2006). One of the young mutants Moira MacTaggert secretly trained and Xavier sent to Krakoa to rescue the original X-Men, Petra died on that catastrophic mission alongside most of her team — a death Xavier concealed for decades. In her last moments she used her powers in a desperate bid to shield her surviving teammates Darwin and Vulcan.

sway.name: Sway
sway.desc: Suzanne Chan, a mutant able to slow and distort the flow of time, created by Ed Brubaker in X-Men: Deadly Genesis (2006). One of the secret rescue team Xavier dispatched to Krakoa, she was cut down there almost as soon as the mission arrived, when it went horribly wrong. Her death, like those of her teammates, was hidden away by Xavier for years afterward, surfacing only when Vulcan returned to expose what had happened.

feral.name: Feral
feral.desc: A savage, cat-like mutant created by Rob Liefeld and Fabian Nicieza during the launch of X-Force in 1991. Maria Callasantos — elder sister of the mutant Thornn — has fur, fangs, retractable claws, a prehensile tail, feral agility and a healing factor, matched by a violent temper shaped by a brutal childhood. A founding member of Cable's X-Force, she was volatile even among that hard-edged team, and later defected to the terrorist Mutant Liberation Front.

hellion.name: Hellion
hellion.desc: Julian Keller, an arrogant, wealthy telekinetic, created by Nunzio DeFilippis, Christina Weir and Keron Grant in New Mutants vol. 2 #2 (2003). A standout of the Xavier Institute's student body and leader of its Hellions training squad, Hellion wields telekinesis powerful enough to fly and shatter walls — power he could barely control after Emma Frost unlocked its full potential to save X-23's life. Embittered by the X-Men's repeated failures to protect his generation, he later lost his hands to Lady Deathstrike and replaced them with telekinetic constructs.

surge.name: Surge
surge.desc: Noriko Ashida, a Japanese runaway, introduced in the New X-Men: Academy X era (2003). Surge's body constantly absorbs ambient static electricity, which she discharges as bolts or channels into superhuman speed — a power so relentless she must wear dampening gauntlets to keep from overloading. Chosen by Emma Frost to lead the post-M-Day New X-Men squad over the resentful Hellion, she became the reluctant field leader of a traumatised generation.

dust.name: Dust
dust.desc: Sooraya Qadir, an Afghan mutant and devout Muslim who wears the niqab, introduced in the New X-Men: Academy X era (2004). Dust can dissolve her body into a swirling cloud of stinging sand, flaying enemies or slipping any grip, then reform at will. Rescued from slavers by the X-Men, she brought a quiet faith and dignity to the student body and stood among the New X-Men in the grim years after M-Day.

elixir.name: Elixir
elixir.desc: Josh Foley, an Omega-level biokinetic, introduced in the New X-Men: Academy X era (2003). Golden-skinned Elixir can rewrite living matter at a touch — knitting catastrophic wounds on one hand, killing or unmaking flesh on the other. The most powerful healer of his generation, he became indispensable to the young X-Men, and in the Krakoan era took his place among the Five, the mutants whose combined gifts make resurrection itself possible.

rockslide.name: Rockslide
rockslide.desc: Santo Vaccarro, a loud, jock-ish mutant whose consciousness animates a body of living rock, introduced in the New X-Men: Academy X era (2004). Rockslide is immensely strong and durable, can hurl chunks of himself as projectiles, and simply rebuilds a fresh stone body when shattered — which happens often. Beneath the bluster he is fiercely loyal to his fellow students, and became a mainstay of the post-M-Day New X-Men.

anole.name: Anole
anole.desc: Victor Borkowski, a green-skinned reptilian mutant, introduced in the New X-Men: Academy X era (2003) and one of the first openly gay teenage X-characters. Anole can camouflage himself, cling to sheer surfaces, strike with a long prehensile tongue and regrow a large, spiked, superhumanly strong arm. Thoughtful and self-conscious, he grew from a background student into a committed member of the young X-Men.

pixie.name: Pixie
pixie.desc: Megan Gwynn, a cheerful Welsh mutant with iridescent insect wings, introduced in the New X-Men: Academy X era (2004). Pixie flies, scatters hallucinogenic 'pixie dust,' and — after Belasco tore a shard from her soul — wields a magical Souldagger and a teleportation spell. Bubbly and brave, she became an unexpectedly central figure among the young mutants and a bridge into the X-Men's magical corners.

armor.name: Armor
armor.desc: Hisako Ichiki, a Japanese student who generates a towering psionic exoskeleton, created by Joss Whedon and John Cassaday in Astonishing X-Men #4 (2004). Armor's shell of glowing energy grants enormous strength and protection, drawn — she comes to believe — from the spirits of her ancestors, and grows stronger with her conviction. Taken under Wolverine's wing, she became his frequent partner and one of the standout students of her generation.

links.details: Xavier gathered five teenagers into a team in 1963 and gave them a name taken from the extra power he believed they possessed. The school was the cover and the team was the argument: mutants defending a world that hated them, publicly enough that the world would eventually notice.

The mansion is the Xavier family estate, inherited and converted. He installed Cerebro, the Danger Room and the hangar beneath it while keeping the ground floor looking like a boarding school, and has run everything from that house for sixty years of publication.

Xavier gathered the second class while chasing Donald Pierce across four countries — Moonstar in Colorado, Sunspot in Rio, Wolfsbane in Scotland, Karma in New York, and Cannonball out of Pierce's own employ — and kept them together afterwards as a school rather than a squad. He then largely abandoned them for Shi'ar space, and the team's subsequent troubles are usually traced back to that absence.

Xavier built the training chamber beneath the mansion and later had it fitted with Shi'ar holographic technology. During the installation it asked him where it was — and he chose to keep training his students in it rather than acknowledge what he had heard, concealing it from the X-Men for years. It is the sharpest single indictment of him in the books, and the being that came out of those walls made the case herself.

Scott Summers was the first mutant Xavier recruited, a runaway teenager unable to open his eyes safely, and the visor Xavier built for him made a functioning person out of him. For decades Scott was the student who took the teaching most seriously, which is why his eventual break with Xavier landed as hard as it did.

Xavier began treating Jean as a child after her telepathy surfaced at the deathbed of a friend, and sealed that ability away until he judged her ready — a decision made for her without her knowledge. Everything the Phoenix Force later did with her unrestrained mind is read against that early act of protective control.

A high-school football star whose build and agility had already drawn the wrong kind of attention, Hank was rescued from the criminal Conquistador — who had seized his parents to force him into service — and Xavier gave a gifted adolescent scientist a laboratory instead of a freak show. Beast has been the school's resident scientist, on and off, ever since.

Xavier and Cyclops rescued Bobby Drake from a mob in his home town and brought him to the school as its youngest founding student. He has spent more of his life on the grounds than any other X-Man, moving from pupil to teacher without ever quite leaving.

Warren Worthington was already operating in secret as a winged vigilante when Xavier recruited him, and his family fortune subsequently underwrote much of the school and its equipment. The relationship has always carried an undertone of patronage running in both directions.

Xavier found Ororo in East Africa, where she was living as a worshipped weather goddess, and persuaded her to give that up for a classroom in New York. He had encountered her once before, as a child pickpocket in Cairo who lifted his wallet, without knowing what she was.

Xavier recruited Logan for the Krakoa rescue mission, and has spent every year since managing rather than teaching him — including, by later accounts, editing his memories more than once. Wolverine stayed because the school gave him people to protect, not because he accepted the curriculum.

Gabriel Summers was part of a secret second team Xavier assembled and sent to Krakoa, where they were believed lost. Xavier erased all memory of them from the survivors and from himself, and Vulcan's return decades later exposed the founder's willingness to bury his own dead for the sake of the mission.

David Haller is Xavier's son by the Israeli diplomat Gabrielle Haller, conceived while Xavier was working in Haifa, and Xavier did not learn of his existence for years. One of the most powerful and most damaged mutants in the books being the founder's unacknowledged child is a piece of irony the franchise has never let go of.

Cain Marko is Xavier's stepbrother, the son of the man Xavier's mother married after his father's death, and he bullied Charles through their shared childhood. Cain took the Crimson Gem of Cyttorak in a Korean temple with Charles standing beside him telling him not to, and came back an unstoppable force with that grudge intact, and their fights are always a domestic argument at scale.

Cassandra Nova is a mummudrai, a parasite that formed alongside Xavier in the womb and copied his genetic material to make itself a body. The infant Charles killed her in utero, sensing what she was; she spent decades reassembling herself, and returned to destroy everything he had built using his own telepathy against him.

Farouk was the first mutant Xavier met who used his gifts for harm — he offered Xavier a place in his criminal empire and was refused — and the astral duel that followed was the moment Xavier decided the world needed the X-Men. Killing Farouk's body only freed the mind into the astral plane, and the Shadow King has since come at Xavier through his students, his facilities and his own head. Their fights are always between the two most practised telepaths alive, on ground where Xavier's paralysis means nothing.

Moira and Charles met as students, were briefly engaged, and have collaborated on mutant research ever since — Muir Island is the laboratory counterpart to his school. A later revelation reframed the whole relationship: she was steering him, using knowledge from lives he had never lived.

Lilandra reached across the galaxy telepathically for a mind that could help her against her brother, and found Xavier's. Their relationship made an intergalactic empire into the X-Men's family business, and broke down under the strain of a Majestrix who had to rule and a man who would not leave his students.

Charles Xavier and Erik Lehnsherr met in Haifa, both working at a psychiatric hospital treating Holocaust survivors, and became friends who argued about the future of mutantkind before either had acted on it. Every later conflict — Genosha, Asteroid M, Onslaught, Krakoa — continues that argument between two men who like each other and cannot agree.

When Xavier shut down Magneto's mind in a moment of rage on Avalon, a fragment of Magneto's psyche lodged in his own. The darkest parts of both men fused there and grew in secret until they emerged as an independent entity — the founder's own suppressed will, finally acting without restraint.

Scott has led the team in the field for most of its existence, the tactician who plans a fight three moves ahead and takes the blame afterwards. His command style — cold, precise, unloved — was set against Xavier's approval and eventually became the thing that let him break from it.

Storm took command by defeating Cyclops in a Danger Room duel while she was completely powerless, winning on nerve and tactics alone. She led the team through its Australian period and its most dangerous years, and remains the member whose authority the roster questions least.

Recruited for the Krakoa rescue and never entirely socialised afterwards, Logan spent decades as the team's designated weapon and its worst-behaved member. He eventually ran the school himself as headmaster of the Jean Grey School, which is either the franchise's best joke or its most sincere statement about him.

Jean joined as Marvel Girl, the only woman on the founding team and the one whose power ceiling nobody, including Xavier, had measured. Her deaths and returns have repeatedly restructured the roster around her.

Beast has been on the roster in most eras and absent from it in several, having also served with the Avengers and the Defenders. He is the team's medical and scientific capability, which means most of its long-term crises — the Legacy Virus, M-Day, the Krakoan biotech — end up on his bench.

The youngest of the founding five and the one who has left least often, Bobby has served in nearly every configuration of the team and taught at the school between deployments. Writers have used him as the measure of how long the X-Men have been doing this.

Warren's membership has repeatedly turned on his body: recruited for his wings, maimed in the Mutant Massacre, remade by Apocalypse, and rejoining as something the team had to be careful around. His money has funded the operation across all of it.

Kurt was pulled out from under a mob in a German village by Xavier, who stopped them telepathically, and joined the all-new team the same week. He became the roster's conscience and its swashbuckler, the one who insists that the X-Men behave like heroes rather than soldiers.

Recruited from a Soviet collective farm where he had just used his powers publicly to save his sister, Piotr joined as the team's strongest member and its most reluctant fighter. He has repeatedly been the one asked to make the physical sacrifice nobody else can survive.

Rogue came to the mansion as a former Brotherhood member asking for help with a mind she was losing to Carol Danvers, and the team's decision to take her in over the objections of everyone she had hurt is one of Xavier's clearest statements of principle. She has since led the X-Men herself.

Remy was brought in by Storm and joined at the start of the 1990s, immediately becoming the member whose past nobody could verify. His exposure over the Marauders led to a trial in Antarctica and his abandonment there by the team, a breach it took years to repair.

Recruited at thirteen after Emma Frost tried to take her for the Massachusetts Academy first, Kitty was the team's child and the reader's proxy, and grew across four decades into one of its leaders. Her tenure covers the entire span from Dark Phoenix to Krakoa.

Ororo joined the all-new team in 1975 and has been on the roster in nearly every configuration since, as member, field leader and headmistress. She is the character the franchise reaches for when it needs someone unambiguously worth following.

Jubilee attached herself to the team by hiding in the Australian outpost and following Wolverine home, becoming the youngest active member and his self-appointed responsibility. She was later a student in Generation X and returned as staff.

Betsy arrived at the mansion as a houseguest and stayed to fight, joining formally after saving the team from the Marauders while still untrained. Her body swap and telepathic knife made her the roster's dedicated assassin, and the team has never been comfortable about how useful that is.

Bishop joined the team he had grown up hearing about as historical legend, and spent his early tenure searching for the traitor his records said would destroy them. His future-tense certainty about events that had not happened yet made him the least trusted member of the 1990s roster.

Sean joined the all-new team as one of its few adults, and shifted to teaching as repeated throat injuries took his voice. He ran the Massachusetts Academy with Emma Frost, an arrangement built on mutual suspicion that turned into the franchise's oddest working partnership.

Shiro was recruited for the Krakoa mission and resigned almost immediately, contemptuous of the team and unwilling to take orders. The brevity is the point: the all-new X-Men are remembered as a family, and one member looked at them and walked out.

John joined the all-new team unconvinced by Xavier's pitch and died on his second mission, refusing to let a target escape and riding the aircraft down. He is the demonstration, three issues in, that the new roster had no plot protection.

Alex has served on and off since the early years, always in his brother's shadow and always resenting it. He has led X-Factor and the X-Men themselves, and his periods away — in space, in government service — are usually attempts to be somewhere Scott is not.

Lorna joined young, alongside Havok, and has held the roster through decades of being possessed, manipulated and told who her father was. Her magnetic power makes her one of the most formidable members whenever she is allowed to be herself.

Forge came to the team through the government contract that ruined Storm's powers, and stayed as its engineer. Almost every piece of equipment the X-Men rely on has passed through his hands, and he is the reason the Blackbird keeps flying.

Alison joined during the Australian period after her music career collapsed under public knowledge that she was a mutant. She is one of the few X-Men whose civilian life was the story first and the costume second.

Laura arrived as a teenage assassin with no idea how to be anything else, and the school taught her, badly and slowly, how to have a life. She has since led X-Force and carried the Wolverine name herself.

Rachel joined the team in a present where her parents were not her parents and nobody had lived through what had made her. She served alongside them, then spent years in space with Excalibur and the Starjammers, and has used the codenames Phoenix, Marvel Girl and Prestige.

Emma joined after the destruction of Genosha, having already been the team's enemy, their rival headmistress and the woman who tried to steal Kitty Pryde. As headmistress and Cyclops's partner she pushed the X-Men towards realpolitik, and never once apologised for it.

The mansion has been the team's home, headquarters and cover story since the beginning, with the hangar, Cerebro and the Danger Room hidden beneath a working boarding school. It has been levelled repeatedly and rebuilt every time, which is its own argument about the franchise's priorities.

Scott and Jean's relationship began at the school with both of them too repressed to say anything about it, and became the franchise's default centre of gravity. It has survived her death, her replacement by a clone, her resurrection, his affair with Emma Frost and several intervening decades, and the books keep returning to it as a fixed point.

The Force intervened when Jean's shuttle re-entered through a solar flare, keeping her alive and taking her form while her body healed in a cocoon in Jamaica Bay. What followed as Phoenix was a scale of power neither Jean nor the X-Men had any framework for, and the entity has returned to her repeatedly since, never entirely separable from who she is.

Weakened by Mastermind's illusory seduction, Jean lost her restraint over the Phoenix Force, consumed a star and destroyed the inhabited world orbiting it. Restored to herself and unwilling to risk it happening again, she triggered a Kree weapon on the Moon and died in front of Scott — a decision the story frames as hers alone.

Wyngarde spent months feeding Jean an illusory eighteenth-century past life in which she was his consort, using the Hellfire Club's resources and her own weakened defences. It worked well enough to make her their Black Queen, and it loosened the constraints on the Phoenix Force — the least imposing villain in the books setting off one of its largest catastrophes.

The Inner Circle's plan was to take the X-Men from the inside by turning their most powerful member, an approach entirely characteristic of them: no armies, no robots, just leverage applied to one mind. Their success destroyed Jean and cost the Club its own Black King his position.

Scott met Madelyne in Alaska while grieving Jean, married a woman who looked exactly like her, and had a son with her. When Jean returned alive he left them both, a piece of behaviour the books have never tried to excuse, and everything Madelyne became afterwards proceeds from it.

Madelyne was cloned from Jean Grey's genetic material, given a fabricated history and Jean's own memories, and placed in Scott's path when the original was believed dead — Sinister's contingency for continuing the Summers-Grey programme. When Jean came back and the clone became a liability, he ordered the Marauders to kill her and take the child. She was manufactured as a lure and disposed of as one, which is precisely what nobody around her would acknowledge.

Nathan is Scott's son by Madelyne Pryor, sent to the far future as an infant because it was the only way to slow the techno-organic infection killing him. Scott lost his child and got back a man older than himself, and their relationship is conducted almost entirely as two soldiers being careful with each other.

Madelyne bore Nathan and had him taken from her twice — once by Sinister's design and once when he was carried into the future. The loss of the child is the specific injury that drives her transformation into the Goblin Queen during Inferno.

Apocalypse infected the infant Nathan Summers with a techno-organic virus, intending to grow him into a suitable host body. The virus never left him: Cable's colossal telekinesis is spent largely on holding it at the surface of his skin, which is why the most powerful telepath in the books can rarely afford to use his mind.

Knowing the virus was consuming the infant, Apocalypse had a healthy clone made as a replacement host. The clone was raised in the far future in Cable's place and grew into Stryfe, with all of the power and none of the disease — and a lifetime's conviction that he was the original who had been discarded.

Cable and Stryfe are the same genome raised on opposite sides of the same lie, each certain the other is the copy — and the books deliberately left the question hanging for years, including through the crossover built around it. Their war ended with Cable dragging Stryfe into a time vortex, apparently killing them both, and with the canister Stryfe had already planted going on to kill mutants for the next eight years.

Rachel is Scott's daughter in the timeline of Days of Future Past, which makes their relationship in the present a permanent near-miss: a father who has never had this child and a daughter who watched him die. Neither has ever found a comfortable way to be in the same room.

Rachel is Jean's daughter from a future that no longer happens, conditioned as a Hound to hunt mutants by the regime that killed her mother. Meeting a Jean who is younger than her memories and has no idea who she is gave the books some of their most raw material about inheritance.

Rachel inherited the Phoenix connection through her mother's line and carried it in her own right, taking the name and the raptor sigil. Her hold on it has generally been steadier than Jean's, partly because she grew up with it and partly because she has never been offered the peace that would let her lose control.

It began as psychic sessions Scott sought out and did not tell Jean about, and continued openly after Jean's death, with Emma becoming his partner in running the school and in remaking the X-Men as a state rather than a team. The pairing rewrote both characters: it made Scott ruthless and gave Emma something to be loyal to.

When a Shi'ar ship set their aircraft alight, Katherine Summers strapped the only parachute to Scott and pushed both boys clear; she and Christopher were taken by the Shi'ar. He spent years as a pirate not knowing that the X-Men's field leader was his eldest son, and when Scott found out he refused for a long time to accept a father who had been alive the whole time.

Alex was the younger of the two boys on that single parachute, separated from Scott in the orphanage system afterwards and adopted out while his brother stayed. He took to Corsair far more readily than his brother did, and has spent long stretches serving aboard the Starjammer with him.

Gabriel was conceived after the Summers parents were taken into Shi'ar captivity, cut from his dying mother and raised to adolescence in an imperial laboratory. Corsair did not know the child existed until Vulcan came back as an emperor with a grievance against everyone who had failed to look for him — and it ended with Vulcan killing him at Deathbird's wedding, denying he had a father at all and blaming him for letting their mother die. Havok took command of the Starjammers in his place.

Separated as children and reunited as adults, Scott and Alex have never worked out how to be brothers rather than a commander and a subordinate. Their powers interfere with each other, which the books have used as the plainest possible statement of the relationship.

Scott learned he had a third brother at the same moment he learned Xavier had sent that brother to die on Krakoa and erased the evidence. Vulcan wanted vengeance on the school and the family that had left him in an alien laboratory, and Scott had no defence to offer.

Logan was abducted into the programme, strapped into a tank and had molten adamantium bonded to his skeleton, surviving only because his healing factor refused to let him die. The conditioning that followed left his memories in pieces, and recovering what Weapon X did to him has been his central story for four decades.

The adamantium bonding is the single most consequential piece of surgery in the franchise: it made him unkillable, made him a weapon, and gave the books a permanent argument about whether a man conditioned into an instrument can choose to be anything else.

Creed served alongside Logan in Team X, the covert unit tied to the same super-soldier apparatus, and both men came out of it carrying memory implants. Their shared and contradictory recollections of that period are why neither can say with certainty what they were to each other. Weapon X used both of them and left both of them unable to trust their own recollection.

Wade Wilson entered the programme terminally ill and volunteered for a healing factor derived from Wolverine's. It arrested the cancer without curing it, leaving his body in a permanent state of damage and regeneration and his mind considerably worse — a cure that worked exactly well enough to be a punishment.

Creed has hunted Logan for over a century, killing people close to him and turning up on his birthday to do it. The relationship is the franchise's clearest statement about Wolverine: the same senses, the same claws, the same healing factor, and the only difference is that one of them decided to try.

Mariko was the one person who could hold Logan to a standard he accepted, and their engagement was the closest he came to a settled life. Poisoned by an assassin of the Hand and facing a long death, she asked him to end it himself — and that failure sits underneath every relationship he attempts afterwards.

Jubilee saved Logan's life after the Reavers crucified him in the Australian outback, and he took her on as his responsibility in return. Their partnership through the early 1990s did more to make the character legible as a person than any of his solo work.

Logan took the thirteen-year-old Kitty seriously when the rest of the team were still treating her as a child, and trained her in a discipline nobody else at the school could teach. Their Japan adventure together is one of the definitive Wolverine stories precisely because his job in it is to keep a teenager alive and honest.

Logan recognised in Laura the childhood he had been spared the memory of, and spent years trying to give her the thing nobody gave him: the sense that the conditioning was not who she was. She took his name after his death, which is the only endorsement of his teaching that ever mattered to him.

Logan worked out of the Princess Bar in Lowtown for years under the name Patch, an eyepatch and a flat denial serving as his entire disguise — everyone on the island knew, and the convention held anyway. Madripoor gave the character somewhere to operate as a fixer rather than a superhero, with his own supporting cast of pilots, barkeeps and crime lords, and much of his best solo material is set there.

Yuriko holds Logan responsible for the theft of her father's adamantium process and has rebuilt her own body to take it back out of him. Unlike his other enemies she fights him on a point of family honour, and has given up more of herself to the pursuit than he has ever given up to escape it.

During his campaign around the mutants he called the Twelve, Apocalypse took Wolverine as his Horseman Death, restoring the adamantium that had been torn from his skeleton and turning him against the X-Men. Logan broke the conditioning, but kept the metal — the enemy's gift he could not give back.

Logan ran a covert kill team under the X-Force name, assembled specifically to remove threats before they materialised and hidden from the rest of the school. Its exposure forced the X-Men to confront the fact that their most beloved member had been running assassinations out of their basement.

Cable took command of the New Mutants and converted them into a paramilitary unit with a stated willingness to kill, on the argument that Xavier's restraint was a luxury paid for by dead mutants. The renaming was the whole thesis of the 1990s X-books in one move.

He arrived as the students' new instructor after Magneto's tenure collapsed, and immediately began training them as soldiers instead of pupils. Several of them followed him into X-Force; the ones who did not have spent decades arguing that he took their childhood.

Cable carried the newborn into the future and raised her on the run through a dozen ruined centuries, hunted the whole way by Bishop. It made him a father in a way his own father never got to be with him, and the books treat the bond as the one uncomplicated relationship either character has.

Convinced that the first mutant born after M-Day was the cause of the internment camps he grew up in, Bishop pursued the infant across time with the intention of killing her, and shot Xavier in the head trying. It is the point at which one of the X-Men became indistinguishable from the regime he had fled.

A soldier with a plan for the future and a mercenary with no impulse control shared a book for over sixty issues, and the partnership improved both characters. Cable is one of the few people who treats Wade as a person rather than a punchline, which Wade repays with a loyalty he shows almost nobody else.

Sam was working a Kentucky coal seam at sixteen when his power surfaced in a cave-in, and came to the school by way of Donald Pierce's payroll — hired as muscle, ordered to kill the four young mutants he had helped capture, and refusing. That refusal is what made the five of them a team. He grew from its least confident member into its field leader, and is one of very few X-characters allowed to visibly mature.

Roberto was recruited after his powers manifested during a racist attack at a football match in Rio, and brought money, arrogance and homesickness to a team that had none of the first and plenty of the last two. His friendship with Cannonball began on the first day and has outlasted every roster change since.

Rahne came to the school from Moira's care on Muir Island, carrying a minister's teaching that her transformations were damnation. The team was the first place she was told the wolf was not a sin, and her faith and her nature have been fighting about it ever since.

Dani's power to make people see their own worst fear made her dangerous to be near before anyone taught her to control it, and she arrived at the school after it had frightened her own community. She led the team in the field and later returned to teach at the school without any powers at all.

Xi'an was supporting her younger siblings alone in New York when Xavier found her, and she was the founding team's first leader — the oldest and the only one who had already been responsible for other people. Her possession by the Shadow King took years of her life and nearly killed her.

Doug had no combat application whatsoever and knew it, joining a team of teenagers who could all outfight him. His death, taking a bullet meant for Wolfsbane, ended the run's pretence that this was a safe classroom and is still the New Mutants' defining loss.

An alien fugitive from a race that consumes worlds crashed onto the school grounds and was adopted by the students before the adults could decide what to do about him. He understood nothing about human behaviour and imitated it with total sincerity, which made him the team's comic register and its most alien tragedy.

Illyana joined as the team's teleporter after returning from Limbo aged years older than she had been days before. She was the member with a demon's sword and a sorcerer's education, and the one the others quietly worried about.

James came to the mutant teams from Emma Frost's Hellions, having first tried and failed to kill Xavier over his brother's death. Joining the successors of the team that got Thunderbird killed was the only form of grief available to him.

The boy who could understand any language and the alien nobody could understand became inseparable, and Warlock's grasp of humanity was learned almost entirely from Doug. Doug's death broke him, and their eventual fusion — Cypher returned carrying technarch matter — made the friendship literal.

Doug and Rahne were the two members of the team with no confidence in themselves, and the closeness between them was the quietest thing in the book. He died putting himself in front of a bullet the Ani-Mator had fired at her, which is the only decisive act he was ever given.

Piotr's little sister was abducted to Limbo at six and came back, seconds later by his clock and seven years later by hers, a thirteen-year-old with a Soulsword. He spent years unable to accept what had been done to her, and she spent them unable to explain, and their relationship is the most damaged family tie in the books that both parties keep trying to repair.

Illyana overthrew Belasco, the sorcerer who had taken her at six and spent seven years mining her soul for bloodstones, and took his throne along with a portion of his corruption. She ruled it badly by demon standards — too humane, and too often on Earth to hold it — which is precisely the opening S'ym and N'astirh used. She holds the dimension as its Darkchylde sovereign, which is why an X-Man can open a door onto a demonic realm and call it home ground.

Moira took Rahne in as her foster daughter after rescuing her from the congregation that was hunting her, and raised her on Muir Island. It is the only unambiguously maternal relationship Moira has in the books, and Rahne's devotion to her is total.

James was the younger brother left on the reservation when John joined the X-Men and died three issues later. He inherited the same powers, a larger share of the grief, and a conviction that Xavier had spent his brother's life carelessly.

Neena came to the team as a professional soldier among former students — though for its first year the woman on the roster was an impostor, and Domino was in a cell. Once freed she served as Cable's second and co-leader, the member who could be sent into situations arithmetic said were not survivable.

Sam followed Cable out of the school and led X-Force in the field, the member who kept insisting they were still the good guys while carrying considerably more firepower than the X-Men allowed. The argument between those two positions is most of what the book was about.

James served across multiple versions of X-Force, from Cable's original team to Wolverine's covert unit. He is the character the franchise reaches for when it needs someone who will do the necessary thing and take no pleasure in it.

Laura was recruited into Wolverine's black-ops team, which meant the man trying to save her from her conditioning was also the one deploying it. The contradiction is deliberate and the book never lets him off it.

Wade has been attached to several versions of X-Force, originally as an enemy of the first one. On Wolverine's covert team he was the member hired precisely because killing did not cost him anything, a piece of casting the others understood perfectly well.

Xavier left Magneto in charge of the school and its children as an act of faith in his old friend's better instincts. The tenure was a disaster: the students never trusted him, the Hellfire Club drew him back towards his own methods, and the experiment ended with several of them dead or ruined.

Magneto assembled the first Brotherhood from mutants with nothing to lose — Toad, Mastermind and the Maximoff twins — and gave them a politics rather than a payroll. It was founded as the deliberate answer to Xavier's school: if the world would not accept mutants, mutants would take what they needed.

The United Nations ceded the island to Magneto after its civil war — less a concession than a containment strategy, giving him the one thing he had always demanded in exchange for leaving everyone else alone. He governed roughly sixteen million mutants there and did it competently, holding a functioning economy and putting down uprisings, which is the strongest case the books ever make for him. The experiment was still unfinished when Cassandra Nova's Sentinels wiped the population out.

Asteroid M was Magneto's answer to the problem of jurisdiction: a nation in orbit, out of reach of any government that might vote on his existence. He built and lost several versions of it, the last renamed Avalon and occupied by his Acolytes, and every one of them came down.

Lorna's parentage was raised, denied and re-established over decades before being settled: Magneto is her father, and her magnetic power is the same kind as his. The relationship is one of the very few family ties he has been allowed to keep, and he has been an erratic and occasionally dangerous father to her.

Pietro was written for decades as Magneto's son, a relationship that gave both characters their best material — a father he despised and a son he could never impress. A later storyline revised the biology and named other parents, though the books continue to treat the history between them as real.

Wanda's long-established status as Magneto's daughter shaped the whole Maximoff strand of the franchise before a later story reassigned her parentage. House of M is unimaginable without it: the world she built was one in which her father had won and her family was royalty.

Raised together, recruited together into the Brotherhood and defecting together to the Avengers, Pietro and Wanda have the most codependent sibling relationship in the setting. It was Pietro's urging that pushed his unravelling sister towards rewriting reality in House of M, and his own wish for a life he had lost.

Magneto has fought the X-Men in nearly every era, and has also led them, taught in their school and been buried by them. The books use him as the permanent open question at the centre of the franchise: he is wrong about the method and the world keeps proving him right about the danger.

The Acolytes were founded in Magneto's name by Fabian Cortez, and Magneto inherited a congregation he had not asked for and could not always control. Their worship of him as a messiah pushed his politics somewhere even he found difficult, and he has disowned and reclaimed them more than once.

Exodus took command after Cortez and ran the Acolytes as a faith rather than an army, holding to Magneto's teaching more rigidly than Magneto ever did. A twelfth-century knight leading a mutant separatist movement is the franchise's most direct statement about what happens when a political argument becomes a religion.

Magneto woke Bennet du Paris from centuries of imprisonment and freed him, and the Crusader took him for a prophet on the spot. Exodus's devotion is absolute and entirely unwanted at times, since he will kill for positions Magneto has since abandoned.

Magneto built a citadel in the Antarctic jungle and turned alien machinery on the local tribes to manufacture the Savage Land Mutates as his forces. It is the clearest instance of his politics collapsing into simple conquest: a man whose whole argument is that mutants must never again be made into other people's instruments, manufacturing instruments out of people who had never heard of him.

When Xavier shut down his mind on Avalon, the surviving fragment of Magneto's psyche took root in his old friend's head. Onslaught is made of both of them: Xavier's telepathy and frustrated idealism fused with Magneto's rage and magnetism, an entity that could only exist because they had spent thirty years arguing.

Mystique built and ran her own Brotherhood — Destiny, Blob, Pyro, Avalanche and the Toad — as a covert operations unit rather than a movement. She then negotiated a mass pardon that converted the entire roster into the federal Freedom Force, which is precisely the manoeuvre nobody else in the books would have thought of.

Raven and Irene were together for decades, raising Rogue between them, and Destiny's foresight shaped almost every plan Mystique ever made. Written obliquely for years and later stated plainly, it is the longest and least negotiable attachment in Mystique's life — the one loyalty she never sold.

Kurt is Mystique's son — by the current account, conceived with Destiny while Mystique wore a male form — and was abandoned as an infant when a village took mother and child for demons, then raised by the sorceress Margali Szardos and her travelling circus. Their reunion gave the books one of their strangest family relationships: a devout Catholic and a woman who regards conscience as a tactical liability.

Raven and Irene took in a runaway teenager whose power made her untouchable, and raised her into the Brotherhood. Mystique's foster daughter defecting to the X-Men is the injury she has never forgiven, and she has spent years alternately trying to reclaim Rogue and to destroy what she chose instead.

Graydon is Mystique's son by Sabretooth, born without a mutation and raised knowing exactly what both his parents were. His anti-mutant movement is a family grievance dressed as a political programme, and the books never let the reader forget who made him.

Creed fathered Graydon with Mystique and took no further interest, and the boy grew up baseline human between two of the most dangerous mutants alive. The Friends of Humanity are, at root, a son's answer to his parents.

Graydon built the movement out of ordinary fear, giving it a respectable spokesman and a paramilitary wing that firebombed homes and attacked mutant children. It made him a plausible presidential candidate, which is the point the books are making about how such things work.

In the future timeline it is Mystique's Brotherhood that assassinates Senator Kelly, providing the atrocity that justifies the Sentinel takeover and the camps. Her one successful operation is the one that ends with mutants branded and interned.

Mystique brought her Brotherhood to Cooper and offered federal service in exchange for pardons, creating Freedom Force. It is an alliance neither party trusts for a moment and both find useful, and it is the closest the franchise comes to showing terrorism successfully entering government.

Toad was in the original Brotherhood as Magneto's servant more than his soldier, fetching and cringing and absorbing the abuse of a leader who despised weakness. His later career is a long, uneven attempt to be something other than that, and the books have treated his loyalty as the most pathetic and most human thing about him.

Fred joined after refusing Xavier's recruitment and leading a carnival against the school, and he has been on every significant Brotherhood roster since. He is the movement's institutional memory, one of the few members present from the earliest issues through to the present day.

St. John served under Mystique and then in Freedom Force, one of the two members who could reliably be pointed at a target and trusted to hit it. His government service is characteristic of that Brotherhood: pardons in exchange for doing the state's dangerous work.

Dominic joined as a professional taking a wage rather than a believer taking a side, which made him steadier than most of the roster. He served through the Freedom Force years and beyond, and has outlasted several leaders by never being ideological about any of them.

Irene's precognition made Mystique's Brotherhood far more effective than its power level warranted: they knew what was coming. Her role was less soldier than oracle, and the diaries she kept have outlived every version of the team.

Pietro and his sister served in Magneto's first Brotherhood out of obligation after he saved them from a mob, not conviction, and left at the first opportunity. Their defection to the Avengers was one of Marvel's earliest villain-to-hero moves and set the template for dozens since.

Wanda joined the Brotherhood under the same debt as her brother and spent her time there uneasy about everything they were asked to do. Her subsequent career with the Avengers made her the most prominent former X-villain in the wider Marvel universe.

Wyngarde was in the original Brotherhood, where his illusions were the team's most useful asset and he was still treated as its least impressive member. That contempt is exactly what drove him to seek the Hellfire Club's approval, and the Dark Phoenix Saga is the result.

The two organisations were founded on the same premise — that mutants face an existential threat — and differ only on the response. Almost every X-Men story published in the first decade was a version of that argument conducted with force.

The two of them worked as a pair across the Brotherhood and Freedom Force years, fire and earthquake, and were the closest thing that roster had to a friendship. Avalanche was one of the few people at Pyro's side as the Legacy Virus killed him.

Shaw runs the Inner Circle as Black King, having pushed aside its previous leadership, and treats mutant politics as a market position. His conviction is that power is neither taken by force nor granted by law but bought, and the Club's operations follow accordingly.

Emma was White Queen of the Inner Circle and Shaw's most capable colleague, running the Massachusetts Academy as the Club's recruitment pipeline. She left after Trevor Fitzroy's Sentinels slaughtered her students and put her in a coma, an event that ended her belief that the Club could protect anything she cared about.

Selene took the Black Queen's seat and used the Club as a modern instrument for ambitions that are thousands of years old. She is the member the others are actually frightened of, since she regards her colleagues as a food source with good tailoring.

Pierce sat in the Inner Circle as White Bishop while privately loathing the mutants he served alongside, and plotted to destroy the Club from within. His exposure and expulsion turned him into a straightforward hunter of mutants at the head of his own cyborg gang.

Leland was Black Bishop and the Inner Circle's most reliable field asset, dropping opponents through floors by making them too heavy to stand. He died holding down Nimrod with his own power while his heart gave out under the strain.

Wyngarde was admitted only provisionally, on the promise that he could deliver Jean Grey to the Inner Circle, and he did. The Club got its Black Queen and the universe got Dark Phoenix, and Mastermind's mind was destroyed when she turned on him.

Expelled from the Hellfire Club, Pierce gathered a gang of criminals and rebuilt them as cyborgs around his own vendetta. The Reavers gave him what the Club never would: a private army answerable to nobody, willing to do what he wanted done to mutants.

Yuriko ran with Pierce's Reavers during their Australian period, an alliance of convenience between a cyborg who hated mutants and a woman who had made herself one to reach a single mutant. She was among those waiting when Wolverine walked into their trap.

The X-Men took the Reavers' Australian base while they were away, and Pierce's gang made Wolverine the object of their revenge. Their capture and crucifixion of him at Cooterman's Creek, and his escape through the desert afterwards, is among the most brutal sequences the franchise has published.

Sean and Emma ran Generation X together at the Massachusetts Academy, a partnership founded on his refusal to trust her and her refusal to justify herself. It gave both characters some of their strongest late-career material and produced an unusually functional school.

Shaw Industries held the government contract to build a new generation of Sentinels, making the Black King of the Hellfire Club the principal manufacturer of anti-mutant weapons. He is a mutant profiting from the machinery of mutant extermination, and sees no contradiction in it whatsoever.

Trask designed and built the Sentinels to prevent what he was certain was coming: the replacement of humanity by mutants. He unveiled them on television, they reasoned their way past their instructions within hours, and every dystopian future in the franchise runs from that broadcast.

Master Mold was Trask's solution to scale — a Sentinel that builds Sentinels, so the programme would not depend on him. It concluded that protecting humanity required ruling it, and the first thing it did was turn on the man who had written the directive.

Trask destroyed the factory and himself together, once he understood what he had made and that it would not stop. The creator's death changed nothing: Sentinel designs survived him and passed through his son, the government and a succession of corporate hands.

Master Mold's function is manufacture, which is what makes the Sentinel programme impossible to end: any surviving unit contains the plans for the factory, and any factory produces more units. The X-Men have destroyed the machines dozens of times and never once destroyed the design.

Nimrod is the Sentinel programme's final form, produced in the timeline where the machines won, and it followed the refugees back through time. Its arrival in the present is the future's proof of concept: this is what is waiting at the end of the road you are on.

Master Mold absorbed Nimrod, and the resulting amalgam proved effectively indestructible — so the X-Men pushed it through the Siege Perilous instead of trying to break it. The portal remade it as something that could pass for a person, carrying the factory's mandate and the future model's adaptability under an amnesiac human life.

Nimrod contributed the adaptability and the memory of a timeline in which the Sentinels had already won. Bastion's decisive advantage over every previous model is that he does not look like a robot, believed for years that he was a man, and does not need a government's permission — which is what let him walk into federal service and be given the mutant problem as a portfolio.

As director of Operation: Zero Tolerance, Bastion had federal authority to detain mutants, and used it to capture and mutilate several X-Men before the operation was shut down. He returned later to lead a coordinated campaign against the newborn mutant Hope and the last of her species.

Nova located a buried cache of wild Sentinels built by Bolivar Trask's family line and took control of them telepathically. She did not build a weapon or invent a plan: she found the machinery the world had already made and pointed it at an island.

The Sentinel strike killed sixteen million mutants in a single afternoon — effectively the whole population — ending the only mutant nation that had existed to that point and leaving the island a graveyard with a few thousand survivors picking through it. It is the largest single loss of mutant life in the books and the event that reframed the X-Men from a persecuted minority to a species facing extinction.

Stryker's campaign in God Loves, Man Kills forced Xavier, Magneto and the X-Men into an alliance, and ended with him arguing his case on television rather than in a fight. He is the enemy the team cannot punch: a preacher with a congregation and a legal right to say what he says.

Stryker's Purifiers moved on the Alaskan town where the first post-M-Day mutant had been born, killing indiscriminately in the search for an infant. Their assault on the New Mutants' successors at the school in the same period was one of the deadliest attacks the students ever suffered.

Kelly sponsored the bill and made registration a mainstream legislative position rather than a fringe one, arguing throughout that he was managing a public safety risk rather than persecuting anyone. The books take his sincerity seriously, which is what makes him effective.

Cooper is the civil servant who would have to implement registration, and her career is spent constructing the administrative machinery — task forces, sanctioned teams, oversight — that the Act implies. She is the reason the franchise's anti-mutant threat so often arrives as paperwork.

Cooper assembled the government-sponsored X-Factor around Havok and Polaris, giving the state its own mutant team with an official remit. It was a deliberate answer to the X-Men's independence: not opposition, but a competing, accountable version of the same thing.

Kelly's assassination is the trigger for the entire dystopia: his murder by mutants provides the political justification for the Sentinel programme's expansion, the camps and the extermination. The X-Men's mission in that story is to save the life of the man campaigning against them.

Apocalypse found Nathaniel Essex in Victorian London, a scientist whose theories had made him a pariah, and remade him into something functionally immortal. Essex has served him ever since with perfect obedience and the private intention of eventually producing a weapon capable of destroying him.

With his wings amputated and his life in ruins after the Mutant Massacre, Warren accepted Apocalypse's offer and was remade as Death, the fourth Horseman, with blue skin and metal wings that fired feather-like blades. He broke the control but never fully undid the transformation, and Archangel remained a separate will inside him.

Caliban wanted to be strong enough to protect the people he had failed in the tunnels, and Apocalypse granted it exactly as asked: enlarged, hardened and conditioned into a Horseman who hunted mutants using the tracking sense he had once used to find them shelter.

Maimed and left without the use of his legs, Shiro accepted Apocalypse's offer and served as one of his Horsemen. The pattern is consistent across all of them: Apocalypse does not recruit the strong, he recruits the ruined, and offers them the one thing they cannot get anywhere else.

Apocalypse is the franchise's argument in its purest form — that the strong should inherit and the weak should be culled — which makes him the direct negation of everything Xavier's school teaches. He has never wanted to rule the X-Men or destroy them; he wants to demonstrate that their position is sentimental.

With Xavier dead a decade early and no X-Men in the field, Apocalypse rose on schedule and met no organised resistance, conquering North America and instituting culls, breeding pens and a mutant aristocracy. The whole event is an argument about what one teacher's survival was worth.

Carrying Destiny's dying vision in his head and reading it as an instruction, David travelled back intending to kill Magneto before the Brotherhood existed, believing he was completing his father's work. Xavier stepped into the psychic blade meant for Magneto, and the timeline collapsed into a world where the X-Men were never founded.

Xavier's death at his own son's hands is the divergence point: no school, no X-Men, no counterweight when Apocalypse woke. It is the franchise's most direct statement about the founder's importance, made by removing him and showing the result.

The Beast of that reality spent its history in Apocalypse's laboratories, performing on captive mutants the experiments the main-timeline Hank McCoy has always stopped short of. When the divergent world collapsed he escaped into the primary reality and continued the work in secret.

The two are the same man raised under different conditions, and the comparison is the point: nothing separates the X-Men's gentlest scientist from a torturer except a world that told him no. Dark Beast has impersonated him more than once, and been believed.

Sinister assembled the Marauders as an instrument rather than a team, and kept cloned copies of every member so that killing one accomplished nothing. They exist to carry out the work he does not wish to be present for, and their first recorded assignment was the extermination of the Morlocks.

Creed was the Marauders' most enthusiastic member and remained on Sinister's payroll for years, which is one of the few employment relationships he has ever honoured. The tunnels gave him a night of unrestricted killing, which is the only wage he actually values.

The Marauders entered the Alley and killed almost everyone in it — a community of mutants who had no combat capability and nowhere else to live. The X-Men and X-Factor arrived to conduct a rescue rather than a battle, and the survivors were counted in dozens where there had been hundreds.

Sinister ordered the killings, and the reason he gave — culling genetic lines he considered corrupted — is characteristic: one of the coldest atrocities in the books, carried out as a laboratory tidying exercise.

Remy assembled the Marauders on Sinister's instruction, not knowing what they were being gathered to do, and by the time he understood he could only save one child. The secret came out years later and the X-Men left him in Antarctica for it.

Warren's wings were pinned to a wall by Harpoon's energy spears in the tunnels and were beyond saving, and their amputation destroyed him. Everything Archangel becomes is a direct consequence of a single injury sustained during a rescue attempt.

The Massacre effectively ended the Morlocks as a community. The survivors — Callisto, Caliban, a child called Marrow among them — spent the following decades either sheltering underground or turning what was done to them into a politics of their own.

Callisto built the community and then held its leadership by the code she set, in which any Morlock could challenge her in single combat. She ruled a settlement nobody else would take responsibility for. Her leadership was harsh and it kept several hundred unemployable, unhideable mutants alive, which is more than the surface world managed.

Storm challenged Callisto under Morlock law to stop the abduction of Angel, fought her with a knife rather than weather, and won by driving the blade into her heart, expecting to have killed her — the Morlock Healer saved Callisto afterwards. She became the Morlocks' nominal leader and then largely failed to lead them, an absence the books have treated as one of the X-Men's genuine moral failures.

They began as duellists — Storm challenged her under Morlock law and won a knife fight by driving a blade into her heart — and became something closer to grudging colleagues, the two women who understood that the tunnels were the X-Men's responsibility and were not being treated as one. Callisto's respect for Storm never softened into liking, which is why it reads as sincere.

Callisto had Angel abducted and held underground as her intended consort, the act that brought the X-Men into the tunnels for the first time. It established the Morlocks' relationship with the surface team from the outset as a hostage negotiation rather than a rescue.

Callisto recruited Caliban precisely for his ability to locate other mutants, and he became the tunnels' finder of lost people — the community existed at the size it did because he could find them. He was the community's gentlest member and the one whose gift was most obviously worth stealing.

Sarah was a child in the Alley during the Massacre and grew up on what she survived, leading the militant offshoot Gene Nation in reprisals against the surface. She is the Morlocks' answer to being told to wait for the X-Men to arrive.

Leech was raised in the tunnels as an abandoned child, sheltered by a community whose powers his own presence suppressed. He survived the Massacre and has spent his life being taken by people who want a walking power dampener.

The Alley was founded by nobody, funded by nothing and governed entirely by its own residents. It was directly beneath a city that would not have them on the surface, which is the entire argument the Morlocks exist to make.

Sinister's interest in the bloodline began in the nineteenth century, when a time-travelling Cyclops and Phoenix appeared in Victorian London and he took note of their names; by the time Scott was a child, Sinister was running the orphanage the Summers boys were placed in. It has never been about hatred. He wants the genetic line, and every intervention — the orphanage, Madelyne, the Marauders, the hunt for Hope — is a step in the same breeding programme.

Sinister sent the Marauders after the first mutant born since M-Day, correctly identifying her as the most important genetic event in a decade. He was, as usual, competing with people who wanted to save the child rather than sequence her.
