Stryfe brought the plague back from the future — a strain built on a virus Apocalypse had developed there — and handed it to Mister Sinister in a canister he said contained two thousand years of Summers DNA. Sinister's assistant opened it after Stryfe's apparent death and released it. It was pure spite, aimed at a world he blamed for his own manufacture, and it killed for eight years after he was gone.

Illyana contracted the virus after being returned to childhood, and died of it as a seven-year-old in the mansion's medical bay with her brother beside her. It is the moment the epidemic stopped being a background threat in the books and became personal to the X-Men.

St. John spent his final months visibly deteriorating, and used what he had left saving Senator Kelly from an assassination attempt — a man whose politics he had fought for years. The virus made no distinction between the X-Men and their enemies, which was part of its point.

Beast's cure required a mutant's death to disperse it into the atmosphere, and Piotr injected himself without telling anyone, having already watched his sister die of the disease. It ended the epidemic and cost the X-Men the member least likely to be asked to make that kind of decision.

Hank spent years on the virus and found the cure that ended it, and also spent those years unable to stop it killing people he knew. The storyline is where the franchise's optimistic scientist learned that being the smartest person available is not the same as being enough.

Moira's facility was the front line of the research, and she became the first human to contract the mutated strain while working on it. She found the cure — and was fatally injured when Mystique's Brotherhood attacked the Centre, holding on long enough to pass the formula to Xavier's mind. Beast built the antidote from her work, and Colossus dispersed it with his own death.

The Mutant Research Centre is Moira's life's work, conceived with Xavier in the early days and built on her own family's land: a laboratory, a hospital and, when it had to be, a prison. Mutants whose powers are killing them are sent there because nowhere else will take them — and she was mortally wounded in its ruins, having just found the cure for the plague that had been killing them for years.

Kevin is Moira's son by a violent marriage, and his reality-warping power destroyed his own body before he was grown. She confined him on Muir Island for years — an act she has defended as containment and never quite as care — and he escaped by consuming the people sent to check on him.

With Proteus loose in a Scottish town and burning through host bodies, the X-Men worked out that metal disrupted his energy form. Piotr, who does not kill, was the only one who could end it, and did — a scene the books have returned to whenever they want to show what he carries.

The Shadow King took Xi'an after an explosion left her vulnerable, possessed her for the better part of a year, and indulged his own appetites through her body until it was grossly changed — and her teammates believed her dead throughout. Magik and her own will eventually broke his hold. It is one of the most sustained violations in the franchise, and her recovery ran across the rest of the New Mutants.

Farouk spent months quietly corrupting the island's residents before taking them outright, turning Moira's patients and the ad hoc team stationed there into thralls and using Xavier's own son Legion as his principal host — through whom he also stirred what remained of Proteus. Ending it took X-Factor and the X-Men together and levelled the facility, leaving Legion catatonic. The Muir Island Saga is also the story that reunited the two teams into one.

Onslaught's emergence meant the X-Men's founder had become the enemy, using everything he knew about them against them — Xavier had even written contingency plans for killing each of his students, and Onslaught destroyed them only after making sure they had been read. The crisis spread across the whole Marvel line and ended with the Avengers and the Fantastic Four apparently dead, and the X-Men publicly blamed for it.

Abandoned by Scott, hunted by the Marauders on Sinister's order and told to her face that she had been manufactured as a copy, Madelyne took the power N'astirh offered and became the Goblin Queen. The demon wanted her son sacrificed to hold the gates between Limbo and Earth open permanently, and she agreed — the story's centre, and the X-Men's difficulty is that every grievance driving her is legitimate.

The invasion came through Limbo, which Illyana ruled, and ending it required her to close the gateway and unmake her own demonic self — returning her to the child she had been when Belasco took her. She lost the years she had spent becoming powerful in order to stop what that power had opened.

Scott spent the crossover trying to recover the son he had left behind from the woman he had left behind, with Jean Grey beside him. It is the story that forces the franchise to reckon with his behaviour in Alaska, and it does not go well for anyone involved.

Wanda remade the world into one where mutants ruled and everyone had what they most wanted, and when the heroes recovered their memories and came for her she ended it with three words. The Decimation that followed cut the global mutant population from millions to a few hundred.

It was Pietro who pushed his unravelling sister towards rewriting reality, terrified of what the assembled heroes had gathered to decide about her. His protectiveness is the proximate cause of the catastrophe that followed.

In the world Wanda built, Magneto ruled and his family were royalty — the life her father had wanted made real by a daughter trying to please him. Its collapse cost him both children's trust and left him living in the ruins of the only version of his politics that had ever worked.

The infant at the centre of the crossover was hunted by four separate factions before she could hold her head up, and the X-Men fractured over what to do with her. Cable took her into the future because leaving her in the present had already cost them Xavier.

Xavier was shot in the head by Bishop during the fight over the child, an injury that removed him from the books for a long stretch. The founder being taken out by one of his own students, over a baby, is the franchise's summary of what M-Day had done to it.

Hope's return to the present coincided with the first new mutant manifestations since M-Day, a wave of adolescents whose powers came online around her. Whether she caused it or merely accompanied it is left open, and either way she ended the extinction the X-Men had been living under.

After M-Day, Hank was given the task of finding out what had happened to the gene and whether it could be restored, and pursued it to the point of collaborating with people he should not have. The franchise's science of mutation is largely whatever Beast has most recently established about it.

Cerebro works by detecting the gene, which makes Xavier the person who decides who counts as a mutant and who gets found first. Every registration scheme in the books is a cruder version of a machine he built and keeps in his basement.

The Friends of Humanity campaigned for registration as a first step and made no secret that they wanted the list for their own purposes. Their support is the clearest illustration of why the X-Men treat a database as an existential threat rather than an inconvenience.

The Force is the story's engine and its unresolved question: an entity that is not evil and cannot be reasoned with, amplifying a woman's own appetites until they consume a star. Nothing in the X-Men's experience gave them a way to fight it, which is why the saga ends in a choice rather than a victory.

Lilandra was required by Shi'ar law to demand the execution of the being that had destroyed an inhabited system, and the being was her lover's student. She granted the X-Men a trial by combat on the Moon and prepared to have them all killed if they won, which is exactly the position her throne put her in.

The empire's case was straightforward: billions of its subjects were dead and the entity responsible was still walking around. Introducing an outside legal authority with a legitimate grievance is what elevates the story above a supervillain fight — the X-Men are not defending an innocent.

Gladiator led the Imperial Guard in the duel on the Blue Area of the Moon, and fought a team he had no personal quarrel with because the throne had ruled. The X-Men lost, which is the outcome that forces Jean's own decision.

The team fought the Hellfire Club, then the Phoenix, then an alien empire, and lost each time in a way that mattered. The saga's lasting effect on the franchise is that it established the X-Men as a book where the heroes can be comprehensively defeated and have to live in the aftermath.

The Inner Circle's plan to install Jean Grey as their Black Queen was a straightforward corporate acquisition of the X-Men's most valuable asset. It worked, and it removed the last restraint from a cosmic entity, which is more consequence than the Club had budgeted for.

Lilandra inherited the throne after the Crystal destroyed her brother's mind, and held it through repeated coups — a soldier ruling a military empire she kept trying to make less brutal. Her reign is the period in which the Shi'ar are the X-Men's allies as often as their prosecutors.

The throne came to D'Ken by default, his elder sister having forfeited it by murdering their mother, and he governed by terror once he had it. His pursuit of the M'Kraan Crystal threatened the structure of the universe itself and ended him: thrown into the Crystal by one of the Starjammers, he emerged permanently catatonic, which is how Lilandra came to inherit an empire rather than win one.

Exiled for the murder of her mother, Cal'syee has taken the throne twice, once as usurper and once as consort, and lost it both times. Her claim is the permanent instability in Shi'ar succession, and she has allied with the Empire's enemies whenever it advanced her.

Gabriel Summers took the imperial throne by killing his way through the succession — reviving D'Ken only to murder him at his own wedding — and marrying Deathbird — a mutant conceived in a Shi'ar slave pen ending as the emperor of the people who made him. It is the rare case of an X-Men antagonist achieving everything he set out to do.

As praetor of the Imperial Guard, Gladiator serves the throne rather than whoever occupies it, which has made him the instrument of tyrants and reformers alike. That obedience is his defining flaw and eventually his qualification: he ends up emperor largely because he is the one figure everyone trusts.

Lilandra led an open rebellion against her brother when it became clear his obsession with the M'Kraan Crystal would kill everyone, and reached across the galaxy for outside help to do it. It is the fracture that defines the imperial family for the whole run of Shi'ar stories.

Deathbird considers herself the rightful heir and Lilandra a usurper twice over, and has spent her life trying to take the throne back. Between the two of them and D'Ken, the imperial siblings have deposed each other more often than any external enemy has.

Two dispossessed claimants with grievances against the same empire married and ruled it together, each entirely aware of what the other was. It is a political alliance the books also treat as a genuine attachment, which makes it the strangest functional marriage in the franchise.

Corsair escaped Shi'ar slavery with three other prisoners and turned them into a crew, taking the ship and the name from the man who had held them. The Starjammers are a revenge operation that grew into a family, which is the only kind of family Christopher Summers has managed to keep.
Alex has served long stretches aboard the Starjammer, taking to his father's crew far more easily than his brother ever could. Space is the one place where he is not Cyclops's younger brother.

Rachel spent years in space with the Starjammers, serving alongside a grandfather from a family that is not quite hers. It is characteristic of her: the Summers relatives she can actually be close to are the ones with the loosest claim on her.

The crew were made by the empire — its slaves, its prisoners, its casualties — and have raided its shipping ever since. They have also repeatedly fought for Lilandra's claim, which makes them pirates whose politics depend entirely on who currently holds the throne.

It was D'Ken's ship that shot down the Summers family aircraft, and D'Ken who had Corsair's wife killed in front of him. Everything Christopher Summers became — pirate, exile, absent father — proceeds from one emperor's boredom.

Mojo holds power over a civilisation whose population is physically addicted to broadcast, which means his authority is measured in ratings and can be lost by being boring. It is the only tyranny in the franchise that can be overthrown by changing the channel.

Mojo had Betsy blinded and fitted with cybernetic eyes that transmitted everything she saw as programming, turning an X-Man into a camera without her consent. It is the single most invasive thing done to her, and it happened before any of the body-swapping that followed.

Mojo abducted Alison to star in his programming, correctly identifying a performer as the most useful kind of hostage. The pairing of a light-show mutant with a dimension made of television is one of the franchise's better jokes about itself.

Mojo has abducted the X-Men repeatedly for entertainment, at one point reducing them to children and at another televising their deaths for ratings. He is the only antagonist whose motive is that they make good viewing, which the books treat as a comment on the reader.

Betsy's route into the X-Men ran through the Mojoverse, where she was captured, mutilated and made into a broadcast unit. She arrived at the mansion already having been through the worst thing that happens to her, which is unusual in the books and shapes everything after.

With the X-Men believed dead, Kurt and Kitty founded a new team in Britain around Captain Britain, Meggan and Rachel Summers. It gave both of them several years of something like a functioning household, and gave the franchise its lightest and least self-serious book.

Kitty was still a teenager when she co-founded Excalibur while recovering from injuries sustained in the Mutant Massacre. The team is where she stopped being the X-Men's youngest member and started being someone who runs things.

Rachel joined Excalibur after the team that knew her history had gone, and it is the only place in the books where she was allowed a settled life. Her time there, and her long stretch afterwards in space, is the closest the character comes to peace.

Excalibur was founded from X-Men survivors and has always been the franchise's British annexe, sharing members and crises without taking orders. The two teams have folded into each other repeatedly, and the lighthouse has sheltered the mansion's refugees more than once.

Xavier established a sovereign mutant nation on the living island, abandoning the school, the dream of assimilation and, effectively, his own politics. It is the moment the franchise's founder concluded that sixty years of teaching coexistence had not worked.

Magneto stood beside Xavier as co-founder of a mutant state with its own laws, borders and diplomatic recognition — the thing he had demanded since 1963, granted at last by his oldest opponent. His line about humanity having new gods is the whole Krakoan era in one sentence.

The nation was built on Moira's knowledge: nine previous lifetimes of watching every other strategy fail, delivered to Xavier and Magneto as a set of instructions, down to the timing of the Nimrod problem. She was the third founder and the one almost nobody knew about, working from a hidden facility, which is precisely how she had planned it.

For several years the X-Men were citizens of a country rather than a team in a house, with gateways growing between continents, a resurrection protocol that undid death and a seat at international negotiations. The books used it to ask what mutants would do with everything they had ever asked for.

Two women who could see how it ends, working from opposite directions: Moira from lives already lived, Irene from futures not yet reached — and a precognitive is the one thing a woman resetting the timeline cannot allow, because a seer can see her. Destiny killed her in an earlier life for pursuing a cure for mutation, and Moira's price for building Krakoa was that Destiny must never be resurrected on it. When Mystique broke that condition, the two of them came for her together and took her power away.

Every X-Man's competence is built in the room, which simulates opponents at lethal settings and has killed people when it malfunctioned. It is where the books stage their training, their arguments and, once the room woke up, their guilt.

The chamber sits beneath the school alongside the hangar and Cerebro, which is the whole architecture of the place in one image: a boarding school on top of a war room. Students are taught mathematics upstairs and survival downstairs.

The Acolytes occupied the orbital station, renamed Avalon, and ran it as a sanctuary for mutants willing to accept Magneto as their prophet. It offered genuine refuge on terms that amounted to a conversion, and it came down like every other version of the asteroid.

Emma was on Genosha when the Sentinels came and survived by shifting into her diamond form, one of a handful left alive out of sixteen million. She emerged from the rubble and joined the X-Men, and the experience is the hinge between her two careers.

The Antarctic jungle is where the X-Men go to be unreachable: crashed, hiding, presumed dead or fighting Magneto's Mutates far from any satellite. It has served as refuge and battleground often enough to count as an outpost.

David was found catatonic and housed on Muir Island, where Moira treated him for years and where his personalities were first catalogued. One of the most dangerous mutants in the books spent his childhood as a patient in a Scottish research station.

Kevin was held in a specially built cell on the island, kept alive and kept contained by his own mother. His escape turned the facility from a hospital into the site of one of the franchise's ugliest family stories.

Sean and Moira were together for years, and Muir Island became his second home as his voice failed him. It is one of the few adult relationships in the books conducted without a love triangle, a resurrection or a possession, and it ended only with her apparent death.

Forge built the weapon that stripped Ororo of her powers, then found her, sheltered her and fell in love with her before she learned what he had made. Their relationship never recovered its footing after that, and their repeated near-marriages are the franchise's most sustained study of a couple who cannot get the timing right.

Rogue, who cannot touch anyone without harming them, and Gambit, who lies by reflex, have been the X-Men's central couple since the 1990s, their obstacles almost entirely internal. They eventually married — something the books treated as an achievement earned over thirty years rather than a plot resolution.

Piotr Rasputin and Kitty Pryde began their romance as teenagers newly arrived at the school. It was interrupted by Colossus's death, Kitty's own brush with death, his corruption in Limbo and an abandoned wedding, and never quite ended — one of the franchise's longest-running romances, and the one most defined by bad timing.

Alex and Lorna have been together, apart and together again across five decades, both of them repeatedly possessed, mind-controlled or presumed dead in the intervals. They are the franchise's most durable couple by sheer persistence rather than by anything either of them does well.

Logan's feelings for Jean were unreciprocated for most of their history and largely respected, which is unusual for him. The triangle with Cyclops shaped both men for decades, and the books use it to measure Wolverine's self-control rather than his appetite.

The team's most violent member and its most devout are the closest friends on the roster, and the friendship is written as genuinely uncomplicated. Kurt's steady refusal to think of Logan as an animal is one of the few things that has consistently kept him honest.

Emma taught Jubilee at Generation X after having previously tried to destroy the X-Men, a reversal none of the students were asked to be comfortable with. Her teaching style — cold, exacting, entirely without reassurance — produced better results than anyone expected.

The Facility, a successor to the original programme, used a damaged sample of Wolverine's genome to produce Laura, and raised her from birth as an assassin. She was conditioned with a trigger scent and sent on contracts as a child — the same institution's methods applied to someone with no life before it.

Cain has walked through the mansion's walls more times than any other opponent, and the team have never found a reliable way to stop him — only ways to make him fall over, get buried or be talked down. His fights are family arguments in which the X-Men are furniture.

Logan was among those who put Rossovich into suspended animation decades earlier, and Omega Red woke with that grudge and a need to drain life energy to survive. Their conflict is one of the few in the books where the villain has a legitimate complaint about being imprisoned without trial.

The Sentinels are the enemy the X-Men can never defeat, because destroying the machines does not touch the political will that funds them. Every generation of the team fights a new model, and every model is built by someone who has decided the last one was insufficiently thorough.

In that timeline the Sentinels were given the mutant problem and reasoned outward from it to the whole of human affairs, taking control of North America and interning the survivors. The story's warning is not that the robots rebel but that they do exactly what they were built to do.

The consciousness of the adult Kate Pryde was sent back into her thirteen-year-old body to stop the assassination that started it all, making the team's youngest member the one carrying the future. The mission succeeded and the future persisted anyway, as its own separate reality.

Rachel grew up in that timeline, interned and conditioned as a Hound to hunt her own kind, and escaped into the present carrying the marks. She is the story's living evidence: the future the X-Men averted still happened to somebody.

The Friends of Humanity cannot fight the X-Men and do not try; they attack the people the X-Men are supposed to be protecting, and then hold a press conference. They are the franchise's demonstration that the ordinary threat to mutants is a neighbour with a can of petrol.

Selene's schemes against the X-Men have ranged from possessing their students to raising an army out of the mutant dead of Genosha in an attempt at godhood. She is one of the few antagonists who treat the franchise's accumulated casualties as a resource.

Leland held the Sentinel down with his own power during the Hellfire Club's confrontation with it, increasing its mass past what it could move. The strain killed him — a corporate lawyer dying to stop a machine that had come back from a future where his side had lost.

Colleagues in the Inner Circle for years and then permanent antagonists, Shaw and Emma understand each other precisely because their methods are identical. Her departure from the Club and eventual alignment with the X-Men made her the one person who knows exactly how he operates.

Gabriel returned to a school that had erased him, a founder who had buried the evidence and brothers who had never been told he existed. His war on the X-Men is a grievance the books cannot argue him out of, because he is substantially right about what was done to him.

Shiro and Mariko are cousins within Clan Yashida, and his fierce, prickly nationalism is set directly against her attempt to steer the family towards legitimacy. The clan connection is also what repeatedly puts him in the same room as Wolverine, a man he has never liked and has fought beside anyway.

Logan has served under Ororo's command longer than under anyone else's and follows her orders when he follows nobody's, largely because she beat Cyclops for the job while powerless and he respects the arithmetic. Their partnership through the Australian and Morlock years is the roster's most reliable working relationship.

Hank co-founded X-Factor with the other four original X-Men after Jean's return, on the premise of posing as human mutant-hunters while secretly rescuing those they caught. It fed exactly the panic it was meant to defuse, and abandoning the deception took the team years.

Scott left Madelyne and their infant son in Alaska to rejoin the original five in X-Factor, a decision the books have never let him live down. The team was founded on Jean Grey's resurrection, and the wreckage of that choice produced Inferno.

Alex commanded the government-sponsored X-Factor under Valerie Cooper's oversight, running a mutant team that answered to Washington rather than to Xavier. It is the closest he came to a role that was his rather than his brother's.

Lorna served on the government team alongside Havok, in a period when both of them were more useful to the state as a demonstration than as soldiers. Her possession by the Marauders' Malice happened in the shadow of that work.

Rahne moved from the New Mutants to the government X-Factor and later to its incarnation as a detective agency, making her one of the few characters to serve in almost every version of the team. The wolf's periodic ascendancy is a running problem across all of them.

Warren's fortune funded X-Factor, and the team's public front was built on his money and his contacts. He lost his wings during its first year, which turned the founder into the casualty the book was then about.

X-Factor exists because Jean was found alive in a cocoon in Jamaica Bay, retroactively separating her from everything Dark Phoenix had done. Reuniting the original five around her return was the entire premise of the book.
Bobby joined the reunion of the original five and spent the run as the member least convinced by the mutant-hunter cover story. His objections were the book's own conscience about its premise.

Kitty was the one mutant the Krakoan gateways refused to let through, an exclusion nobody could explain and which she took as a verdict on her. She ran the nation's smuggling operation by sea instead, and eventually died and was resurrected into a place that had rejected her.

Irene's diaries were among the most sought-after objects on Krakoa, since they recorded futures the nation's founders were trying to avoid. Her resurrection was resisted by Xavier and Moira precisely because a precognitive could see what they had chosen not to disclose.

Storm led the X-Men team that first exposed Genosha's treatment of its mutate caste, and the encounter is one of the franchise's most direct confrontations with a state built on racial servitude. She returned to the island repeatedly, including after it became a graveyard.

Kurt's relationship with his mother alternates between attempted reconciliation and open opposition, since she keeps giving him reasons to fight her and he keeps declining to give up on her. He is the only person whose good opinion Mystique appears to want and cannot obtain.

Rogue's first appearance was as a Brotherhood member attacking the Avengers, and her permanent absorption of Carol Danvers happened in that service. She left because the powers she had taken were destroying her mind and the X-Men were the only people equipped to help.

Sinister cut away a portion of Remy's brain to bring a power that was consuming him back under control, and collected the debt by having him assemble the Marauders. Remy was carrying the excised tissue in a vial on the night the killing started. The relationship is the reason Gambit's past is a permanent liability rather than a colourful backstory.

Cable was raised in a future ruled by Apocalypse, told from childhood that he existed to end him, and came back to the past to make sure that future never arrived. It is the only mission he has, and it has outlasted several deaths on both sides.

Jubilee found Logan strung up by the Reavers and cut him down, then nursed him through the desert afterwards. Their partnership reversed the usual arrangement: the teenager was the one who saved the indestructible man, and both of them knew it.

Fighting Sentinels is the X-Men's most frequent activity and their least productive, since each victory removes the machines and leaves the appetite for them untouched. The books use these fights as a recurring measure of how bad the political weather has got.

Bishop's hunt for the infant Hope put him in direct opposition to Cable and the teams protecting her, and he pursued them across centuries with no willingness to be argued out of it. He was an X-Man fighting X-Men over an outcome none of them could verify.

Xavier designed and built Cerebro to extend his own telepathy to planetary range, and every recruitment drive in the franchise begins with him sitting in that chamber. It also makes him the sole holder of a complete register of mutant life on Earth, a fact the books return to whenever they want to make his benevolence uncomfortable.

The chamber sits in the sublevels alongside the Danger Room and the hangar, shielded so that its amplification does not spill into the minds upstairs. Its physical location beneath a boarding school is the school's whole double nature in one room.

Stryker's plan in God Loves, Man Kills turned Xavier's own amplifier against mutantkind, using a captive telepath and the machine's reach to attempt mass killing at a distance. It is the clearest demonstration of why a register of every mutant alive is dangerous regardless of who built it.

On Krakoa the technology was rebuilt to record copies of mutant minds at regular intervals. The bodies were grown by the Five — Hope Summers, Proteus, Elixir, Tempus and Egg, whose powers combined into a single circuit — from genetic material Mister Sinister kept on file, and Xavier then downloaded the stored mind into the new body. It made Cerebro the mechanism of mutant immortality and put the authority to restore or withhold a life in the hands of whoever operated it.

Xavier does most of his real fighting on the astral plane, where his power is at its greatest and his paralysis is irrelevant — he appears there as he imagines himself, walking. Nearly every duel he has had with the Shadow King has been fought and lost or won on that ground.

Killed in his physical body during his first encounter with Xavier, Farouk survived as pure psychic presence and has lived on the astral plane ever since, taking bodies as he needs them. He cannot be killed in the ordinary sense, only driven back into a realm he owns.

David's fractured personalities occupy a landscape inside his own mind that functions as a private region of the astral plane, complete with terrain and inhabitants. Treating him has repeatedly meant sending telepaths inside to walk through it, and several have not come out unchanged.

Betsy's psychic knife — the focused totality of her telepathic power — is an astral weapon that cuts a mind rather than a body, and her fights with the Shadow King were conducted there. It is the discipline that survived every change to her physical form.

The metal was bonded to Logan's skeleton and claws by Weapon X in a procedure that would have killed anyone without a healing factor, and that he has no reliable memory of consenting to. It made him unkillable and it made him a weapon, and the books have never entirely separated the two.

The Facility coated Laura's claws in adamantium while she was still a child, extracting them from her hands to do it. Where Wolverine's bonding was done to an adult soldier, hers was part of raising a person as equipment from birth.

Yuriko had her own skeleton laced with the alloy her father devised, choosing surgically what was inflicted on Wolverine involuntarily. The irony is deliberate: she gave up her body to punish a man for having been given the same thing without asking.

The programme's central achievement was working out how to bond the alloy to living bone before it cured, a procedure that requires a subject capable of surviving the process. Everything Weapon X is remembered for follows from having solved that engineering problem and then looking for someone to test it on.

En Sabah Nur found a buried Celestial ship and used its technology to make himself effectively immortal, and it is the same equipment he uses to remake his Horsemen. The franchise's oldest villain runs entirely on borrowed alien machinery he does not fully understand.

The wider Marvel universe attributes humanity's capacity for superhuman mutation to Celestial experiments on prehistoric populations, which places the X-gene at the end of a procedure nobody consented to and no one has ever explained. It also means the thing mutants are persecuted for was installed by outsiders.

Apocalypse recruits four servants each time he wakes and remakes them with Celestial technology, refilling the roles from whoever is available. He does not choose the strong: he chooses people whose lives have just collapsed, and offers them power on the only terms they will still accept.

Warren became Death with his wings replaced by metal ones that fired blades, taken up at the moment his own had been amputated and his life had ended in every way that mattered to him. He broke the conditioning and kept the body, which is why Archangel never entirely stopped being a Horseman.

Caliban accepted the offer wanting to be strong enough to protect the Morlocks he had failed, and was enlarged, hardened and turned into a hunter of his own people. It is the cruellest of the appointments because the wish behind it was entirely decent.

Maimed and unable to walk, Shiro took Apocalypse's offer and served as one of the four, a proud man accepting from an enemy what nobody else could give him. The recruitment followed the usual pattern precisely.

Logan was taken as Death during Apocalypse's campaign around the Twelve and had the adamantium restored to his skeleton as part of the conversion. He broke free, and the metal Apocalypse gave back is still in him, which is the one gift from an enemy he has never managed to return.

Jean-Paul joined the X-Men after years with Alpha Flight and taught at the school, bringing an abrasiveness that made him useful in a roster full of people trying to be liked. He has since been killed, resurrected, brainwashed by the Hand and returned to teaching, which is roughly standard service.

Two Canadians with a shared Alpha Flight history and no patience for each other's methods, they have worked together for decades on the understanding that neither is going to apologise. Northstar is one of the few people who will tell Logan directly that he is being stupid.

Northstar joined the mansion's teaching staff, taking students on the physical training that his own athletic career equipped him for. His presence on the faculty is one of the clearest signs of the school functioning as a school rather than a barracks.

In the Age of Apocalypse, that reality's Sinister engineered Nate from Scott Summers's and Jean Grey's genetic material as the weapon capable of killing Apocalypse — the same programme the main-timeline Sinister has pursued for a century, brought to completion in a world with fewer restraints. Nate escaped before he could be aimed.

Nate carries Scott's genetic material without ever having been his child, produced in a laboratory in a reality where the two never met. Scott's encounters with him are a version of the same problem Cable and Rachel present: a grown offspring from a life he did not live.

Nate was engineered from Jean's genome in a world where she had died young, and his telepathy is recognisably hers taken to an extreme no body can sustain. Their meetings are among the few in the franchise where a Summers-Grey descendant is treated with straightforward warmth.

Two versions of the same idea — the son of Scott and Jean built to be the most powerful mutant alive — one raised as a soldier in the far future, the other decanted from a tank in a collapsing timeline. Cable's power is spent holding a virus at bay; Nate's has no restraint on it at all, which is the whole comparison.

Nate was that reality's last weapon and its most powerful mutant, and his fight with Apocalypse is where the story ends. When the timeline collapsed he was thrown into the main universe, one of a handful of survivors carrying the memory of a world nobody else lived in.

Sean taught Paige at the Massachusetts Academy and spent much of that time trying to slow her down, since she trained harder than any student he had and enjoyed none of it. His steadiness was the counterweight to Emma's demands on the same class.

Emma pushed Paige exactly where she was already pushing herself, which produced results and very nearly produced a breakdown. The relationship is the clearest illustration of what Emma's teaching does to a student who cannot be told she has done enough.

Sam and Paige are the eldest two of the Guthrie children, and she spent her adolescence studying mutant powers in order to follow him. He has spent his career trying to keep her out of the field she insisted on entering, and losing that argument.

Paige graduated from Generation X onto the senior roster, one of the few students to make the transition the school is supposedly for. Her tenure has been marked by the physical toll of a power that requires her to destroy her own body to use it.

Sean took in a student who could not eat, speak aloud or be looked at without comment, and taught him without ever treating the injury as the interesting thing about him. It is one of the franchise's strongest arguments for the school's existence.

Emma taught Jonothon telepathic speech and, characteristically, refused him any sympathy about needing it. Her flat refusal to be gentle with him was more use to the character than kindness would have been, which the book knew perfectly well.

Jonothon served on the senior roster after Generation X, one of the few X-Men whose mutation is a permanent visible injury rather than an ability with a costume attached. He has spent most of his time since trying to be treated as a colleague rather than a case.

Everett was the most naturally capable of the Generation X students and the easiest to teach, since his power required him to pay close attention to everyone around him. Sean's death and his own both fell on that class harder than anything else it went through.

Emma taught a student whose ability was to borrow other people's, which meant training him in a dozen powers he would only hold for minutes at a time. He is the one member of the class she never had to force into working.

Everett was among the dead restored by Krakoa's resurrection protocols, decades after being killed as a student. He was then sealed in the Vault, a facility where time runs fast, and spent a subjective lifetime inside it with Laura Kinney and Darwin before getting out.

Tabitha arrived by way of the X-Terminators and never entirely stopped behaving like a runaway, which made her the least disciplined student on a roster of teenagers. Her plasma bombs are the most casually destructive power any of them had.

She followed the team into Cable's paramilitary version of it and spent the entire run objecting to the seriousness of everyone around her. She is the character the book used to keep reminding itself that these soldiers were nineteen.

Tabitha and Sam were together on and off through the whole X-Force period, an unstable pairing of the team's most responsible member and its least. Their arguments about the work were also arguments about growing up, which is what the run was mostly about.

Shatterstar joined the team out of an arena, understanding combat completely and everything else not at all, and was one of its most lethal members from the first day. Learning that Earth does not resolve disputes by duel took him considerably longer than learning to use its weapons.

Cable took command of a gladiator raised to kill on camera and had to teach him restraint before anything else, which is not a subject Cable is qualified in. Their relationship is the sharpest version of X-Force's central problem: a soldier training soldiers and calling it a school.

He was bred and trained in the Mojoverse for arena broadcast, and escaped into the rebellion against its regime before crossing to Earth. His origin has been rewritten more than once — construct, refugee, descendant of Longshot — and the books have never settled it.
Shatterstar was produced by the system Mojo runs, escaped it, and returned repeatedly with a rebellion at his back. He is the one former performer who came back to shut down the studio.

Xavier reached Kurt in the German village of Winzeldorf as a mob overwhelmed him, froze every one of them where they stood, offering a school to a young man who had been told his whole life that he was a demon. Of all the founder's students, Kurt is the one who accepted the teaching most completely and questioned the teacher least.

Xavier recruited Piotr from a Soviet collective farm hours after the boy had used his powers publicly for the first time, stopping a runaway tractor bearing down on his small sister Illyana. He gave a farm labourer a classroom, and then spent thirty years asking him to be the one who takes the hit.

Xavier recruited Kitty at thirteen, beating Emma Frost to her by a matter of days, and admitted a child young enough that the school had to be an actual school again. She is the student who most consistently held him to his own stated principles, including when he did not want to hear it.

Xavier took in a former Brotherhood member over the objections of a team she had recently tried to kill, on the grounds that she had asked for help and nobody else could give it. It is his clearest single demonstration that the school is a school rather than a recruitment pipeline.

Xavier sought Dani out at her grandfather's insistence, after her power to show people their own worst fear had frightened her own community. She became the New Mutants' field leader under his teaching and eventually returned to the school as staff.

Xavier found John on the Apache reservation at Camp Verde, running down a bison on foot, and recruited him by telling him he was needed — the only argument that worked on a man who thought the whole enterprise was a rich man's hobby. Three issues later John was dead, and Xavier's recruitment of him has been thrown back at him repeatedly since.

Xavier brought Shiro onto the all-new team despite a first encounter as enemies, and Shiro resigned almost at once. It is the shortest teaching relationship in the founder's career and the one that most directly rejects his premise.

Xavier debated Trask on live television, arguing that mutants were not a threat while the Sentinels the man had built stood behind him. He lost the argument in the room and won it a few hours later when the machines seized their creator, which is not the way he wanted to be proved right.

Xavier tried to recruit Fred Dukes out of a carnival, was refused, and attempted to wipe the encounter from his memory when he left — a failure that brought the entire sideshow down on the school. It is an early, unflattering demonstration of what the founder does when persuasion does not work.

Jubilee lived in the mansion's tunnels for weeks before anyone realised she was there, having followed the X-Men home from a Californian mall. The house has been her only fixed address since, through her time as a student, an X-Man and eventually a member of staff.

Emma moved into the school she had spent years competing with and became its headmistress, teaching in the building she had once tried to empty. Her presence in the staff room is one of the strangest continuities in the franchise.

Laura arrived at the school with no experience of living anywhere that was not a facility, and the mansion is where she was taught the ordinary parts of being a person. She has since taught there herself, which the books treat as the measure of how far she got.

Xi'an returned to the school as a teacher after her years of possession by the Shadow King, taking a faculty post rather than a field roster place. The New Mutants' first leader teaching a later generation is one of the school's quieter continuities.

Remy moved into the mansion in the early 1990s and spent his residence there being the member nobody could verify, with a past that surfaced in pieces. It is also where the trial over his role in the Mutant Massacre was held before the team left him in Antarctica.

Alison took a room at the school after her music career collapsed under the public knowledge that she was a mutant. Living in the house was, for her, the end of a civilian life rather than the beginning of a heroic one.

Sarah moved into the mansion as an X-Man having grown up in the tunnels beneath a city whose surface residents would not have her, and she was openly contemptuous of the comfort. Putting a Morlock in the guest wing is the closest the books came to answering for the Alley.

Bishop moved into a building he had only known as a preserved ruin in his own century, where his people's history was kept as relics. Living in the intact version of a museum he had grown up visiting shaped everything about how he behaved there.

Mortimer has worked at the school as caretaker for extended stretches, employed by the organisation he spent years attacking. The books use it as the least dignified and most honest ending available to a career spent being the least impressive mutant in every room.

The room began as mechanical traps, flamethrowers and presses; the holographic technology that turned it into a simulator able to generate any opponent came from the Shi'ar. The X-Men's training facility runs on imperial military hardware, which is also why its governing intelligence was sophisticated enough to wake up — and why nobody at the school understood what they had installed.

The friction began over Jean Grey and hardened into a genuine disagreement about how the X-Men should operate, with Logan calling Scott a bureaucrat and Scott calling Logan a liability. Decades later they had swapped positions entirely — the soldier running a militant state, the berserker running a school — without ever getting on.

Storm challenged Scott for command and beat him in the Danger Room while she had no powers at all, which he took worse than losing to anyone else would have been. Their disagreements about leadership have run for forty years and have never once been personal, which is what makes them serious.

During the conflict with the Avengers the Force arrived seeking a host and was split across five X-Men, Scott among them. He used the power to end drought and famine, and then to break anyone who questioned him, and finally took all of it into himself — the most complete demonstration the books have given of what the entity does to conviction.

Emma held a fifth of the Force and found it magnified exactly what she already was: certainty without hesitation. Her period as one of the Phoenix Five ended with the power stripped from her and her judgement permanently in question among people who had only just started trusting it.

Hope was the host the Force had been travelling towards, and she took it fully at the end of the conflict with the Avengers. She used it to restore the mutant gene across the world, undoing M-Day — the one occasion in the franchise where the Phoenix repaired something instead of burning it.

The grievance predates Jean by centuries: a Shi'ar host called Rook'shir carried the Force and devastated much of the galaxy before the Imperial Guard put him down, and his descendants were contained or killed. Dark Phoenix confirmed the doctrine, and the empire has hunted hosts and the Grey bloodline ever since. Their position is not paranoia: they are among the few powers in the setting to have actually counted the dead.

Madelyne is Jean's clone, grown from her genetic material and given a life while Jean was dead in a cocoon in Jamaica Bay. Neither woman chose the arrangement, and the books have generally sided with Jean while making it clear that Madelyne was the one who was wronged.

The rivalry began with Emma's psychic affair with Scott and became something more interesting after Jean's death, when Emma took her place at the school and beside him. Their few conversations as equals — including Jean's decision to train Emma rather than fight her — are among the better things either character has been given.

Storm recruited Alison to the X-Men when her career had collapsed and she had nowhere else to be, and has been the person on the roster who takes her seriously since. A weather goddess and a light-show performer turn out to have a good deal to say to each other about being looked at.

Irene raised Rogue alongside Mystique and, being precognitive, knew what the girl's power would do to her long before it manifested. Her care for Rogue is the one part of Destiny's life she never treated as a move in a longer game.

Kurt and Kitty co-founded Excalibur together and have been each other's closest friend since she arrived at the school as a thirteen-year-old frightened of the man with the tail. Their years at the lighthouse are the nearest thing either of them has had to an ordinary life.

Kitty and Doug were the school's two computer-literate teenagers and friends before either had a codename, which made his death one of the first she had to absorb. She has spoken for him repeatedly since to people who dismissed his power as useless.

Illyana and Kitty became inseparable when both were children at the school, and Kitty was the person who most refused to accept that Limbo had taken her friend. She was there when Illyana died as a seven-year-old, and the friendship has survived both of their subsequent resurrections.

Betsy fought the Shadow King on the astral plane during his takeover of Muir Island and was among the few who could meet him on his own ground. He has used her repeatedly as a route into the X-Men, and her psychic knife exists partly because of what he taught her about that kind of fight.

The empire took Christopher Summers's freedom, killed his wife and grew his third son in a laboratory, and he has raided its shipping ever since. His piracy is one long personal reprisal that happens to have become a political force.

The Majestrix and the pirate raiding her empire's convoys have repeatedly fought on the same side, since Corsair's quarrel is with the throne's occupants rather than the throne. Her willingness to use him, and his to be used, is the most functional relationship either has with Shi'ar politics.

Forge served on the government-sponsored team as its technical capability, building for a state agency the equipment he had previously built for a school. His presence made explicit what X-Factor was: mutants doing sanctioned work with public money.

Pietro served on the government X-Factor, a former Brotherhood member and former Avenger working for the American state and irritating everyone in the building. It is the most conventional employment of his career and he lasted about as long as could be expected.

Sam and Roberto met on their first day at the school and have been each other's closest friend across four decades, through the New Mutants, X-Force and Roberto's eventual purchase of a terrorist organisation. It is one of the longest uninterrupted friendships in the franchise.

Betsy took the mantle of Captain Britain and led a later incarnation of Excalibur, tying her back to her brother's legacy and to the magical Otherworld the team is bound up with. It is the point at which the character's British origins stopped being background detail.

Roberto followed the New Mutants into Cable's paramilitary version of the team, and his money kept it operational when it had no institution behind it. He is the member who understood earliest that the fight was as much about resources as about firepower.

Neena and Nathan have been together, apart and professionally entangled for most of their publication history, an attachment between two soldiers who never expected to survive long enough for it to matter. She is also the person most willing to tell him his plans are lunacy.

Cable was raised by the Askani, the order Rachel founded in the far future, which makes her something between his sister and the origin of his entire upbringing. The two of them are the franchise's clearest example of a family assembled out of timelines rather than households.

Bishop comes from his own Sentinel-ruled future — a separate timeline from the one Kate Pryde was sent back from, with mutants interned, branded and hunted much the same way. He reached the present chasing the killer Trevor Fitzroy, and stayed carrying his century's history as record rather than prophecy.

Their worst encounter came when Magneto tore the adamantium out of Logan's body through his pores, an act of deliberate cruelty that nearly killed him and left him with bone claws for years. It is the only time an enemy has taken the thing that made Wolverine what he is, and it is why he is the one X-Man who will never entertain Magneto's arguments.

Raven and Victor's relationship produced Graydon Creed, and neither of them took any further interest in the child. It is the least sentimental pairing in the books and its only lasting consequence is a human demagogue who built a movement out of what his parents were.

Wyngarde's illusions are the mechanism of the whole story: months of a fabricated past life, feeding Jean a version of herself in which cruelty was elegant. He wanted a seat in the Inner Circle, and the Force he loosened destroyed his mind when it turned on him.

Scott fought the duel on the Moon knowing he could not win it and stayed with Jean at the end, and the saga is the point at which the character's discipline stops looking like coldness. Everything he becomes over the following decades is written against that day.

Emma was White Queen when the Inner Circle captured the X-Men and put Jean in Hellfire costume, making her a direct participant in the manipulation that produced Dark Phoenix. That she later took Jean's place at Scott's side, in Jean's school, is the fact the books keep returning to.

Apocalypse found Bennet du Paris in the twelfth century, unlocked his latent power and then sealed him away when he refused to serve. Magneto woke him a thousand years later, which means the most devout Acolyte was made by the enemy his prophet spent a lifetime fighting.

Sinister took and kept Jean's genetic material, cloning it into Madelyne Pryor and using it in his long project to combine the Summers and Grey lines. She is a specimen in his files rather than an enemy, which is precisely what makes him harder for her to fight than anyone who hates her.

The Marauders were assembled for this one job and carried it out over several nights in the tunnels beneath Manhattan. Sinister's habit of cloning them meant the X-Men could kill members of the team and find the same faces waiting at the next confrontation.

Callisto survived the slaughter of the community she had led and spent the years afterwards protecting the handful left. Whatever the surface world thought of her methods, she was the only person who had ever taken responsibility for those people.

Sarah was a child in the Alley when the Marauders came through, and everything she became was formed in the days after it. Gene Nation's attacks on the surface were carried out by survivors who had waited a long time for the X-Men to do something about it.

Piotr was gravely injured in the tunnels, and the massacre is also where he killed one of the Marauders — a line he had not crossed before and has never been comfortable about since. The team that came out of that week was not the team that went in.

Kitty was struck by Harpoon's energy spear and left unable to hold solid form, phasing out of existence by degrees for months afterwards. Her recovery took her out of the X-Men and into Excalibur, and the injury is one of the reasons that team exists at all.

A cache of wild Sentinels, built outside any government programme, was turned on the island and killed its entire population in a single afternoon. It is the machines' largest recorded success and it required no new technology at all — only someone willing to give the order.

Lorna was on Genosha when the Sentinels came and survived the destruction of sixteen million people around her, an experience the books have treated as the source of her worst subsequent breakdowns. She is one of the very few characters written as carrying that day rather than referring to it.

Selene later raised the mutant dead of Genosha as an army in her attempt at godhood, turning the island's mass grave into a resource. It is the most grotesque use anyone in the franchise has made of the atrocity, which is presumably why it was given to her.

Nimrod is what the Sentinel programme eventually produces if nobody stops it: self-repairing, adaptive, human-sized and able to pass as a person. It arrived in the present from the future that the machines won, which makes it the programme's own finished product rather than anyone's invention.

Bastion commands Sentinel forces rather than merely being one, having been built from the fusion of a factory and a future model. Under him the machines stopped needing a government sponsor, which is the point at which the anti-mutant threat became self-directing.

Rachel came from the timeline Nimrod was built in and had been hunted by it before she reached the present, which is why she recognised what had arrived when nobody else did. Fighting a machine from her own childhood in a decade that had not produced it yet is the exact shape of her whole existence.

Alison was outed as a mutant at the height of her music career, and the registration debate reached her as a matter of contracts, venues and audiences rather than raids. Her book is the franchise's most sustained look at what the politics does to a public life.

Kelly spent years as the political enemy of every mutant terrorist including Pyro, and was saved from an assassination attempt by him — a dying man using what he had left on a politician who had campaigned against his existence. The act changed Kelly's position, and he was killed by an anti-mutant extremist not long afterwards.

Kelly's legislative campaign and Trask's engineering were two halves of the same programme: the political will to treat mutants as a threat and the machinery to act on it. Kelly's continued sponsorship of Sentinel funding after Trask's death is what turned one man's project into permanent state capability.

Both men built careers on the mutant question and had nothing else in common: Kelly was a legislator who believed he was managing a risk, Creed a demagogue running a movement. Creed's presidential campaign was an attempt to take the ground Kelly had made respectable and use it for something far worse.

Stryker had Xavier abducted and used him as an amplifier for mass murder, and then debated him on television — a preacher and a professor arguing about whether mutants are people, in front of an audience. Xavier's inability to simply win that argument is the whole point of God Loves, Man Kills.

Kitty's confrontation with Stryker's movement, and her refusal to let a slur pass unchallenged in front of a crowd, is one of the most quoted moments in X-Men publishing. The franchise's youngest member making the case that the adults could not is a deliberate piece of construction.

Rahne was raised on Muir Island by Moira after being rescued from the congregation hunting her, and returned there whenever her life elsewhere collapsed. It is the only place she has consistently treated as home.

In the reality created by Xavier's death, Magneto founded and led the X-Men in his friend's memory, married Rogue and fought Apocalypse for a decade. It is the franchise's most direct answer to the question of what he would be if he had lost the argument with Xavier by having Xavier die for him.

The infant at the centre of the Goblin Queen's sacrifice was Nathan Summers, and the crossover ends with the baby saved and his mother dead. Everything Cable becomes proceeds from a night in which both his parents' families tried to decide what he was for.

Emma sat on the Quiet Council, negotiated Krakoa's pharmaceutical trade with the human nations and ran the Hellfire Trading Company that carried it. The state's economy was built by its most practised manipulator, and it worked.

Doug is the mutant who learned to speak with the island itself, which made the least regarded power in the franchise the foundation of an entire nation's language, laws and architecture. Krakoa's founding documents exist because he could translate them.

After his sister's death from the Legacy Virus, Piotr left the X-Men and joined Magneto's followers, having concluded that Xavier's approach had failed the people he loved. It is the one period in which the team's most reliable member walked out, and he did it quietly.

The invasion came out of Limbo, animating New York's own objects against its residents and turning the city into a landscape of the dimension's making. Ending it required Illyana to close the gateway permanently at the cost of everything she had become there.

The unstoppable man and the strongest X-Man have fought repeatedly, and Colossus has never once stopped him — only slowed him, redirected him or gone through a wall with him. The relationship inverted when Piotr took the power of Cyttorak himself to protect Kitty and his sister, becoming the Juggernaut for a long stretch and losing his judgement to it before the war with the Avengers stripped it away.

Creed was among the operatives involved in Rossovich's original containment and betrayed him in the process, which put Omega Red on his trail as soon as he woke. Their conflict is one of the few in which Sabretooth is the one being hunted.

Two mercenaries who have worked the same contracts and the same teams for decades, with Neena treating Wade's behaviour as an occupational hazard rather than a personality. She is one of the very few people who neither indulges him nor writes him off.

Hank and Bobby were the two youngest of the original five and have been friends since before either had a codename, a friendship conducted mostly in mockery. It is one of the few relationships that survived every schism the team has had.

Jubilee was among the mutants stripped of their powers on M-Day and kept working without them, which is not the choice most depowered characters were given room to make. Her later transformation into a vampire happened while she was still living as a former mutant.

Dani lost her powers on M-Day and stayed at the school as staff, teaching students who had abilities she no longer possessed. The New Mutants' field leader carrying on without a mutation is one of the more dignified things the Decimation was used for.

Lorna was depowered on M-Day, losing the magnetism that had defined and troubled her whole life, and later had it restored. The stripping of a power that had been used to tell her who her father was is one of the crueller applications of the event.

Magneto returned from presumed death offering mutants sanctuary aboard Avalon, answered the UN's Magneto Protocols with a global electromagnetic pulse, and tore the adamantium out of Wolverine when Wolverine came close to gutting him. It is the storyline that ended his long ambiguity and put him back where he started.

Xavier led the strike team to Avalon in a Shi'ar exoskeleton, and after watching Magneto strip his friend's skeleton he reached into his oldest opponent's mind and shut it down completely. The founder crossing that line is the point of the story, and the piece of Magneto left behind in his head became Onslaught.

Logan lost the adamantium that had defined him, extracted through his own pores, and left the X-Men afterwards with bone claws and a healing factor wrecked by the trauma. He spent years in that state, which is the longest the books have ever gone without their most reliable weapon.

Grieving his sister's death from the Legacy Virus and no longer able to believe in Xavier's approach, Piotr walked out of Illyana's funeral and joined Magneto's Acolytes on the spot. He stayed with them afterwards, telling himself it was to keep them in check.

Avalon was the Acolytes' sanctuary and the platform from which Magneto proposed to finish humanity, and their recruitment of Colossus at a funeral is the crossover's opening move. Xavier's strike team began by jettisoning them into escape pods, which is roughly the regard the story has for their theology.

Onslaught was conceived in the moment Xavier shut Magneto's mind down on Avalon: a fragment of the man he had just erased lodged in the mind of the man who erased him. Everything the entity later did was seeded by a single act at the end of this storyline.

Bastion ran the operation as a federal director with a budget and a mandate, detaining and mutilating mutants under legal authority. It is the closest the books have come to showing extermination arriving as policy rather than as an attack.

The operation's Prime Sentinels were ordinary people converted by nanotechnology without their knowledge, who lived normal lives until the moment they activated. It made the Sentinel programme untraceable: anybody in the room might already be one.

Several X-Men were captured and interrogated, the mansion's defences were stripped and the team spent the storyline scattered and hunted by their own government. The operation was eventually shut down politically rather than defeated in a fight, which is the point.

Bastion sealed Utopia and the Bay Area inside a dome nothing could breach, ordered every teleporter the X-Men had killed first, and opened a portal to his own home timeline to bring Nimrod-series Sentinels through. Stryker's Purifiers, the Sapien League and Cameron Hodge's forces were all working to his order. It is his most complete operation and the closest the anti-mutant side came to finishing the job.

Kurt teleported Hope across the country in a series of jumps that drained him past his limits, and when Bastion cut them off he put himself in the way of the killing blow. He died on Utopia having got her home, and the X-Men lost the member who had held them to being heroes.

Cable brought Hope home and died holding a portal open so that X-Force could return from the Sentinel future on the other side of it. Having spent his life as a soldier arguing that someone has to pay for the future, he paid.

Hope came into her powers during the siege and ended Bastion herself, in front of an audience of mutants who had spent two years arguing about whether she was worth the losses. Both her foster father and the man who carried her across the country died getting her there.

Stryker's Purifiers were among the forces Bastion assembled, and they hit Cable and Hope within hours of their arrival in the present. Their function in the campaign was to make the country impassable while the machines closed the net.

Scott ordered a teenage student to use lethal force in the middle of a battle, on the reasoning that mutants were nearly extinct and could not afford scruples. It was the end point of a decade of hardening, and it cost him the half of the team that still thought of the X-Men as a school.

Logan — the killer, the one the school had spent thirty years managing — was the one who refused to let children fight, and walked out to reopen the mansion as a school. The two men had swapped positions completely since 1975, and the story knows exactly how strange that is.

Quire's stunt at the arms conference, forcing world leaders to confess their worst acts on camera, destroyed any chance of the world's Sentinel stockpiles being dismantled and triggered the attack that split the X-Men. He was fifteen and entirely pleased with himself.

Scott raised the island rather than submit to Osborn's occupation of San Francisco, declared it sovereign and governed it as a head of state with an army — which is what the X-Men had become by then. Nearly every mutant left alive after M-Day lived there under his protection and, increasingly, his command, and the fact that he had built his nation on Magneto's foundations was not lost on either of them.

For several years the team operated from a rock in San Francisco Bay rather than a house in Westchester, with no cover story, no school and no pretence of being anything other than the armed force of a besieged people. Magneto himself came to live there, which tells you how far the X-Men had moved. Bastion sealed it under a dome, the Schism split it, and the war with the Avengers sank it.

After the Schism Logan took half the roster back to Westchester and reopened the mansion as the Jean Grey School for Higher Learning, with himself as headmaster. The franchise's least academic character running its school is the joke and the point at once.

The Force returned to Earth destroying worlds on its way, and the entire war turned on a disagreement about what it was coming for: restoration, in Cyclops's reading, or extinction in the Avengers'. It arrived and split five ways rather than settling the argument.

Scott held a fifth of the Phoenix, then took all of it, and used it to end hunger and drought before turning on anyone who questioned him. He killed Charles Xavier when Xavier tried to shut him down, and was arrested as the most dangerous mutant alive — having been, on the central question, right.

Emma held a share of the Phoenix and found it amplified her certainty into something without brakes, and Scott took her portion from her by force at the end. The experience left her power diminished and her judgement in question among people who had only just started to trust it.

Piotr took a fifth of the Force alongside his sister, a man who had already accepted a demon's bargain once to protect other people. It is the second time he has been handed enormous power at a cost he did not fully understand.

Illyana held a share of the Phoenix and used it with rather more relish than the others, which is entirely in character for someone who already ruled a demonic dimension. The Five's decline into tyranny was quickest to arrive in the two Rasputins.

One fifth of the Force bonded to Colossus during its arrival on the Moon, giving the team's gentlest member the power to level cities. What it amplified in him was not cruelty but conviction, which turned out to be almost as dangerous.

Illyana's portion of the Phoenix sat comfortably alongside the Limbo sorcery she already carried, and she was among the last of the Five to be talked down. The entity has always found the least reluctant hosts the easiest to work with.

Wanda spent the war being blamed by every mutant alive for M-Day, and ended it working alongside Hope to expel the Phoenix from Cyclops. Their combined act broke her own spell, restoring the mutant gene she had switched off seven years earlier.

Hope was the host the Phoenix had been travelling towards, and the reason both sides went to war over her. She took the whole of the Force at the end, used it to repair the damage Cyclops had done, and then let it go — spending the power on restarting her species rather than keeping it.

Xavier sided with the Avengers against his own students and died trying to shut down the one he had recruited first. For a character defined by intervening in other people's minds, being killed mid-intervention is as pointed an ending as the books could give him.

Orchis spent years preparing: subverting Krakoan medicines, taking control of the gateways, and manufacturing a Nimrod. The strike at the third Hellfire Gala was staged so that the world would see a mutant atrocity against human guests, and it worked.

Nimrod dropped into the Gala the moment a new X-Men team had been announced and killed most of it within seconds, then melted Iceman and fought the Juggernaut through the building. It is among the most effective things any Sentinel has done in the franchise's history.

The team lost its nation, its resurrection protocols and the public standing it had spent a decade building, in one evening. What followed was imprisonment, hiding and scattered resistance — the X-Men returned to being fugitives after the only period in which they had won.

The Krakoan age ended at the Gala. The gateways that had made the island a country became the route by which Orchis's forces arrived, and the medicine that had bought mutants diplomatic recognition was turned into the evidence against them.

Everett had just been elected to lead the X-Men alongside Talon when Nimrod attacked, and watched most of the team die in front of him within moments of the announcement. Having already lost several lifetimes inside the Vault, he came out of the Gala as one of the era's most damaged survivors.

Stripped of the reincarnation that had let her keep trying, and having already decided the answer was to depower mutantkind rather than save it, Moira joined the organisation dedicated to ending it and rebuilt herself as a machine for the work. The third founder of Krakoa became one of the architects of its destruction — and the trade was mutual: Orchis acquired ten lifetimes of intelligence on how mutants win.

Karima Shapandar founded Orchis carrying the memories of a future in which the machines had already won, and built an organisation designed to make that future arrive on schedule. A woman turned into a Sentinel against her will became one of the most effective planners the programme ever had.

Doctor Alia Gregor built the Nimrod for Orchis in the present day, using the mind of her dead husband as its seed — the one thing Moira's lifetimes of foresight had identified as the point of no return for mutantkind. The X-Men's raid on the Mother Mold delayed it by a matter of months.

Orchis beat the X-Men on preparation rather than power: no manifesto, no costumes, a public relations strategy and a decade of patience. It won, and the franchise spent years afterwards on what losing looks like.

Mystique ran repeated operations against the Orchis Forge, including the bombing that destroyed the first Nimrod before it could stabilise. Her war with them is personal in the way most of her wars are: she was doing it for Destiny, on the promise of getting her back.

Sean took the headmaster's post at the Massachusetts Academy and spent the run doing what Xavier had stopped doing: teaching frightened teenagers, in a building he did not trust, alongside a colleague he trusted less. It is among the strongest work the character was ever given.

Emma reopened her school for a second class after Fitzroy's Sentinels killed the first, this time with an X-Man watching her every move. Teaching students she had not recruited as weapons is the whole of her turn, conducted without a single apology.

The class lived and trained at Emma's school in western Massachusetts rather than at Xavier's mansion, which kept them at a deliberate distance from the X-Men. The Academy closed permanently when the book ended, and the students who survived moved on to the senior teams.

The Academy was Emma's own institution long before it was a school for heroes — a genuine elite boarding school used as a screen for locating mutant children before Xavier reached them. She ran it through both of its incarnations.

Emma's first class trained at the Academy as the Hellfire Club's junior team, drilled specifically against the New Mutants. The building's second class inherited the same corridors and a headmistress who had already buried one set of students in them.

Emma trained the Hellions as the Club's next generation and as the answer to Xavier's students, and grew genuinely attached to them in the process. Their deaths broke both her allegiance to the Hellfire Club and, for a while, her.

James joined Emma's Hellions as a teenager, recruited on the strength of his rage over his brother's death and pointed at Xavier. Leaving them for the New Mutants was the first decision he made about his brother rather than because of him.

Fitzroy's Sentinels came through the Hellfire Club's doors and killed almost the entire class in minutes, to score points in the Upstarts' competition. It is one of the coldest massacres in the books: children killed as a scoring move in a rich man's game.

Jubilee arrived as the only student who had already been an X-Man, which made her the class's veteran at sixteen and its most sceptical member. Being sent from Wolverine's side to a school run by Emma Frost was not something she forgave quickly.

Paige had spent years studying mutant abilities in preparation for a place at a school like this one, and arrived as the hardest-working and least relaxed student in the building. Her brother's example is what she measured herself against, unfavourably and constantly.

Jonothon came to the Academy with half his body destroyed by his own power and no way to speak except telepathically, which made him the class's outsider by physical fact rather than temperament. His refusal of pity carried the book's best material.

Everett was the most naturally gifted student in the class and the one who held it together socially, since his power required him to pay attention to everyone in the room. He was killed at the Academy by a bomb planted by the headmistress's own sister, and it is the class's defining loss.

Monet arrived apparently perfect — strong, fast, telepathic and entirely certain of it — which made her insufferable and, as the book eventually revealed, not always actually present. Her family's interference in her life is the longest-running mystery of the run.

Clarice was among the young mutants the Phalanx captured in the crossover that formed the team, and she died turning her teleportation on her captors so the others could get out. The class existed because of her; she never got to join it.

Mystique negotiated the arrangement herself and ran the team through its entire existence, which made her the rare X-Men villain to talk her way onto a federal payroll. She held it together by being the one person who understood exactly how expendable they all were.

Cooper took Mystique's offer of service in exchange for pardons, and set the price of the deal as a demonstration: bring in Magneto. It gave the government mutant capability it could direct, staffed entirely by people whose freedom depended on results.

Irene followed Mystique into federal service as she had into everything else, and her precognition made the unit far more effective than its roster suggested. She was killed on a Freedom Force mission to Muir Island by Legion, who was under the Shadow King's influence at the time — a death she foresaw precisely and allowed, to keep Mystique out of the way of it.
